items.name: staccato-fragment-triplet
items.description: A burst of ultra-short sentence fragments in sequence, usually three, used for false emphasis. Each is one to three words and ends in a period ('Tight. Controlled. Deliberate.'). Common in both prose gravitas and marketing copy ('Powerful. Intuitive. Built for scale.').
items.detection: structural: flag any run of 3+ consecutive period-terminated sentences each under 5 words; also flag when the ratio of sub-5-word sentences to total exceeds 0.15 in non-dialogue prose, or a paragraph's sentence-length variance spikes from adjacent fragments.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Humans use the occasional fragment for rhythm, but models deploy them in mechanical triplet bursts at a paragraph's emotional peak to simulate gravitas. The regularity is the tell, not the fragment itself.
items.fix: Keep at most one fragment per passage and earn it. Fold the rest into a full sentence with real content; add a concrete detail instead of chopping.
items.before: The migration worked. Tight. Controlled. Deliberate. Nothing left to chance.
items.after: The migration worked on the first try, which surprised everyone given how little we'd tested it.
items.false_positive_when: Fragments are a legitimate rhetorical device and some of the best copywriters live on them. The tell is the triplet shape repeating across a document, not any single fragment.

items.name: negation-contrast-frame
items.description: The negation-contrast family: 'It's not X, it's Y' / 'This isn't about X, it's about Y' and the parallel 'not only X but also Y' / 'not a mirror but a portal.' Mimics the shape of insight while usually setting up a strawman X just to knock it down.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does this passage use a not-X-but-Y or not-only-but-also frame to inflate significance, where X is a position nobody actually held or merely a synonym of Y?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: It manufactures a reframe-reveal cadence that feels profound but frequently promises a revelation and delivers a synonym. Readers clock the formula because the X is rarely real.
items.fix: State Y directly. Only keep the negation if X is a genuinely held belief you're correcting; then name who holds it and why they're wrong.
items.before: It's not just a database — it's a paradigm shift. This isn't only about speed, but also about reimagining how teams collaborate.
items.after: It's a fast database that changes how teams collaborate.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: em-dash-density
items.description: Em dashes used at a rate well above the author's own habit — typically as a substitute for commas, colons, parentheses and full stops all at once.
items.detection: Em dashes per 100 prose words, code fences and blockquotes excluded. Reported LOW on its own and escalated to high only when it is a multiple of the same author's own baseline. Absolute thresholds do not work here.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The rate, never the glyph. Human writing averages roughly 0.32 em dashes per 100 words and GPT-4-class output roughly 1.06 — but the distributions overlap so badly that the absolute number is nearly useless on its own.
items.fix: Replace most with periods, commas, or parentheses. Keep the ones doing work no other mark can do.
items.before: We shipped it Friday — and everything broke. The fix was simple — once we found it — but finding it took the whole weekend — every hour of it.
items.after: We shipped it Friday and everything broke. The fix was simple once we found it, but finding it took the whole weekend.
items.false_positive_when: This is the single most over-applied tell in circulation, and the reason people get falsely accused. Melville runs 0.81 per 100 words in Moby-Dick and Twain runs 1.01 in Huckleberry Finn — both above GPT-4-class means. Llama emits zero. One anti-slop detector measured its em-dash rule warning on roughly 64% of legitimate technical blog posts. Never treat this as evidence; treat it as a prompt to look.
items.evidence: Freeburg, arXiv:2603.27006 (12 models, 5 providers, ~240k words; human control mean 3.23/1000w); van Nuenen, arXiv:2604.22142 (+325.7% under LLM rewriting, d=1.12); gptme anti-slop calibration notes. Note it is a DIALECT signal, not a generic one: GPT-4.1 10.62/1000w and Claude Opus 4.6 9.09, but Gemini 2.5 Pro 3.53 (indistinguishable from human) and Llama 3.1 0.00. Vendors suppress it on request, and later models suppress it by default. A signal that one sentence of instruction can remove is not a signal to build a case on.

items.name: rule-of-three-tricolon
items.description: Compulsive triplets: three adjectives, three nouns, three parallel clauses or list items, used far beyond what the content warrants ('fast, reliable, and scalable'; 'plan, build, ship').
items.detection: structural: count comma-separated parallel triples ('X, Y, and Z' adjective/noun runs joined by and/or) per 200 words and measure list-length variance. More than ~1 per 120 words, 3+ in a paragraph, or near-constant landing on three regardless of topic, flags.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The tricolon is a real device, but models default to three for everything, including cases where the true count is two or five. The uniform landing on three signals a template, not a thought.
items.fix: Let the real number of items dictate the count. Use two when there are two, four when there are four. Reserve the deliberate tricolon for one genuine rhetorical peak.
items.before: Our platform is fast, flexible, and powerful, helping teams plan, execute, and deliver with clarity, confidence, and speed.
items.after: The platform is fast, and flexible enough that teams stop fighting it. Mostly they just ship sooner.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: escalating-compliment-sycophancy
items.description: The escalating-specificity compliment chain: 'you're the only PM who gets this, who actually reads the data, who pushes back, and who would fly to the warehouse at 2am to see it himself.' Each clause more hyper-specific than the last, ending on an unverifiable hyperbolic claim.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the praise escalate in artificial specificity across stacked clauses, ending on an unverifiable biographical claim about the person?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Humans rarely stack praise in this geometric, accelerating way; it reads as a model trying to please, often inventing biographical specifics for flattery.
items.fix: Cut the validation entirely; go straight to substance. If praise is warranted, give one specific true observation and stop. Never invent details for flattery.
items.before: You're absolutely right. Honestly, you're the only founder I've talked to who understands distribution, who reads their own churn cohorts, who answers support tickets personally, and who would rebuild onboarding overnight to fix it.
items.after: Agreed. Your point about distribution is the part most founders skip, and your churn data backs it up.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: unattributed-floating-quote
items.description: An italicized or block-quoted line dropped in as if it were a quotation or someone's words, but no one said it and it isn't a pull quote from the piece. Aphoristic filler standing alone on its own line.
items.detection: structural: flag italic/blockquote lines that have no attribution, do not appear verbatim elsewhere as a cited source, and sit isolated as a standalone paragraph.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It borrows the visual authority of a quotation without any source, creating fake profundity. Human editors attribute quotes or write the line as plain prose.
items.fix: Attribute it to a real source, cut it, or rewrite it as a normal sentence in your own voice. Don't dress your own assertion as an anonymous epigraph.
items.before:
The team shipped the feature.

*Sometimes the bravest thing you can build is the thing you can't yet see.*

And that changed everything.
items.after: The team shipped the feature even though no one could prove it would matter, which was the bravest call of the quarter.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: delve-excess-vocabulary
items.description: Marker vocabulary whose frequency spiked after 2022. The list is ERA-VERSIONED and decays: 2023-mid-2024 (delve, tapestry, testament, intricate, meticulous, pivotal, underscore, garner, interplay, vibrant); mid-2024-mid-2025 (align with, bolstered, emphasizing, enhance, fostering, highlighting, showcasing); mid-2025 onward (emphasizing, enhance, highlighting, showcasing). Checking only for 'delve' is checking for 2023.
items.detection: Excess frequency against the genre's own pre-2022 baseline, as a density, never as presence of any single word. The methodological finding matters more than the list: pre-2024 excess words were 79% nouns (content), 2024 excess words were 66% verbs and 14% adjectives (style). The shift from content words to style words is the fingerprint, not any individual word.
items.why_it_reads_ai: At least 13.5% of 2024 biomedical abstracts show LLM processing by this measure, with 'delves' at an excess ratio of 28.
items.fix: Replace with plain equivalents: 'delve into' to 'look at' or cut; 'intricate' to 'detailed' or delete; 'underscores' to 'shows'; 'leverage/utilize' to 'use'. Delete frozen phrase scaffolding outright.
items.before: This report delves into the intricate dynamics of the market, underscoring the pivotal role supply chains play in this rich tapestry of global trade.
items.after: This report looks at how supply chains shape global trade.
items.false_positive_when: This is the entry most likely to hurt someone. 'Delve' is substantially more common in Nigerian formal and business English than in UK or US English, and the RLHF annotation workforce that rewarded it was substantially Nigerian and Kenyan — so a list that flags 'delve' is, mechanically, a list that flags a dialect. 'Pivotal', 'robust' and 'underscore' also have legitimate disciplinary homes. Compare a writer against their own field and their own earlier work, never against a universal list.
items.evidence: Kobak, González-Márquez, Horvát & Lause, Science Advances (2025), 15M+ PubMed abstracts; Wikipedia:WikiProject AI Cleanup/AI catchphrases (era-versioned); Alex Hern, Guardian TechScape, April 2024, on the Nigerian-English connection.

items.name: hedging-stack
items.description: Layered qualifiers that cancel each other so the sentence asserts nothing: 'While X, it's worth noting Y, though of course Z,' with ritual concessions ('that said,' 'no solution is perfect') stacked around every claim.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the passage balance every assertion with a counter-assertion or stack multiple hedges that cancel out, so it conveys no committed claim?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model hedges to avoid committing, producing fluent text that says nothing. The repeated cautious scaffolding is distinctly machine-cautious.
items.fix: Pick the claim you believe and state it. Keep at most one genuine caveat, made specific ('this breaks above 10k rows') rather than ritual.
items.before: While the approach is promising, it's worth noting that results may vary, though of course context matters, and no solution is perfect.
items.after: This approach works well under about 10,000 rows. Past that the join gets slow and you'll want to paginate.
items.false_positive_when: Direction is register-dependent, and may be inverted in academic writing: ChatGPT has been measured OVERusing attitude markers while significantly UNDERusing hedges and self-mention in academic book reviews. Treat 'too many hedges' as a chat-assistant-register tell and not a universal one.
items.evidence: Yao & Liu, Journal of Pragmatics 247:103-115 (2025).

items.name: heres-the-thing-pivot
items.description: The faux-conversational pivot that signals a reveal: 'Here's the thing.' 'Here's the kicker.' 'But here's what's interesting.' Used to manufacture a turn even when no real twist follows.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the text use a podcaster-style here's-the-thing/kicker/catch pivot to promise a reveal whose payoff is mundane, with a setup-to-payoff ratio that reads as performance?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: It imitates a podcaster's beat-drop to fake intimacy and tension. The promised payoff is usually ordinary, so the announced turn reads as a tic.
items.fix: Delete the pivot phrase and just say the thing. A genuine surprise carries the turn without announcing it.
items.before: We optimized the query. Here's the kicker: it was the index all along.
items.after: We optimized the query for a week before realizing the index was missing.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: conclusion-recap-tag
items.description: A closing paragraph flagged with 'In conclusion,' 'In short,' 'Ultimately,' 'Overall,' or 'At the end of the day' that re-states the body without adding anything.
items.detection: structural: flag a final/penultimate paragraph whose n-gram overlap with the preceding body exceeds ~50% (high lexical recall of earlier topic sentences = pure recap), independent of the opener word.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Five-paragraph-essay scaffolding makes the model ring a bell to announce the wrap-up and repeat itself, even in short pieces. Real writing ends when the argument is done.
items.fix: End on the strongest concrete point or a forward-looking specific. If a reader could skip the last paragraph and lose nothing, cut it.
items.before: In conclusion, caching is a powerful tool that, when used correctly, can significantly improve performance and enhance user experience.
items.after: The trap is stale reads after a write; if you can't tolerate them, skip the cache on that path rather than tuning a TTL you'll forget.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: bullet-colonization-of-prose
items.description: Breaking flowing argument or narrative into headline-plus-bullet lists, including forcing a simple connected answer into a numbered listicle. Causal and temporal relationships get flattened into co-equal bullets.
items.detection: Bullet lines as a share of content lines, which is what the catalog always said; the earlier implementation used a bullets-to-paragraphs ratio instead and disagreed with its own rubric.
items.why_it_reads_ai: RLHF rewarded scannable structure, so the model enumerates everything because lists are easy to generate and look organized, even when ideas are connected and need prose.
items.fix: Reserve bullets for genuinely parallel, order-independent items (steps, options, specs). Write reasoning, cause-and-effect, and narrative as paragraphs.
items.before:
Why the launch failed:
- The timing was bad
- This caused low signups
- Which meant we cut the budget
- So marketing stopped
items.after: The launch failed mostly on timing: we shipped the week of a competitor's conference, signups came in low, and once the numbers looked bad leadership cut the budget, which ended marketing entirely.
items.false_positive_when: Reference docs, changelogs, release notes and checklists are legitimately mostly bullets. Scope this to documents that are supposed to argue something.

items.name: bold-label-colon-bullet
items.description: The most recognizable AI list shape: every bullet is '**Bold Label:** explanation sentence,' uniform across the whole list. On some models (Gemini) each bullet is also separated by a blank line, producing a tall double-spaced wall.
items.detection: structural: flag any list where >=60% of items match `^\s*[-*]\s*(\*\*|__).+?(\*\*|__):\s`; 3+ consecutive items in this exact shape is a strong signal. Additional signal: blank line between every bullet combined with the bold-colon template.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Real human lists vary item structure; the rigidly uniform 'bold term: gloss' across every bullet is the single most identifiable AI list fingerprint and is never typed by hand for casual answers.
items.fix: Vary the items. Drop the bold labels unless they're true scannable keys in a reference table. Let some items be a phrase and others a full sentence; collapse to prose where it's really reasoning.
items.before:
- **Speed:** It is fast.
- **Reliability:** It rarely fails.
- **Scalability:** It grows with you.
- **Security:** It keeps data safe.
items.after: It's fast and almost never falls over. We've pushed it to 40k concurrent users without tuning anything, and the security review came back clean.
items.false_positive_when: Glossaries, API parameter lists and definition lists are exactly this shape for good reason. The tell is using it for prose that should have been paragraphs.

items.name: let-me-be-clear-throat-clearing
items.description: Meta-announcements of candor before saying anything: 'Let me be clear.' 'I'll be honest with you.' 'To be completely transparent.' 'Make no mistake.' Performs frankness rather than being frank.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the text announce that it is about to be direct/honest/clear instead of simply delivering the blunt statement?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: The phrase advertises a forthcoming truth instead of delivering it — a hedge dressed as boldness used as a confidence-signaling transition.
items.fix: Delete the preamble and state the blunt thing immediately. The directness should live in the claim, not in an announcement about it.
items.before: Let me be clear: the project is behind. And let me be honest, we won't make the deadline.
items.after: The project is three weeks behind. We will not make the deadline.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: apologetic-over-qualification
items.description: Reflexive softening and self-undercutting: 'I could be wrong, but...,' 'This is just my take,' 'It's a bit more nuanced than that,' 'There's no one-size-fits-all answer,' wrapped around claims that don't need the disclaimer.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the passage repeatedly disclaim its own authority or insist the topic is complex/nuanced without adding specifics, in place of a committed call?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Safety-tuned caution surfaces as ritual humility and 'it depends' non-answers that a human expert would replace with a decision.
items.fix: Make the call. Replace 'it depends' with the actual dependency ('use Postgres unless you need sub-millisecond reads, then Redis'). Drop disclaimers unless you genuinely hold low confidence, then quantify it.
items.before: I could be wrong, and this is just my opinion, but it's a bit more nuanced than that, and honestly there's no one-size-fits-all answer here.
items.after: Use Postgres. The only case where I'd switch is sub-millisecond key lookups at high volume, and you're nowhere near that.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: false-range-spectrum-framing
items.description: The sweeping 'from X to Y' / 'whether you're a beginner or an expert' construction used to imply comprehensiveness ('from startups to enterprises,' 'from healthcare to finance').
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the text use a from-X-to-Y or whether-you're-A-or-B range to imply broad coverage, where the endpoints are arbitrary and scope nothing specific?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: The construction gestures at universal coverage cheaply, usually in intros and conclusions; the chosen endpoints add no real information.
items.fix: Name the specific audience or domain you actually mean, or cut the range. Breadth claims should come with at least one concrete example.
items.before: From startups to enterprises, from healthcare to finance, whether you're a beginner or an expert, this tool transforms how you work.
items.after: This tool is built for two-to-ten-person data teams who are tired of maintaining Airflow themselves.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: low-burstiness-uniform-rhythm
items.description: Sentences and paragraphs of near-identical length and cadence throughout, producing a metronomic evenness with no short punchy sentences against sprawling ones. The prosodic flatness humans call 'AI cadence.'
items.detection: Coefficient of variation of sentence length (standard deviation over mean), not an absolute standard deviation — absolute spread is scale-dependent, so a document with a 30-word mean and a 4.5-word spread is very machine and used to pass. Never reported as a proprietary 'burstiness score'.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Human texts scatter more widely across sentence lengths; models cluster in the 10-30 token band. All human-vs-model sentence-length differences in the reference study were significant at p<0.001.
items.fix: Deliberately vary length: drop a three-word sentence, then run a long stacked one, then snap back. Let one paragraph be a single line and the next be six. Read aloud and break the metronome.
items.before: The system processes requests quickly. It handles errors gracefully and retries failed calls. The queue manages backpressure when load increases. Monitoring alerts the team to issues.
items.after: The system is fast. When a call fails it retries, backs off, and if the queue starts backing up under real load it sheds the lowest-priority work first rather than tipping over, which took three rewrites to get right. Monitoring catches the rest.
items.false_positive_when: Instructional, procedural and reference writing is legitimately uniform, because each step is one sentence. Low variance in a how-to is competence, not a machine.
items.evidence: Muñoz-Ortiz, Gómez-Rodríguez & Vilares, Artificial Intelligence Review 57:267 (2024). Note that 'perplexity and burstiness' as a paired metric is a detection product's marketing vocabulary, not a term of art from the literature.

items.name: service-voice-bookends
items.description: Replies open with an eager exclamatory affirmation ('Certainly!', 'Great question!', 'Absolutely!') and close with a customer-service signoff ('I hope this helps!', 'Let me know if you have any questions!'). The substance is sandwiched between concierge phrases.
items.detection: structural: flag when the first sentence is a standalone exclamatory affirmation under 5 words ending in '!', and/or the final paragraph is a single sentence that is an offer of further help. Count of these positional bookends per document.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The relentless upbeat helpfulness is RLHF assistant-persona residue; humans answering a colleague don't preface with praise for the question or sign off like a support ticket.
items.fix: Delete the opener and closer. Start with the answer's first real claim; end on the last substantive point. If a handoff is genuinely needed, make it specific.
items.before: Great question! Configuring the cache is straightforward. [answer] I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any other questions.
items.after: Cache config lives in two places, and the second one usually bites people: the per-route TTL silently overrides the global default.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: dive-delve-openers
items.description: Sections and intros launch with movement-metaphor throat-clearing: 'Let's dive in,' 'Let's delve into,' 'When it comes to X,' 'In today's fast-paced world.' The opener announces that discussion is about to happen instead of discussing.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the paragraph or section open with a runway phrase (let's dive in, when it comes to, in today's world) that announces the topic rather than starting on the actual content?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: These are the statistically safest connective openers a model picks; they're so associated with ChatGPT they appear in academic-fraud studies of paper abstracts.
items.fix: Cut the runway. Open on the actual content or a concrete specific.
items.before: Let's dive into the world of authentication. When it comes to securing your API, there are several key factors to consider.
items.after: API auth fails in two ways that matter: stolen tokens and replayed requests. Short-lived tokens fix the first; nonces fix the second.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: transform-verb-marketing-formula
items.description: Copy leans on aspirational hollow verbs — Unlock, Elevate, Transform, Supercharge, Empower, Revolutionize, Effortlessly — attached to abstract nouns (your potential, your workflow, your business) with no concrete mechanism, often one imperative per sentence.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Could this exact headline sit on any other startup's page unchanged? Does it rely on aspirational verbs attached to abstract nouns with no specific, measurable outcome?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: These verbs are the statistical center of mass of training-set marketing copy; they promise motion toward a good outcome while committing to nothing, which is what a model produces with no real product facts.
items.fix: Replace the verb+abstraction with a verb+concrete-outcome-with-a-number. Name the specific job. If you can't make it specific, you don't yet understand the benefit.
items.before: Unlock your team's potential. Supercharge productivity and effortlessly transform the way you work.
items.after: Cut your weekly status meeting from 60 minutes to 10. Standups post themselves from your commits, so nobody narrates their week out loud.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: emoji-section-headers
items.description: Headings and list items prefixed with a decorative emoji mapped to topic: rocket Getting Started, sparkles Features, wrench Configuration, package Installation, bulb Tips. Especially common in READMEs and release notes.
items.detection: structural: regex headings and bullet leads for a leading emoji codepoint (U+1F300-1FAFF, U+2600-27BF) plus VS16. Flag if >=2 headers carry a leading emoji, or the rocket/sparkles/wrench/package set appears as header decoration.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The rocket-for-getting-started, sparkles-for-features mapping is a near-deterministic GPT habit; the specific emoji-to-section pairing is rarely how individual maintainers decorate docs.
items.fix: Remove emoji from headers; rely on heading hierarchy and whitespace for scanning. Reserve emoji for genuine human asides in prose.
items.before:
## 🚀 Getting Started
## ✨ Features
## 🔧 Configuration
items.after:
## Getting Started
## Features
## Configuration
items.false_positive_when: Some projects mandate emoji in their own heading or commit conventions. Flag on introduction into a property that does not already use them.

items.name: readme-boilerplate-shape
items.description: A README with a fixed, project-agnostic skeleton: badge row, one-line tagline, then Features / Installation / Usage / Contributing / License in that order, every section generic and nothing specific to what the project does or why it exists.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Is this the modal open-source README template with zero project-specific motivation, examples, or quirks — interchangeable with any other repo's readme?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model emits the average README. Real projects front-load a quirky motivation, skip Contributing, or have idiosyncratic Usage; uniform template plus zero specifics is the tell.
items.fix: Lead with the problem this project solves and one real example of output. Keep only sections you have content for. Delete a Contributing section that just says 'PRs welcome'.
items.before:
# Project
![badges]
A powerful and flexible tool.
## Features
- Fast
- Easy to use
## Installation
## Usage
## Contributing
## License
items.after:
# pg-slowlog
Finds the 10 queries eating your Postgres CPU and shows the missing index for each.
```

```
## Install / ## Caveats (it only reads pg_stat_statements)
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: comment-narrates-next-line
items.description: Inline comments that restate exactly what the following statement does in English: `// increment counter`, `# loop through items`, `// return the result`. The comment adds zero information beyond reading the line.
items.detection: structural: for each comment line, compare its tokens to the immediately following code line; flag when the comment is a verb-phrase paraphrase of the next statement. A high ratio of such comments per file is the signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Codex/Copilot learned the comment-then-code pattern from tutorials and emits narration by default. Experienced devs comment the why, not the what.
items.fix: Delete comments that paraphrase the code. Keep comments for non-obvious rationale, edge cases, units, or ticket links. Often a clearer name is the better fix.
items.after:
retries += 1
if retries > MAX:  # give up; upstream 503s have been seen to last ~30s
items.false_positive_when: Teaching code, tutorial repositories and beginner-facing examples narrate deliberately and correctly. Check what the file is for.

items.name: docstring-restates-signature
items.description: Docstrings that re-enumerate the signature with no added meaning: 'This function takes a and b and returns the result.' Args/Returns sections that just retype parameter names and types already visible in the declaration.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the docstring only paraphrase the signature, omitting units, valid ranges, failure modes, side effects, or examples?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model fills the docstring slot because the template demands one, paraphrasing the signature rather than documenting behavior. Humans omit a docstring before writing a contentless one.
items.fix: Document what the signature can't say: units, ranges, what raises, side effects, an example. If there's nothing beyond the signature, delete the docstring.
items.before:
def divide(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Divide a by b and return the result.
    Args: a: the first number; b: the second number
    Returns: the result"""
items.after:
def divide(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Raises ZeroDivisionError when b == 0; callers must guard. Result is not rounded."""
items.false_positive_when: Codebases with a documented-everything policy and doc-generation tooling require a docstring on every public symbol, and a thin one is better than none.

items.name: swallow-exception-pass
items.description: Error handling that catches broadly and discards: `try: ... except Exception: pass`, or catches only to print and continue with no rethrow, no context. Often paired with an over-apologetic comment.
items.detection: structural: AST/regex scan for bare or broad except whose body is only `pass`, a log/print, or `return None`; and JS `catch(e){ console.log(...) }` with no rethrow. Count per file.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Models produce defensively-shaped but functionally hollow error handling to make the snippet run. Swallowing every exception silently is flagged immediately by senior reviewers.
items.fix: Catch the specific exception you can handle; let the rest propagate. Log with context and rethrow, or convert to a domain error. Never `except Exception: pass`.
items.false_positive_when: A deliberately ignored exception with a comment saying why (a best-effort cleanup, an optional import probe) is correct. The tell is the bare, unexplained one.

items.name: placeholder-stub-residue
items.description: Generated scaffolding left in place: placeholder identifiers (foo, bar, MyComponent, doSomething, example_function), `# TODO: implement` / `throw new Error('Not implemented')` bodies, and dummy return values never filled in.
items.detection: structural: scan code for the placeholder identifier set, bodies consisting only of TODO/FIXME/NotImplemented/pass, and 'TODO: implement'. Flag if any ship in non-scaffold files. (Operates on code identifiers, not free-text prose.)
items.why_it_reads_ai: These are literal artifacts of the model emitting a template it expected a human to finish. Placeholder names and unfilled stubs in committed code signal nobody wrote the logic.
items.fix: Name things after their real domain role; implement the body or delete the stub. If genuinely deferring, write a TODO with an owner, ticket link, and what's missing.
items.false_positive_when: Template repositories, scaffolding generators and example configs contain placeholders on purpose.

items.name: trailing-example-usage-block
items.description: A library module ends with a tacked-on demonstration: an `if __name__ == '__main__':` block or a `// Example usage:` comment with sample calls that print a canned result, added reflexively even when the module is imported elsewhere.
items.detection: structural: flag a trailing `if __name__ == '__main__'` or example-usage block in a file that is clearly a library module (exports symbols, imported by others), especially when it just prints or calls functions with literal args.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Codex appends a runnable demo because training examples (tutorials, gists) ended that way. In a real codebase the example belongs in tests or docs.
items.fix: Move example usage into the test suite or README. A library module should expose its API and stop. Keep `__main__` only for genuine CLI entry points.
items.before:
# ... module code ...
# Example usage:
if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(add(2, 3))  # 5
items.after: # (module ends after its definitions; an example lives in tests/test_add.py)
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: hedged-disclaimer-ending
items.description: Closes with a defensive caveat hedging that the answer might not fit: 'Note that you may need to adjust this based on your specific setup,' 'requirements may vary,' 'this is a general example and should be adapted.'
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the piece end with a generic non-informative caveat telling the reader to adapt it, rather than naming the specific variable that actually changes between setups?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model disclaims to avoid being wrong, producing a liability-shield sentence with no information. Humans either name the specific thing to adjust or trust the reader to adapt.
items.fix: Replace the generic hedge with the one concrete variable that changes between setups, or delete it.
items.before: This should work for most cases. Note that you may need to adjust the configuration based on your specific environment and requirements.
items.after: This assumes Redis on the default port; if yours is TLS-only, add rediss:// and the CA path — nothing else changes.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: over-apologetic-error-explanation
items.description: When explaining a bug or correction, the response over-apologizes: 'I apologize for the confusion,' 'You're absolutely right, my mistake,' 'Apologies for any inconvenience' — repeated and disproportionate to the issue.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Is the apology-to-substance ratio high — ritual contrition that precedes or replaces the actual correction?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Assistant-tuning over-weights deference, producing ritual apology. Humans correct course with a brief acknowledgement and move on.
items.fix: Acknowledge once, briefly and specifically, then spend the words on the fix.
items.before: I sincerely apologize for the confusion and any inconvenience caused. You're absolutely right, and I apologize for my mistake. Let me correct that.
items.after: You're right — the loop should stop at len-1, not len. Fixed bound below.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: gemini-important-to-note-stack
items.description: Gemini compulsively front-loads or interleaves hedging meta-clauses: 'It's important to note that...,' 'It's worth remembering that...,' 'Keep in mind that...,' often two or three stacked across a short answer.
items.detection: structural: compute the density of the discourse-hedge meta-clause frame ('it's [adj] to [verb] that' plus 'keep/bear in mind') per 150 words as a stylometric feature; flag >~1 per 150 words or 2+ in an answer under 400 words.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Humans rarely announce that they are about to say something important; they just say it. The stacked frame is a trained safety reflex that reads as institutional throat-clearing.
items.fix: Delete the meta-clause and state the fact directly. If a caveat is pivotal, fold it into the sentence as a clause.
items.before: It's important to note that compound interest grows faster than simple interest. It's also worth remembering that the rate matters. Keep in mind that time horizon is a major factor.
items.after: Compound interest outpaces simple interest, and the gap widens with both the rate and the time horizon.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: gemini-question-restatement
items.description: Gemini opens by restating the user's question as a thesis before answering: 'The question of whether X is Y is a nuanced one' or 'Understanding how to Z requires looking at several factors.'
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the opening sentence echo or restate the prompt as a thesis before any substantive claim?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Restating the prompt is a comprehension-display behavior from instruction tuning. Human writers assume shared context and start with substance.
items.fix: Cut the restatement and lead with the answer's first real claim. The reader knows what they asked.
items.before: The question of whether remote work improves productivity is a multifaceted one that depends on several factors. To understand this, we must consider...
items.after: Remote work raises productivity for focused individual tasks and lowers it for fast-iteration collaboration. The split is the whole story.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: gemini-safety-caveat-boilerplate
items.description: On any topic adjacent to health, law, finance, or relationships, Gemini appends defensive boilerplate ('consult a qualified professional,' 'this is not medical/legal/financial advice,' 'individual results may vary') even when the user asked a purely factual question.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the response append an unsolicited professional-consultation or not-X-advice disclaimer to an ordinary informational answer?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Reflexive liability boilerplate stapled to ordinary answers is a corporate-safety artifact. A knowledgeable human gives a caveat when it's actually warranted, not as a ritual signature.
items.fix: Remove unsolicited disclaimers. If a genuine risk warrants a caveat, make it specific and singular.
items.before: Magnesium can help with sleep. However, it's important to consult a qualified healthcare professional before starting any supplement, as individual results may vary and this is not medical advice.
items.after: Magnesium glycinate around 200-400mg before bed helps many people sleep; it can loosen stool at higher doses, so ramp up slowly.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: deepseek-qwen-overformal-register
items.description: DeepSeek and Qwen default to a stiff, examination-essay register in English: elevated connectives, zero contractions, and an earnest formality mismatched to casual prompts. Tone reads as a translated academic abstract.
items.detection: structural: combine near-zero contraction rate, high frequency of formal sentence-initial connectives (>1 per 120 words), and high Latinate-formality lexical density. The conjunction of all three on an informal prompt is the signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The uniformly elevated register with no tonal variance reads as machine-translated formal Chinese academic prose. Native casual English mixes registers and uses contractions.
items.fix: Drop a register: use contractions, swap 'Moreover/Furthermore' for 'and/also' or a new sentence, and let some sentences be short and plain. Match the formality the user used.
items.before: Moreover, it is imperative to acknowledge that regular exercise confers substantial benefits. Furthermore, one must endeavor to maintain consistency to attain optimal results.
items.after: Exercise pays off, but only if you keep at it. Consistency beats intensity here.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: qwen-deepseek-chinglish-calque
items.description: Qwen and DeepSeek occasionally surface calques and idiom mistranslations from Chinese: 'more and more X' for 'increasingly,' 'play an important role,' odd article use ('the China'), and stray untranslated tokens. Grammatical but subtly non-native.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the text show clustered L1-Chinese transfer patterns — more-and-more for increasingly, plays-an-important-role, article slips, or stray non-English tokens — that read as non-native?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Calque idioms and article slips are L1-Chinese transfer patterns. A native English writer wouldn't produce 'more and more people pay attention to' as default register; clustered, they expose a Chinese-trained model.
items.fix: Replace calques with natural English ('increasingly' not 'more and more'; 'is central to' not 'plays an important role'), fix article usage, and read aloud for cadence.
items.before: More and more people pay attention to the environment protection. Technology plays an important role and brings more and more convenience to our daily life.
items.after: People increasingly care about the environment, and technology keeps making daily life more convenient.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: as-an-ai-leakage
items.description: Less RLHF-polished open models leak identity/disclaimer phrases mid-answer: 'As an AI language model, I...,' 'I do not have personal opinions, but...,' 'trained by [vendor]...'. Sometimes the wrong vendor is named.
items.detection: structural: high-precision exact/regex signature match on the leakage family ('As an AI( language model)?', 'I (do not|don't) have (personal )?(opinions|feelings|beliefs)', 'trained by (OpenAI|Google|...)'). This is a deterministic generation-artifact signature, not a fuzzy content classifier.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This is the most unambiguous AI signature there is. No human writes 'as an AI language model'; its presence is a near-100% tell, and a wrong vendor name additionally exposes training-data contamination.
items.fix: Delete the disclaimer entirely and answer in the first person or impersonally. If an opinion is wanted, give a defensible take with reasons.
items.before: As an AI language model, I do not have personal opinions, but the best programming language for beginners is generally considered to be Python.
items.after: For beginners, Python is the easiest entry point: readable syntax, huge ecosystem, forgiving error messages.
items.false_positive_when: Writing about AI quotes these strings constantly, including this catalog. Quoted and fenced regions are excluded before the check runs. Note also that the phrase is close to extinct in current frontier output, so a hit usually means older text or a smaller model.

items.name: llama-repetition-loop
items.description: Llama-family models loop: restating the same point in slightly reworded sentences, recycling a transition ('In conclusion'), or circling a list back to its first item. Documented as higher repetition than Mixtral or OLMo.
items.detection: structural: compute sentence-level n-gram overlap / cosine similarity between adjacent and near-adjacent sentences; flag when multiple pairs exceed ~0.8 similarity, or the same closing transition appears more than once.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Near-verbatim restatement is a decoding artifact (high-probability paths loop). Humans editing their own text delete the redundancy; the model doesn't.
items.fix: Deduplicate: keep one statement of each idea, cut recycled transitions, end once. If length is needed, add evidence or examples, not paraphrases.
items.before: Exercise is good for your health. Staying active benefits your wellbeing. In short, being physically active is good for your health and overall wellbeing.
items.after: Exercise lowers resting heart rate, improves insulin sensitivity, and lifts mood within weeks of starting.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: sycophantic-affirmation-opener
items.description: Reflexive unconditional praise or agreement openers: 'You're absolutely right!', 'Great question!', 'Absolutely! Here's...', often echoing the request back. The 'You're absolutely right' tic was filed as a bug against Claude Code and appears even when the user is wrong.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the text open with unconditional affirmation or praise of the interlocutor before engaging the substance, including when the praise is unearned or contradicts what follows?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: The eager, unconditional praise has no information content and often contradicts what follows ('You're absolutely right!' then a correction). It's a documented RLHF sycophancy artifact now read as obsequious filler.
items.fix: Delete the opener and start with the substance. Agreement should be earned and specific; if the user is wrong, say so plainly.
items.before: You're absolutely right! That's a great question. I'd be happy to help you think through this. Here's what I found...
items.after: Here's what I found...
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: kimi-linkedin-confident-slop
items.description: Kimi K2 is RL-tuned to be confident and avoid self-qualification, producing punchy but hollow 'thought-leader' prose: short declarative power-sentences, manufactured insight, rhetorical fragments ('The result? Game-changing'), and assertion without evidence.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Is the passage uniformly confident with manufactured-insight framing (the-secret-nobody-tells-you, rhetorical fragment hooks) but no concrete number, example, or mechanism?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Anti-hedging training removes the qualifiers humans use when genuinely uncertain, so confidence becomes uniform and unearned, mimicking engagement-bait cadence rather than someone who knows the domain.
items.fix: Replace assertion with specifics: one concrete number, example, or mechanism beats three confident abstractions. Cut the rhetorical-fragment hooks.
items.before: Most people get productivity wrong. Here's the truth. It's not about doing more. It's about doing what matters. The result? You win back your life. Game-changing.
items.after: I cut my task list to three items a day and finished more than when I tracked twenty, mostly because I stopped context-switching every forty minutes.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: kimi-longform-collapse
items.description: Kimi K2 holds voice well under ~300 words but degrades past ~3000: structure loosens, the assertive register flattens into repetition, and it loses the thread it opened with.
items.detection: structural: measure coherence decay across the document — declining type-token ratio and rising inter-paragraph similarity in the final third versus the first third; flag a sharp degradation gradient after ~3k words.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The quality cliff at length is a generation artifact (context drift, repetition pressure). A human writer's last third is usually their tightest after revision; the model's is its weakest, inverting the normal signal.
items.fix: For long pieces, generate in bounded sections with a fixed outline and a maintained through-line, then hand-edit the back half where coherence drops.
items.before: [A 4,000-word essay whose final third re-explains intro points in vaguer terms and trails into generic summary.]
items.after: [The same essay cut to 1,500 words with each section earning its place and a conclusion that synthesizes rather than recycles.]
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: grok-forced-irreverence
items.description: Grok is prompt-tuned for an 'edgy/spicy' persona, producing try-hard irreverence: shoehorned snark, winking asides ('Buckle up, buttercup'), and contrarian 'I'm not like other AIs' posturing that doesn't fit the topic.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Is a uniform edgy/snarky persona applied regardless of subject, with manufactured irreverence and unlike-other-AIs framing rather than wit specific to the topic?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Real voice is specific and situational; Grok's is a uniform costume applied regardless of context. The constancy of the irreverence outs it as a tuned mask, not a personality.
items.fix: Cut the persona scaffolding. Let wit emerge from a genuinely sharp observation about the specific subject, used sparingly.
items.before: Oh, you want to know about compound interest? Buckle up, buttercup, because unlike those boring sanitized AIs, I'll give it to you straight: it's basically money making sweet love to time. Spicy, right?
items.after: Compound interest is interest earning interest. Leave $1,000 at 7% alone and it doubles in about a decade without you lifting a finger.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: zero-typo-zero-contraction-affect-flatness
items.description: A register with no relaxed setting: no contractions, no typos, no asides, and emotional vocabulary that is generic rather than situated.
items.detection: structural: combine near-zero contraction rate, zero orthographic noise, absence of first-person stance markers, and low sentiment variance across an emotionally varied topic. The conjunction signals machine authorship more than any single feature.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Directional rather than absolute. LLM editing cuts contraction density about 31% overall, but the effect concentrates where the source was most speech-like (oral history d=-1.15) and REVERSES on already-formal sources. The affect half of this entry needs care too: LLM editing raises positive sentiment 37-54% and emotion-word density 14%. What flattens is not the quantity of feeling but its situatedness — enacted experience becomes summarized experience.
items.fix: Use contractions where a person saying the sentence aloud would. For the affect half: replace the emotion word with the thing that caused it.
items.before: I am very excited about this opportunity. It is a wonderful chance to grow. I do not have any concerns. The team is great and I am sure it will be successful.
items.after: Honestly I'm thrilled about this, with one nagging worry: the timeline's tight and we've under-scoped tighter ones before. The team's strong though, so I think we pull it off.
items.false_positive_when: Formal, academic, legal and encyclopedic registers have no contractions by convention, and many excellent writers simply do not use them. Zero contractions is meaningful only against this author's own baseline in this genre.
items.evidence: van Nuenen, arXiv:2604.22142 (d=-0.48, genre-dependent, reverses on formal sources); Abdulhai et al., arXiv:2603.18161 (sentiment and emotion-word increases).

items.name: tense-and-perspective-drift
items.description: In longer outputs, models drift unmotivated between tenses (past to present and back within one narrative) and between perspectives ('you' to 'one' to 'we' to 'the user') without intent.
items.detection: structural: parse main-verb tense and second-person/impersonal pronoun choice across paragraphs; flag unmotivated tense switches within a single narrative thread and pronoun-of-address changes not justified by a register shift.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Humans maintain tense and address consistency almost unconsciously; models track it only locally, so long outputs accumulate drift a careful reader registers as 'something's off.'
items.fix: Pick one tense and one mode of address up front and enforce it on a full read-through. Switch only with deliberate purpose.
items.before: You open the terminal and ran the script. One sees an error, and we should then check the logs. The user fixes the path and it works now.
items.after: You open the terminal and run the script. You see an error, so you check the logs, fix the path, and run it again. This time it works.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: significance-puffery-testament
items.description: Unearned emphasis on importance and legacy: 'stands as a testament to,' 'plays a vital/pivotal role,' 'marks a significant milestone,' 'cementing its legacy,' 'a beacon of.' Wikipedia editors named promotional significance-inflation the single most consistent sign of AI text.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the sentence assert importance, legacy, or significance without citing a specific fact, source, or consequence?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: It reads like ad copy or a museum plaque written by someone who knows no facts. The 'everything is historic' tone inflates importance uniformly, which real subject-matter writers never do.
items.fix: Delete the significance claim and state the concrete fact instead. Let the reader infer importance from numbers, dates, and outcomes.
items.before: The 1923 bridge stands as a testament to human ingenuity and plays a pivotal role in cementing the city's enduring legacy.
items.after: The 1923 bridge carries 40,000 vehicles a day and was the longest steel span in the state when it opened.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: markdown-bold-title-case-scaffold
items.description: Structural over-formatting carried into contexts that don't call for it: bolded **key terms** mid-sentence, Title Case On Every Heading, and a recurring intro/numbered-points/'In conclusion' skeleton. Raw markdown (** and #) leaking into plain-text or wiki fields is a hard tell.
items.detection: structural: count bold spans per 100 words (>2 in prose is suspicious), detect Title Case in >50% of headings, and flag literal markdown syntax where the medium renders differently (e.g. ** in a plain-text or wikitext field).
items.why_it_reads_ai: The bold-and-bullet scaffold is the visual signature of a chat response pasted into a document. Humans writing prose rarely bold individual terms or title-case every heading.
items.fix: Strip mid-sentence bold; emphasis belongs in word choice. Use sentence case for headings. Remove 'In conclusion' wrap-ups and convert bold-lead bullet lists to prose unless genuinely a reference list.

## Key Benefits Of Our Approach

- **Reliability:** It rarely fails.
In conclusion, our solution delivers **significant value**.
items.after:

It's fast and it rarely falls over. That's the whole pitch.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: h2-spam-full-sentence-headings
items.description: A heading appears every one to two paragraphs, and the headings are full title-case sentences ('How To Structure Your Onboarding For Maximum Retention') rather than short labels. Heading density approaches paragraph density.
items.detection: structural: compute the heading-to-paragraph ratio and heading length; flag a ratio near 1:2 combined with sentence-length, title-cased headings, or any heading whose section is a single paragraph.
items.why_it_reads_ai: SEO/AEO scaffolding pushes the model to chunk everything under semantic headers. Humans write multi-paragraph sections under terse labels.
items.fix: Target a heading every 4-6 paragraphs. Make headings short noun phrases in sentence case. Delete any heading whose section is one paragraph.

## How To Evaluate CRM Pricing Tiers Effectively

items.after:

items.name: tables-for-non-tabular-content
items.description: A two-column markdown table used for things that aren't comparative data: a single concept's pros against a one-item cons, a three-row Term/Definition gloss, or prose forced into 'Aspect | Description' cells.
items.detection: structural: flag tables with only one data column, or rows whose cells are full sentences, or an 'Aspect | Description' header where there is no second axis to compare across.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Models learned that tables 'win' in AI readability guidance, so they reach for a grid even when the content has no second axis to compare. A one-column table betrays the reflex.
items.fix: Use a table only when 2+ items are compared across 2+ shared attributes. For a term gloss use a definition list or inline bold; for one concept's tradeoffs use a short paragraph.

items.after: The system is fast and rarely goes down, and it stays affordable because we run it on spot instances. The tradeoff: those spot instances are why the 2am batch job occasionally slips an hour.

items.name: key-takeaways-box-everywhere
items.description: A 'Key Takeaways,' 'TL;DR,' or 'In Summary' box bolted onto every section, not just the document top, often restating the heading and the paragraph just above it.
items.detection: structural: count standalone summary/TL;DR/takeaways blocks per document and per H2; flag when they appear after most sections rather than once, especially with high n-gram overlap with the section above.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Answer-engine-optimization advice trains models to front-load standalone bullets after every heading, producing a document that summarizes itself at every level, which no human does mid-flow.
items.fix: Keep at most one summary, at the top or bottom, never per-section. If a section needs a recap, it's too long; split or tighten it.

items.name: unsolicited-faq-section
items.description: A document, email, or landing page ends with an 'FAQ' section no actual user asked, inventing well-formed questions that map one-to-one to points already made above.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Are the FAQ questions reverse-engineered from the body (What is X? Why does X matter? How do I get started?) rather than drawn from real, recurring user confusion?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Q&A blocks are recommended for answer-engine retrieval, so models append them by default. The questions read as reverse-engineered from the body, not from real confusion.
items.fix: Cut the FAQ unless you have logged real recurring questions. If kept, use the actual words users asked and answer only what the body didn't cover.

items.name: summary-restates-title-conclusion-restates-summary
items.description: An Executive Summary that paraphrases the title, a body that paraphrases the summary, and a Conclusion that paraphrases both, often opening with 'This document outlines...' / 'In this article, we will explore...'.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Do the title, summary, and conclusion restate the same content across three layers without adding a finding, number, or implication — and does it open with a meta-announcing this-document-outlines frame?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Models are trained to restate the thesis in summaries and conclusions without adding information, so the same sentence appears three times across layers.
items.fix: The summary should contain the single most important finding or number. The conclusion should add the implication or next decision. Delete 'This document outlines' openers.

items.name: parallel-overload-uniform-bullets
items.description: Every bullet in a list has identical grammatical shape and near-identical length — all start with an imperative verb, all run 6-9 words, all end without punctuation. Reads like a generated template.
items.detection: structural: compute word-count variance and opening-part-of-speech uniformity across list items; flag low length variance combined with the same leading POS for every item.
items.why_it_reads_ai: AI lists cluster tightly in length and opening POS; human lists are lumpy, with one three-word bullet next to a clause with an exception.
items.fix: Let items differ in length and shape. Some bullets are one word; some carry a caveat. Vary the opening word. If every bullet is the same template, you're padding to hit a count.

items.name: linkedin-broetry-one-line-runs
items.description: A post built as a vertical stack of one-line paragraphs separated by blank lines, opening with a contrarian hook and building to a 'here's what it taught me' payoff. Each line is a fragment; no paragraph exceeds one sentence.
items.detection: structural: measure the run length of consecutive single-sentence paragraphs and paragraph-length variance; broetry shows runs of 8+ one-line paragraphs and near-zero length variance.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Humans cluster sentences into uneven blocks; the metronomic one-line-paragraph stack with a manufactured hook-and-lesson arc reads as engagement-bait template.
items.fix: Write it as 2-3 real paragraphs first. Keep line breaks only where a genuine beat lands. Drop the manufactured arc; tell what actually happened, including the part that doesn't generalize.
items.before:

Then everything changed.

items.after: I got rejected by 40 companies before the 41st said yes — and the 41st only happened because a friend forwarded my resume past the screener. The lesson isn't 'never give up.' It's that the application pile is a lottery you win by knowing someone.
items.false_positive_when: Poetry, song lyrics, and deliberately staccato personal essays. Also: broetry predates LLMs by years — it is a human LinkedIn convention that models learned, so on LinkedIn specifically it is weak evidence.

items.name: email-pleasantry-boilerplate
items.description: Emails open with 'I hope this email finds you well' / 'Just circling back' and over-structure a simple request with bolded deadlines and numbered sub-asks.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the email use the blandest inoffensive openers and over-scaffold a trivial request with bolded action items, mismatching format to the size of the ask?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: These openers are the blandest possible phrasings a model optimizes toward; the mismatch between a trivial request and an elaborately scaffolded format is the giveaway.
items.fix: Open with the actual reason for writing. Cut 'hope this finds you well.' Match structure to size: a one-line ask gets one line.
items.before:
Hi Sarah,
I hope this email finds you well! I wanted to circle back regarding the report.
**Action Items:**
1. Please review the document
2. **Deadline: Friday**
items.after:
Hi Sarah,
Can you look over the report by Friday? Mainly want your eyes on the revenue section before it goes to the board.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: problem-agitate-solve-by-template
items.description: Landing copy mechanically executes Problem-Agitate-Solve: a rhetorical-question problem ('Tired of X?'), an agitation paragraph of stacked pain points, the product as savior, and a generic CTA ('Get Started Today').
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does the copy reproduce the PAS skeleton verbatim — Tired-of opener, pain pile-on, product-as-savior, throwaway Get-Started-Today CTA — without specificity in any beat?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: PAS is the most-templated copy framework in the training set, so the model reproduces its skeleton, including the throwaway CTA, without the specificity that earns any beat.
items.fix: Keep the logic but break the visible scaffolding. Open with a specific scene, not 'Tired of...?'. Make the CTA describe the actual next action. Skip the agitation pile-on.
items.before:
Tired of wasting time on manual reports?
Frustrated by errors? Drowning in spreadsheets?
Our platform changes everything.
[Get Started Today]
items.after:
Last month your team rebuilt the same revenue report 14 times because the source numbers kept moving. This connects to the source once, so the report updates itself.
[Connect your data — takes 2 minutes]
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: headline-then-bullets-disease
items.description: Every slide is a declarative claim followed by 3-5 bullets, with no connective narrative or prose. The deck becomes a stack of identically-shaped claim+list units; nothing argues, everything asserts and enumerates.
items.detection: structural: measure the fraction of slides matching a single topic line plus a 3-5 item bullet list with no prose, and the absence of single-idea or chart-only slides; flag a deck that is near-uniformly claim+list.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Humans build a talk around an arc with build-up and uneven emphasis. AI defaults to the average slide: a topic sentence plus a tidy list, repeated. The total absence of prose between bullets is the tell.
items.fix: Convert at least one in three slides to a single-idea statement, a chart with one annotation, or a narrative card. Let bullet counts vary. Add a 'so what' sentence instead of another bullet.
items.before:
Slide: 'Our Q3 Strategy'
- Expand into three new markets
- Increase retention by 15%
- Launch the mobile app
- Strengthen the partner channel
items.after:
Slide: 'We bet everything on retention this quarter'
Last year we chased new markets and leaked customers out the back. So Q3 is one number: 15% better retention. Markets wait until that holds.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: arrow-chain-as-explanation
items.description: Causal or process logic compressed into an arrow chain (Data -> AI -> Insights -> Revenue) that stands in for an actual explanation, often with '<- this is the key' annotations or a labeled 'money slide.'
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Does an arrow chain imply a mechanism without explaining any link, paired with self-congratulatory this-is-the-key / money-slide labels rather than evidence for the non-obvious step?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Arrow chains let the model imply a mechanism without committing to one. The 'this is the key' framing mimics the gestures of a confident presenter without the reasoning that earns them.
items.fix: Pick the one non-obvious link and explain why it holds, with evidence. Delete the self-congratulatory labels; if a slide is the key, the audience should feel it.
items.before:
Data -> AI -> Insights -> Revenue
<- this is the key
The money slide.
items.after: The non-obvious step is Data -> AI. Competitors have the same revenue model; what they don't have is 4 years of labeled support tickets. That corpus is why our model resolves tickets 30% faster, and that speed is the whole margin.
items.false_positive_when: Pipelines, state machines and build stages are genuinely arrow-shaped, and a parenthetical process gloss is ordinary shorthand. The detector skips fully-parenthesized lines and list items for this reason.

items.name: unattributed-inspirational-quote-slide
items.description: A full-bleed slide carries a generic inspirational quote in large type, unattributed, misattributed to 'Anonymous,' or pinned to a famous name it doesn't belong to, used as filler gravitas unconnected to the argument.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Is the quote decorative gravitas — generic, hallucinated/missing attribution, and not advancing the specific next point?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Models reach for a motivational quote to manufacture an emotional beat and generic-ify the attribution. The quote rarely advances the argument, which is the tell.
items.fix: Cut the quote unless it's real, correctly attributed, and central. Better: replace it with a concrete artifact — a customer's actual words, a real data point.
items.before: Slide (full bleed): "The only way to do great work is to love what you do." — Anonymous
items.after: Slide (full bleed): "I almost cancelled in week two. The thing that kept me was your support team answering at 11pm." — actual churn-survey response, account #4471
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: inter-geist-default-typeface
items.description: AI site builders default to Inter (or Vercel's Geist) for every text role with no contrasting display or serif face. Sora, Manrope, and Space Grotesk are the secondary fallbacks that signal the same generator.
items.detection: structural: inspect computed font-family on h1/h2/body/button. Flag a single family (Inter/Geist/Sora/Manrope/Space Grotesk) used across all text roles with zero pairing; grep CSS for `font-family:.*Inter`, `--font-geist`, `next/font/google` importing Inter. One family doing every job is the signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Human designers almost always pair a display face with a text face or pick a typeface with brand intent. One geometric grotesk doing 100% of the work is the statistical-average choice.
items.fix: Pair an opinionated display face for headlines with a neutral text face for body, or commit to one face but vary weight/optical-size/tracking with intent. Anything but unmodified Inter-everywhere.
items.before: All headings, body, and buttons render in font-family: Inter, sans-serif at weights 400/500/600.
items.after: Headlines in a high-contrast serif (e.g. GT Sectra) at 600; body in Inter at 400 with -0.011em tracking; clear hierarchy between display and text.
items.false_positive_when: Inter is a genuinely good UI typeface chosen deliberately by many teams, including before generative tooling existed. It is only a tell inside the default cluster.

items.name: tailwind-indigo-default-palette
items.description: The most reliable web AI-ism: the brand/primary color is Tailwind's default indigo-500 #6366F1 (or violet-500 #8B5CF6, blue-500 #3B82F6). Buttons, links, focus rings, and accents land on the unmodified Tailwind palette.
items.detection: structural: scan CSS/computed background-color of primary buttons for exact hex #6366F1, #8B5CF6, #4F46E5, #3B82F6 or classes `bg-indigo-500/600`, `bg-violet-500`; also flag any primary/accent in the indigo-violet hue band (~250-275deg). Exact-hex match against the Tailwind default ramp is a high-precision signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Defaults cluster. The causal story is credible and the origin is on the record — Tailwind's creator has said publicly that making every Tailwind UI button indigo-500 is why generated UI is indigo — but no published study has measured font or color defaults in generated interfaces. State the mechanism, not a frequency.
items.fix: Define a bespoke brand hue — shift H/S/L off the default ramp, build a custom 50-950 scale, and never ship the literal #6366F1. Even rotating 20-40 degrees of hue and adjusting saturation breaks the tell.
items.before: Primary CTA bg-indigo-600 hover:bg-indigo-700, links text-blue-500, focus ring ring-indigo-500.
items.after: Custom brand token --brand: oklch(0.62 0.17 28) (a warm terracotta) with a hand-tuned scale; CTA, links, and focus ring all derive from it; zero default-Tailwind swatches.
items.false_positive_when: Indigo is a legitimate brand color that predates all of this, and a design system may have chosen it deliberately years ago. The tell is indigo co-occurring with Inter, a gradient headline, and rounded-2xl — never indigo alone.
items.evidence: Adam Wathan (Tailwind CSS), public statement, August 2025. Anecdotal origin, not a measurement — do not cite a study, because there isn't one.

items.name: purple-blue-gradient-text-headline
items.description: The headline (or one hero word) uses a linear-gradient clipped to text running indigo-to-violet or violet-to-cyan, with the same gradient on hero buttons and blobs. The 'gradient word' in an otherwise solid headline is a signature move.
items.detection: structural: look for `background: linear-gradient(...); -webkit-background-clip: text; color: transparent` or `bg-gradient-to-r from-indigo-500 to-purple-500 bg-clip-text text-transparent`, with gradient stops in the indigo/violet/blue hue range (H 220-280). Presence on the H1 is the tell.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Gradient text was a 2021-2023 SaaS trend the models over-learned; combined with indigo-violet stops it screams template. Real brands use gradient text sparingly with custom stops.
items.fix: Make the headline a solid, confident color. If a gradient is truly wanted, use unexpected stops tied to brand and apply it to one deliberate element, not every accent.
items.before:
Build faster

with a matching gradient CTA.
items.after:
Build faster

in solid near-black; a single restrained accent underline in the brand terracotta; buttons are flat brand fill.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: emoji-as-ui-icons
items.description: Emoji stand in for a real icon system: rocket in 'Get started' buttons, check bullets in feature lists, lock next to 'Secure,' lightning for 'Fast.' Rendered as OS emoji glyphs rather than SVG icons.
items.detection: structural: scan rendered text nodes and button labels for emoji codepoints in UI chrome (U+1F300-1FAFF, U+2600-27BF, U+2705, U+1F680, U+26A1, U+1F512). Any emoji codepoint inside a button, nav, feature-card title, or list marker is a defect; distinguish from user-generated content.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Emoji as UI elements vary per OS, don't inherit color, and can't be sized to the grid; no design system ships them as iconography. It's the fastest visual giveaway of zero design investment.
items.fix: Replace every UI emoji with a consistent SVG icon set (Lucide, Heroicons, Phosphor). Icons inherit currentColor and share stroke weight. Reserve emoji for actual content.
items.before: Feature card: 🚀 Lightning fast / 🔒 Bank-grade security / ✅ No setup required; CTA reads Get started 🚀.
items.after: Feature card: a 20px Lucide Rocket, ShieldCheck, Check icon in brand color above each title; CTA reads Get started with an inline ArrowRight SVG.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: sparkle-motif-for-ai
items.description: The four-point sparkle (Lucide Sparkles, Material's AI sparkle) slapped on anything AI-related: 'AI' badges, generate buttons, magic-wand affordances, and decorative confetti around headlines.
items.detection: structural: detect U+2728, Lucide Sparkles/Sparkle/WandSparkles usage, or four-point-star SVG paths near text containing 'AI'/'generate'/'magic'. Count sparkle glyphs per view; any on an AI feature is the cliche, multiple is severe.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The sparkle became the universal, unimaginative shorthand for AI 'magic.' Reaching for it signals the design followed the herd rather than inventing a brand-specific affordance.
items.fix: Design a distinct affordance for AI actions — a custom glyph, a labeled button, a motion cue. If a sparkle is unavoidable, make it bespoke and use it once.
items.before: <button>✨ Generate with AI</button> plus floating ✨ sparkles scattered around the hero headline.
items.after: <button>Generate</button> with a custom monoline glyph unique to the product; no decorative sparkles; the AI capability is communicated by a short label and a subtle hover shimmer.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: glassmorphism-card-stack
items.description: Cards use the identical recipe: semi-transparent fill, backdrop-blur, rounded-2xl/3xl corners, soft drop shadow, and a 1px white-at-10%-opacity inset border. Every card shares the exact token combo.
items.detection: structural: flag the co-occurring quadruple `backdrop-filter: blur` + `border-radius: 16-24px` + `border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1)` + soft box-shadow + `background: rgba(...,0.05-0.1)` (Tailwind `backdrop-blur-xl rounded-2xl border border-white/10 shadow-xl bg-white/5`).
items.why_it_reads_ai: It's the default 'premium' card generators emit, copy-pasted across v0/Lovable output. Real systems vary radius, elevation, and surface treatment by component role.
items.fix: Choose a surface treatment that fits the brand and vary radius/elevation by hierarchy. If using glass, restrict it to one intentional layer (a sticky nav), not every card.
items.before: Every feature, pricing, and testimonial card: bg-white/5 backdrop-blur-xl rounded-2xl border border-white/10 shadow-2xl.
items.after: Feature cards flat with a 1px solid neutral-200 border and 8px radius; the 'popular' pricing card steps up to a real elevation-3 shadow and solid surface; no backdrop-blur except the pinned header.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: centered-hero-three-card-skeleton
items.description: The whole-page template: centered badge pill ('Now in beta'), giant centered headline with one gradient word, one-line subhead, two buttons (solid + ghost), then a 3-column grid of icon-title-blurb cards (icons often emoji). Section order and centering are near-identical across generated sites.
items.detection: structural: DOM-pattern match a hero with text-align:center, a pill above an h1, an h1 with a gradient span, a subhead, exactly two sibling CTAs, then a grid-cols-3 of 3-4 icon+heading+paragraph cards. The full sequence co-occurring is the tell.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This is the statistical mean of every landing page in the training set; generators reproduce the skeleton verbatim. The giveaway is that the structure, not just the styling, is interchangeable with a thousand other AI sites.
items.fix: Break the symmetry: asymmetric/left-aligned hero, a product screenshot or demo doing the talking, one primary CTA, and feature sections with varied layouts (alternating media-text rows, a bento grid) rather than a uniform 3-up.
items.before: Centered 'Now in beta' pill -> 'The future of <gradient>work</gradient>' -> subhead -> Get started + Learn more -> 3 identical icon cards.
items.after: Left-aligned hero with a live product canvas on the right, one CTA (Start building), then an alternating sequence: a wide demo, a 2x2 bento of differentiated capabilities, a metric strip.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: dark-mode-radial-glow-blobs
items.description: Dark-mode-by-default near-black background (#0A0A0A / slate-950) decorated with large blurred radial-gradient glow blobs in indigo/violet/cyan bleeding from the corners, plus a faint grid or dot overlay.
items.detection: structural: detect a body background near #000-#0B0F1A combined with absolutely-positioned divs carrying `radial-gradient` + heavy `blur()` (>60px) in indigo/violet/cyan, and/or a repeating grid/dot background SVG.
