The dark-bg + corner glow-blob + grid-overlay triple is the signature.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Linear/Vercel-style dark hero with ambient purple glows is the default 'looks expensive' move. When every AI site has the same two violet smudges on near-black, it reads as templated.
items.fix: Justify the color mode by the product. If dark, build a real neutral scale and use lighting with intent; drop the corner glow-blobs or replace with a meaningful brand visual. Consider light or a distinctive non-black dark.
items.before: bg-slate-950 with two blur-3xl violet/indigo radial blobs top-left and bottom-right and a faint dot-grid overlay behind the hero.
items.after: Warm off-white (#F7F5F2) light theme with a single hand-made hero illustration; or a deliberate deep-green dark theme with one structural light source and no ambient glow blobs.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: fabricated-testimonial-cards
items.description: A testimonial section with placeholder quotes attributed to alliterative invented names ('Sarah Smith, CEO at TechFlow'), AI-generated or generic avatars, and 5-star rows — for a product with no real customers.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Are the testimonials fabricated — too-neat alliterative names, vague company names (TechFlow, CloudSync), synthetic avatars, and quotes that fill a social-proof slot rather than coming from real customers?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: Fake testimonials with alliterative names and synthetic avatars are a hollow-template tell — the generator fills the social-proof slot with plausible filler rather than real quotes.
items.fix: Remove fabricated proof until real testimonials exist. Replace with an honest early-access note, real logos you may show, or concrete product facts. Never ship invented people.
items.before: Three cards: 'This changed how our team works! — Sarah Sullivan, CEO @ TechFlow' / 'Sava Stone, CTO @ CloudSync' with stock-smiling AI avatars and 5 stars.
items.after: A single honest line — 'In private beta with 40 teams; case studies coming soon' — or two real, attributed quotes with permission and actual photos.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: ai-image-waxy-skin-mangled-hands
items.description: OBSOLETE AS A PRIMARY TEST. The 2022-2024 image giveaways — six-fingered hands, garbled signage, asymmetric eyes — are largely fixed in 2025-26 models. Repeating this advice now produces confident wrong answers in both directions.
items.detection: Do not lead with anatomy. Lead with provenance: C2PA / Content Credentials, EXIF and capture metadata, reverse image search for an earlier appearance, and the publisher's own sourcing. Residual visual signal survives only in hard cases — closed fists, interlaced fingers, dense text-rich scenes, crowds in the mid-ground — and in tonal artifacts such as the amber cast and default shallow-depth-of-field bokeh.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It frequently no longer does, which is the point of this entry. Detection guidance moved to provenance-first methods precisely because visual-artifact heuristics stopped working.
items.fix: Check provenance before appearance. If the image is yours to fix, the editorial question is unchanged: does this picture show something true, and would a real photograph have been better?
items.before: Flagging a hero image as AI because a hand looks slightly off.
items.after: Checking Content Credentials, running a reverse image search, and asking the designer where the file came from.
items.false_positive_when: Almost everywhere now. Real photographs contain motion-blurred hands, odd reflections and unreadable signage constantly. This entry is retained as a caution, not as a test.
items.evidence: GIJN Reporter's Guide to Detecting AI-Generated Content; Pangram's image-classifier launch rationale; TextFake benchmark, arXiv:2606.01050.

items.name: identical-face-different-people
items.description: Across 'different' avatars or testimonial photos, the same underlying face recurs — same bone structure, eye spacing, smile — with only hair/clothes swapped, plus a shared teal-and-orange grade and creamy bokeh across all images.
items.detection: llm-judge: 'Do the supposedly distinct people share one mean face with cosmetic variation, and do all images share an identical color grade and depth-of-field, indicating one generator produced them?'
items.why_it_reads_ai: A diffusion model collapses toward an attractive mean face, so a batch of generated people look like siblings. The shared grade and identical bokeh confirm one generator made them all.
items.fix: Use distinct real people. If generating, vary seeds/prompts hard and verify faces are genuinely different, or avoid faces entirely. Diversify color grade and depth-of-field.
items.before: Four testimonial avatars that are visibly the same face with different hairstyles, all teal-orange graded with identical background bokeh.
items.after: Four genuinely distinct licensed portraits with varied lighting, framing, and color treatment — or four monogram/initial avatars instead of faces.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: stock-mesh-gradient-background
items.description: The hero or full-page background is a soft multi-stop mesh gradient (pink-purple-blue-teal blend), often the literal default from a mesh-gradient generator, used as decoration unrelated to the brand.
items.detection: structural: detect large conic/radial multi-stop gradients or a mesh-gradient SVG/PNG covering the hero with 3+ pastel stops in the magenta-violet-blue-cyan range, frequently with blur.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Mesh gradients had a moment, so models emit them as instant 'modern' backdrop. A pastel mesh that doesn't echo any brand color is decoration-by-default.
items.fix: Make the background earn its place: a solid brand-tinted surface, a real product visual, a subtle texture, or a gradient built from actual brand colors. Avoid the default rainbow-pastel mesh.
items.before: Full-bleed hero behind the headline is a blurred pink-to-purple-to-cyan mesh gradient lifted from a generator preset.
items.after: Hero sits on a flat warm-neutral surface with a single duotone product screenshot; any gradient uses only the two brand hues at low contrast.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: mixed-icon-sets-one-view
items.description: A single view mixes icon vocabularies: some Lucide line icons, some Heroicons solid, a couple of emoji, maybe a Font Awesome glyph — different stroke weights, corner radii, and fill styles side by side.
items.detection: structural: inventory icon sources in the DOM (lucide-react, @heroicons, react-icons/fa, emoji codepoints, inline SVGs with differing stroke-width). More than one icon system in a viewport, or mixed stroke-width among adjacent icons, is the tell.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generators pull icons from whatever import is handy per snippet, so a page accretes mismatched sets. Humans standardize on one family and weight.
items.fix: Standardize on a single icon library and one style (e.g. Lucide, 1.5px stroke, 24px grid) across the app. Remove emoji from UI. Audit every icon for shared weight, size, and alignment.
items.before: Feature row pairs a Lucide outline Zap (stroke 2), a Heroicons solid LockClosed, and a 🔒 emoji — three visual languages in one line.
items.after: All three are Lucide outline icons at 24px / 1.5px stroke in brand color, optically centered on a shared baseline.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: uncanny-padding-rhythm-uniformity
items.description: Every section uses the exact same vertical padding, every card the same internal padding and gap, every element the same radius token — mechanically uniform rhythm with no focal emphasis or intentional density change.
items.detection: structural: measure section vertical padding and card padding/radius/gap across the page; flag near-zero variance in spacing and radius tokens across semantically different sections (e.g. every section py-20, every card p-6 rounded-2xl gap-6).
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generators apply one spacing scale uniformly because they have no editorial sense of pacing. Designed pages breathe — heroes get more air, dense data less. Perfect evenness feels machine-laid.
items.fix: Introduce intentional rhythm: vary section padding by importance, let a hero be spacious and a table tight, use radius/elevation to signal hierarchy, and add one deliberate irregularity.
items.before: Eight consecutive sections all py-20, every card p-6 rounded-2xl gap-6, identical column widths throughout.
items.after: Hero py-32, feature bento py-24, dense pricing table py-16; a full-bleed quote section breaks the column grid; card radii and padding step with hierarchy.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: badge-pill-now-in-beta
items.description: A small rounded-full pill above the headline with a tiny dot or sparkle and text like 'Now in beta,' 'Introducing X,' or 'New.' Subtle border, muted background, centered — the reflexive hero garnish.
items.detection: structural: detect a rounded-full inline-flex element directly preceding the h1 with a small status dot/icon plus short text (often border-white/10 bg-white/5 text-xs). Its position above a centered h1 plus pill styling is the pattern; also flag text-xs here as failing the 14px legibility floor.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The announcement pill is a Linear/Vercel-ism every generator prepends to heroes automatically, whether or not there's anything to announce. Its presence as default garnish signals templated output.
items.fix: Only show an announcement pill when there is a genuine linkable announcement, and make it a real link. Otherwise delete it. If kept, ensure label text is >=14px or a proper >=600-weight uppercase eyebrow, not text-xs.
items.before: ✨ Now in beta above the centered h1, linking nowhere.
items.after: Either no pill, or a real link pill at 14px to a dated launch post: 'Read: v2 is live ->' — and only when that post exists.
items.false_positive_when: Not yet characterized. Treat as a cue to look, never as evidence of authorship.

items.name: invisible-unicode-artifacts
items.description: Invisible or near-invisible codepoints in the text: U+202F narrow no-break space, zero-width space, word joiner, byte-order mark, soft hyphen. Treat this as evidence the text was PASTED from somewhere, which is not the same as evidence about who wrote it.
items.detection: Count the codepoints. Useful as a normalization step and as a provenance hint, not as an authorship signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It often doesn't any more. U+202F appeared in o3 and o4-mini output in April 2025 and OpenAI removed it within days, calling it a quirk of large-scale reinforcement learning. As of 2026 no mainstream assistant is known to embed hidden characters deliberately.
items.fix: Normalize whitespace before judging anything else, then forget about it. The prose problems are the real work.
items.before: A sentence — with residue in it.
items.after: A sentence — with the residue removed.
items.false_positive_when: Constantly. Microsoft Word emits U+202F and U+00A0 routinely, LaTeX does, French typography requires U+202F before high punctuation by convention, and every web copy-paste carries non-breaking spaces. This was a genuine tell for roughly a week. Treat a hit as 'this was pasted', never as 'a model wrote this'.
items.evidence: OpenAI removed the U+202F behavior days after it was noticed in April 2025; contemporaneous reporting notes Word as a routine source of the same character.

items.name: model-markup-residue
items.description: Vendor scaffolding tokens leaking into shipped text: oaicite, contentReference, turn0search0, attributableIndex (ChatGPT); [cite_start] and (start_span) (Gemini); grok_render_citation_card_json (Grok); ppl-ai-file-upload (Perplexity); lenticular brackets in DeepSeek output.
items.detection: Literal token match against the closed vendor list. Essentially zero false positives outside a document about this very topic.
items.why_it_reads_ai: These are the model's own internal citation and rendering markup. Nobody writes them; they survive a copy-paste that nobody proofread.
items.fix: Grep and delete. Then check whether the citation each token was attached to points at anything real, because it frequently does not.
items.before: The study found a 40% reduction :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}.
items.after: Kobak et al. found a 40% reduction.
items.false_positive_when: Documentation about AI output artifacts (including this catalog) contains these strings deliberately. Wrap such passages in the ignore markers.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing maintains the per-vendor token list.

items.name: tracking-param-residue
items.description: URLs carrying utm_source=chatgpt.com, utm_source=perplexity, or a sibling attribution parameter, pasted straight out of a chat UI.
items.detection: Regex over URLs for utm_source=(chatgpt|openai|perplexity|copilot|claude). A literal fingerprint, not a stylistic inference.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The chat product appends the parameter to links it surfaces. The person pasting never strips it because they never looked at the URL.
items.fix: Strip query parameters from every URL before shipping. While you are in there, open each link and check it says what the sentence claims.
items.before: See the report at https://example.org/report?utm_source=chatgpt.com
items.after: See the report at https://example.org/report
items.false_positive_when: A genuine analytics campaign could in principle use the same parameter value, but no real campaign names itself after a chatbot. Treat a hit as reliable.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing lists utm_source parameters among citation artifacts.

items.name: participial-tail
items.description: A sentence-final present-participial clause bolted onto an already complete sentence, adding commentary instead of information: '..., underscoring its importance', '..., reflecting broader industry trends'.
items.detection: Rate of sentence-final ',' + present participle drawn from a closed set (highlighting, underscoring, emphasizing, reflecting, showcasing, demonstrating, symbolizing, positioning, signaling, cementing, solidifying, fostering, cultivating, encompassing, enhancing, contributing, ensuring, marking). Measured as a rate per 100 words, never as presence.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Measured at 5.3x the human rate with a paired effect size of d=1.38, the top-ranked discriminating feature across a 66-feature grammatical tagset. Wikipedia's editors independently named the same pattern 'superficial analysis': significance asserted without a fact behind it.
items.fix: Delete the clause, or promote it to its own sentence with a subject and a claim someone could check. If it cannot survive being made a standalone assertion, it was filler.
items.before: The library reopened in 2019, underscoring the town's commitment to public education.
items.after: The library reopened in 2019. Voters had approved the bond twice.
items.false_positive_when: Academic and journalistic registers use participial clauses legitimately, and a single one is not a tell. Flag on rate, and never on one instance.
items.evidence: Reinhart et al., PNAS 122 e2422455122 (2025); Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Superficial analysis.

items.name: nominalization-density
items.description: Verbs converted into abstract nouns and propped up with a weak verb: 'the implementation of', 'provides an enhancement to', 'the utilization of'.
items.detection: Count -tion/-sion/-ment/-ance/-ence/-ization suffixes per 100 words. Pure morphology, no topical list.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Measured at roughly twice the human rate. Instruction tuning specifically rewards an informationally dense, noun-heavy register, and the model carries it into genres where it misfits.
items.fix: Turn the noun back into a verb and give it a subject.
items.before: The implementation of the new caching layer resulted in a reduction in latency.
items.after: We added a caching layer. Latency dropped.
items.false_positive_when: Legal, academic, and specification writing are legitimately nominal; a standards document will exceed any threshold honestly. Scope this to prose meant to be read for pleasure or persuasion.
items.evidence: Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025 (2.1x, d=1.23); Abdulhai et al., arXiv:2603.18161 (14-27% relative noun increase under LLM editing).

items.name: copula-avoidance
items.description: Systematic replacement of 'is' and 'are' with inflated substitutes: serves as, stands as, functions as, represents, boasts, features, maintains, offers.
items.detection: Count the closed substitute set against plain copulas and flag when substitutes exceed roughly a third of copular positions.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Grammatical rather than lexical, so it survives the synonym-swapping that defeats word lists. Wikipedia's cleanup project lists copula avoidance as a top-level sign.
items.fix: Restore the copula. If the sentence feels thin with 'is', the problem is the claim, not the verb.
items.before: The building serves as the headquarters of the agency and features a restored atrium.
items.after: The building is the agency's headquarters. Its atrium was restored in 2011.
items.false_positive_when: 'Serves as' is correct when a thing genuinely stands in for another. Real-estate and museum copy have used 'boasts' sincerely for a century.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Avoidance of basic copulas.

items.name: deontic-softening
items.description: Obligation expressed in procedural modals rather than interpersonal ones: 'cannot' where a person writes 'can't', 'need to' where a person writes 'have to', and a general shortfall of 'should'.
items.detection: Ratio of personal deontic modals (should, have to, has to, had to, ought to) to procedural ones (must, need to, cannot, is required to).
items.why_it_reads_ai: Across eleven models the personal deontic modals sit near the 4th percentile of underuse, more underused than 96% of common vocabulary, so it is not a generic frequency artifact. Humans giving advice use them at roughly three times the model rate.
items.fix: Use the modal a person would say out loud. 'Can't' not 'cannot'; 'have to' not 'need to'; say 'should' when you mean should.
items.before: Users cannot modify the config directly; they need to submit a change request.
items.after: You can't edit the config directly — you have to file a change request.
items.false_positive_when: Legal, safety, and standards writing use 'must' and 'shall' deliberately and correctly. RFC-style documents will fail this check by design.
items.evidence: Hart, Allred, Abbas & Alugo, arXiv:2608.18144 (2026), eleven-model replication.

items.name: pronoun-evacuation
items.description: First- and second-person pronouns stripped out, so the writer disappears from their own sentences.
items.detection: First/second-person pronoun density per 100 words, compared against the author's own baseline where one is available.
items.why_it_reads_ai: LLM editing removes 40-61% of pronouns, and voice-preserving prompts recover only 10-15% of that. Users have far more leverage over what a model adds than over what it removes.
items.fix: Put the person back. If the sentence describes something someone did, decided, or saw, name them as the subject.
items.before: The decision was ultimately made to postpone the launch.
items.after: I postponed the launch.
items.false_positive_when: Encyclopedic, technical-reference and news registers exclude first person by convention and should never be flagged for it.
items.evidence: Abdulhai et al., arXiv:2603.18161; van Nuenen, arXiv:2604.22142 (d=-0.57 across 300 personal narratives).

items.name: comma-inflation
items.description: Parenthetical smoothing: every clause acquires an appositive, every sentence a mid-sentence aside.
items.detection: Commas per 100 words. Weak standalone; meaningful as a delta against the author's own earlier drafts.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Measured at +66.6% comma frequency under LLM rewriting, travelling with dash inflation as one punctuation-smoothing dimension.
items.fix: Break the sentence in two instead of adding a clause to it.
items.before: The migration, which had been planned for months, finally shipped, though not without incident, on a Tuesday.
items.after: The migration shipped on a Tuesday. We had been planning it for months, and it still went wrong.
items.false_positive_when: Plenty of excellent human prose is comma-rich. This is a cue only, and should never be reported above low severity without a baseline.
items.evidence: van Nuenen, arXiv:2604.22142 (d=1.40).

items.name: specificity-starvation
items.description: Confident copy about nothing: no proper nouns, no numbers, no dates, nothing a reader could check, date, or attribute.
items.detection: Count mid-sentence capitalized tokens plus numerals per 100 words. Counting specificity is possible; classifying vagueness is not.
items.why_it_reads_ai: People write from particulars — a name, a number, a Tuesday. A model writes from the average of everything, and the average has no particulars in it.
items.fix: Add the specifics you actually know: who, how many, when, which version. If you cannot, you may not have anything to say yet.
items.before: Many teams have found that adopting modern tooling significantly improves their workflow.
items.after: Three of the four teams that moved to Bazel cut CI time from 22 minutes to under 6.
items.false_positive_when: Conceptual, philosophical and instructional writing legitimately carries few proper nouns. A tutorial explaining recursion is not starved; it is abstract on purpose.
items.evidence: Follows from the excess-vocabulary finding that 2024 marker words shifted from content words to style words (Kobak et al., Science Advances 2025).

items.name: challenges-and-future-directions
items.description: The obligatory penultimate move: a 'Challenges and Future Directions' / 'Future Outlook' section whose body runs 'Despite its X, it faces challenges... Despite these challenges, it continues to...'.
items.detection: Heading regex over the closed set, plus body regex for 'Despite (its|these|the)'.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A rigid formula that ends in speculative positive assessment regardless of subject. The model is completing a document template, not finishing a thought.
items.fix: Delete the section. If a real open problem exists, state it as a specific unresolved question with a name attached to it.
items.before:
## Challenges and Future Directions

Despite its rapid growth, the project faces challenges typical of open-source ecosystems.
items.after: Maintainer burnout is the live risk: two of the three core committers stepped back in 2024 and neither has been replaced.
items.false_positive_when: Grant proposals and review articles have a genuine, long-standing convention of a future-work section. Judge the body, not the heading, in those genres.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Outline-like conclusions.

items.name: horizontal-rule-spam
items.description: A thematic break inserted between every section of a document.
items.detection: Count standalone --- / *** / ___ lines outside code fences.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Markdown-shaped training: the model emits a document template rather than a document, and the rule is a boundary it does not trust the prose to signal.
items.fix: Delete them. If two sections need separating, the heading already does it.
items.before:
...end of section.

---

## Next section
items.after:
...end of section.

## Next section
items.false_positive_when: A single rule before a footer, an afterword, or a scene break in fiction is ordinary typography. Three or more across one document is the signal.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Thematic breaks; Freeburg, arXiv:2603.27006, finds markdown structural features suppressible to zero under a prose-only instruction, so their presence is an uninstructed default.

items.name: heading-level-skip
items.description: Heading levels jumped rather than nested — H1 straight to H3, or H1s used where H2s belong.
items.detection: Check monotonicity of heading levels in document order; flag jumps of two or more.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The outline was emitted, not read back. A person writing an outline notices the gap because they see the document as a shape.
items.fix: Renumber the headings contiguously.
items.before:
# Overview
### Installation
items.after:
# Overview
## Installation
items.false_positive_when: Some documentation generators legitimately emit skipped levels from templates. Check whether the file is generated before flagging it.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Skipping heading levels.

items.name: heading-spam
items.description: A heading every paragraph or two, labelling single paragraphs rather than organizing sections.
items.detection: Ratio of headings to paragraph-start lines.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is the outline the model was given, left in place. Scaffolding that was never taken down after the building went up.
items.fix: Cut headings that label a single paragraph. Let the prose carry the transitions.
items.before:
## Why speed matters

Speed matters because users leave.

## Why reliability matters

Reliability matters because users return.
items.after: Speed matters because users leave; reliability matters because they come back. Both are the same argument about attention.
items.false_positive_when: Reference documentation and API docs are legitimately heading-dense, because readers arrive by search and leave immediately. Scope to narrative prose.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Excessive headings.

items.name: title-case-heading-uniformity
items.description: Every heading in the document set in Title Case, with no drift.
items.detection: Share of multi-word headings whose significant words are all capitalized.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A house style nobody chose. Human writers drift between sentence case and title case within a document; generators do not drift.
items.fix: Pick sentence case and use it. It reads faster and dates less.
items.before: ## Getting Started With The New Dashboard
items.after: ## Getting started with the new dashboard
items.false_positive_when: Publications with an enforced Title Case style guide (many US magazines, most marketing sites) are following house style correctly. Check the property's other pages first.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:WikiProject AI Cleanup notes heading-case habits among markdown-shaped formatting signs.

items.name: checkmark-bullet-grid
items.description: List items led by status glyphs — checkmarks, crosses, warning triangles, target and lightbulb emoji — turning every claim into a satisfied requirement.
items.detection: Count list lines whose first character is a status dingbat. Kept separate from emoji headings because a single checkmark is a much milder tell than an emoji H2.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It reads as a compliance table rather than as writing. The glyph asserts that each line has been verified, which is exactly the claim the document has not earned.
items.fix: Use a plain list, or a real table if the items genuinely compare along an axis.
items.before:
✅ Fast
✅ Secure
✅ Scalable
items.after: It handles about 4,000 requests a second, runs in our SOC 2 boundary, and has survived two regional failovers.
items.false_positive_when: Migration checklists, test matrices and compatibility tables use these glyphs correctly and legibly. The tell is using them for claims, not for states.
items.evidence: Observed across README and marketing-copy generation; sibling of emoji-section-headers.

items.name: markdown-leak-in-unrendered-medium
items.description: Markdown syntax pasted into a medium that does not render it — a LinkedIn post, an email body, a Slack message, a YouTube description — so the reader sees literal asterisks and hashes.
items.detection: Count **bold** spans and ATX headings in files whose extension does not render markdown.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Nobody typing into that box would produce them. The syntax is a fossil of the interface the text was generated in, and it survives only because no one previewed the result.
items.fix: Strip the syntax and carry the emphasis in the words. If the emphasis cannot survive that, it was decoration.
items.before: **Key takeaway:** we shipped it. ## What's next
items.after: The key takeaway is that we shipped it. Here's what's next.
items.false_positive_when: Plain-text files destined for a markdown renderer, and anything in a repo where .txt files are processed. Check the destination before flagging.
items.evidence: Widely reported by social-platform users; the literal-asterisk artifact is among the most-named giveaways in platform folklore.

items.name: curly-straight-quote-mixing
items.description: Straight and curly quotation marks or apostrophes both used within one document.
items.detection: Count straight vs curly singles and doubles; flag when both appear at least twice.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Two sources were pasted together. Typed text uses whatever the editor produces; model output uses the other. Consistency is the default within any single writing process.
items.fix: Normalize to one style across the document, then keep it.
items.before: The team's “big bet” was the company's "only bet".
items.after: The team's “big bet” was the company's “only bet”.
items.false_positive_when: Code samples and technical documentation legitimately mix, because code requires straight quotes and prose wants curly. Exclude fenced regions before counting — the detector does.
items.evidence: Widely-reported paste artifact; corroborates the invisible-codepoint family.

items.name: ai-default-token-repetition
items.description: Utility-class tokens repeated across every surface: backdrop-blur, rounded-2xl, bg-gradient-to-r, bg-clip-text, from-indigo, bg-grid-, animate-pulse.
items.detection: Count occurrences of each token in markup. These are structured code identifiers, so counting them is not free-text classification.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The unstyled style of generated UI: the treatment was applied everywhere rather than designed once. Defaults cluster, and the cluster is the tell, not any single token.
items.fix: Keep each effect where it earns its place. Design one deliberate surface treatment and reuse that one.
items.before: Every card: rounded-2xl backdrop-blur bg-gradient-to-r
items.after: One elevated surface with a chosen radius and a real shadow; everything else flat.
items.false_positive_when: A design system that deliberately standardizes on a radius token will repeat it everywhere, correctly. Check whether a token file defines the choice.
items.evidence: Observed across v0/Lovable/Bolt output; see the AI Design Slop catalog in sources.

items.name: decorative-section-divider
items.description: ASCII-art banner comments partitioning a source file into labelled sections.
items.detection: Count comment lines made of runs of =, *, ~ or - , with or without a centered label.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The generated outline made visible. The model organizes a file the way it organizes a document, with signposting rather than structure.
items.fix: Check the surrounding files first. If they have no banners, delete these; if a file needs sectioning this badly, it needs splitting.
items.after: (no banner; the helpers live in their own module)
items.false_positive_when: Many long-standing C and Python codebases use banner comments as house style. This is only a tell as drift from the repo's own convention, which is why it is low severity.
items.evidence: Rule OBVIOUS_HEADER in the grain anti-slop linter; corroborated by maintainer style guides.

items.name: emoji-in-code
items.description: Emoji in source files — log strings, comments, commit-adjacent scaffolding.
items.detection: Emoji codepoints on non-docstring source lines.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generated code decorates its own output. A human adds an emoji to a log line when the team already does; a generator adds one because the training data did.
items.fix: Check the repo's own convention first. If there isn't one, remove them — they break alignment in terminals and grep output.
items.before: print("✅ Migration complete!")
items.after: print("migration complete: 412 rows, 2.1s")
items.false_positive_when: Repos that mandate emoji in conventional-commit types or log levels are following their own documented spec. Flag only on introduction into a file or repo without the convention.
items.evidence: Rule set of the grain anti-slop linter; several repos' commit specs mandate the opposite.

items.name: stance-neutralization
items.description: The piece surveys both sides and lands nowhere. An argument becomes a balanced overview; a recommendation becomes 'it depends on your needs'.
items.detection: Ask: does this text commit to a position the author could be wrong about? Name that position in one sentence, or report that there isn't one.
items.why_it_reads_ai: In a randomized controlled trial, heavy LLM use produced a 68.9% increase in essays that stayed neutral on the topic question rather than arguing either way (p=0.017). This is the tell readers actually resent, because it wastes their time.
items.fix: Make the writer state the claim they would defend, put it in the first paragraph, and cut the counterweight paragraph added to 'balance' it. Balance is a virtue in a survey and a defect in an argument.
items.before: Both approaches have merit, and the right choice depends on your team's context and priorities.
items.after: Use Postgres. The Mongo case only wins if your schema genuinely changes weekly, and yours doesn't.
items.false_positive_when: Surveys, literature reviews, explainers and neutral-point-of-view reference writing are supposed to be even-handed. Ask what genre the piece is before flagging.
items.evidence: Abdulhai et al., arXiv:2603.18161; Shrinking Landscape of Linguistic Diversity, arXiv:2502.11266.

items.name: register-leveling
items.description: The same voice regardless of genre: a Slack message, a postmortem and a wedding toast all arrive in the same measured explanatory register.
items.detection: Name the genre this text is written in. Then name the genre it is FOR. Do they match?
items.why_it_reads_ai: Instruction tuning produces a fixed, informationally dense register that models carry into every genre, even when explicitly prompted to match informal speech. The literature calls the result genre misalignment.
items.fix: Name the target genre out loud, then cut everything that belongs to a different one.
items.before: A Slack message reading: 'Great question. There are a few considerations worth weighing here. First,...'
items.after: yeah it's the pool config. i'll patch it after standup
items.false_positive_when: Some writers genuinely have one register and use it everywhere, and house styles enforce uniformity on purpose. Judge against the destination, not against variety for its own sake.
items.evidence: Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025; Muñoz-Ortiz et al., AI Review 57:267 (2024), on register leveling.

items.name: epistemic-rhetorical-miscalibration
items.description: Rhetorical intensity out of proportion to evidential grounding: confident emphasis attached to claims with nothing underneath them.
items.detection: For each emphatic claim, ask what evidence the text offers for it. Flag emphasis with no substrate.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This is the mechanism under 'it sounds authoritative and says nothing'. Measured as form-meaning divergence across 225 argumentative texts spanning expert, non-expert and generated writing.
items.fix: Either supply the evidence or drop the intensity. Usually dropping it is the honest move and the sentence survives.
items.before: This is absolutely critical to get right, and the consequences of ignoring it cannot be overstated.
items.after: Get this wrong and the migration silently drops rows, which is what happened to us in March.
items.false_positive_when: Polemic and opinion writing are supposed to be intense, and a strong claim with a named stake behind it is good writing, not miscalibration.
items.evidence: arXiv:2604.19768, framework for quantifying epistemic-rhetorical miscalibration.

items.name: vague-attribution
items.description: Claims sourced to an unnamed collective: 'Industry reports suggest', 'Experts argue', 'Observers have noted', 'Some critics contend'.
items.detection: For each such frame, ask whether a named, checkable source is attached within the sentence. Distinct from the unattributed-quote entry, which concerns quotation marks; this concerns unquoted claims.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Presenting one source, or none, as a widely-held consensus. It is a hole in the text wearing the costume of a hedge.
items.fix: Name the source or delete the claim. 'Experts' with no expert is not a hedge.
items.before: Industry observers have noted that adoption is accelerating.
items.after: Gartner put 2025 adoption at 34%, up from 19% in 2023.
items.false_positive_when: Genuinely uncontroversial background ('most linguists agree') is ordinary prose, and a named source appearing in the next sentence resolves it. Read the paragraph, not the clause.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Vague attributions and overgeneralization.

items.name: citation-pathology
items.description: References that exist but do not do their job: DOIs resolving to an unrelated paper, invalid DOIs and ISBNs, links to search results rather than documents, named refs declared and never used, and refs attached to sentences they do not support.
items.detection: Structural for the mechanical subset (DOI/ISBN checksum, HTTP status, '/search?q=' in an href, unused named refs). Judge for the one that matters: does the cited source actually support the sentence it is attached to?
items.why_it_reads_ai: Models use legitimate sources inappropriately and invent plausible ones. Wikipedia's cleanup guidance is emphatic that the highest-yield check is not style at all — it is opening the citations.
items.fix: Open every reference. Delete or replace any that does not support its sentence.
items.before: Latency fell 40% after the migration.[12]  (ref 12 is a 2011 paper about a different system)
items.after: Latency fell 40% after the migration (our own p99 dashboard, 12-19 March).
items.false_positive_when: Almost none, and note this is the ONE finding class in this catalog that is about truth rather than authorship. Act on it with full confidence — you are checking a claim, not inferring an author.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:WikiProject AI Cleanup.

items.name: adjective-inflation
items.description: Nouns arriving pre-modified — comprehensive framework, robust solution, seamless integration, significant improvement — where the bare noun carries the same information.
items.detection: Judge each evaluative adjective: does it carry a measurement, or does it stand in for one? A structural proxy is adjective-to-noun ratio against the author's own baseline.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Measured at 40-87% increases in adjective use even under explicit 'minimal edits' prompts, against a human-editor baseline of under 5% change in any part-of-speech category. This is one of the clearest 'the model cannot help itself' findings available.
items.fix: Delete the adjective. If the sentence loses meaning, replace it with the number or fact the adjective was standing in for.
items.before: A comprehensive suite of robust integration tests significantly improved reliability.
items.after: We added 340 integration tests. Escaped defects fell from 11 to 2 per release.
items.false_positive_when: Marketing copy has used evaluative adjectives sincerely for a century, and some of these words are load-free house vocabulary in a given field. The tell is density, not any one word.
items.evidence: Abdulhai et al., arXiv:2603.18161.

items.name: elegant-variation
items.description: The model refuses to repeat a word, so 'the router' becomes 'the routing component', then 'this networking element', then 'the aforementioned module' — four names for one thing.
items.detection: List every distinct noun phrase used for the same referent. Flag referents carrying three or more names.
items.why_it_reads_ai: LLM rewriting measurably INCREASES lexical diversity (MTLD +52.7%, d=1.59). Technical writing wants the opposite: one name per thing. The model is optimizing a metric readers experience as noise.
items.fix: Pick one name per referent and use it every time. Repetition is a feature in exposition.
items.before: The router forwards the packet. This networking component then hands the datagram to the aforementioned module.
items.after: The router forwards the packet, then hands it to the scheduler.
items.false_positive_when: Literary prose legitimately varies its nouns, and pronouns are not elegant variation. Scope this to technical and reference writing.
items.evidence: van Nuenen, arXiv:2604.22142; Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Historical indicators.

items.name: notability-padding
items.description: Canned proof-of-importance: 'has been featured in local, regional, and national media outlets', 'garnered coverage in trade publications', 'maintains a strong digital presence'.
items.detection: Judge whether any outlet, piece, or date is named. The pattern is performing the criteria for importance rather than reporting a fact.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model is satisfying an implied notability requirement rather than describing anything. Outside an encyclopedia it reads as an about-page protesting too much.
items.fix: Name the outlet and the piece, or cut it.
items.before: Her work has been featured in numerous regional and national publications.
items.after: The Star Tribune profiled her in 2022.
items.false_positive_when: A press page listing real, linked coverage is doing its job. The tell is the unnamed plural.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Canned emphasis on notability.

items.name: connection-vagueness
items.description: Relationships stated indirectly rather than claimed: 'in connection with', 'associated with', 'has been linked to', 'widely associated with'.
items.detection: Judge whether a verb could replace the frame. If 'X founded Y' works, the hedge was doing nothing.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A model hedging a relationship it cannot verify. It reads as legal-department prose in contexts with no legal department.
items.fix: State the relationship with a verb.
items.before: Chen is widely associated with the founding of the lab.
items.after: Chen founded the lab in 2014.
items.false_positive_when: Legal, journalistic and medical writing hedge causation deliberately and correctly — 'linked to' is the honest verb when causation is unproven.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Vague expression of connection.

items.name: title-echo
items.description: The document repeats its own title as its first heading, or opens by restating the title as a sentence.
items.detection: Compare the first heading, and the first sentence, against the document title.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Markdown-shaped training: the model emits a self-contained document that re-announces itself, because in its training the title and the body were separate contexts.
items.fix: Delete the echo and open on the first real sentence.
items.before:
# Caching in Production

## Caching in Production

Caching in production is an important topic.
items.after:
# Caching in Production

We cache three things, and two of them were mistakes.
items.false_positive_when: Some publishing systems require an H1 matching the front-matter title, and generated docs sites do this legitimately.
items.evidence: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, Title heading.

items.name: commit-body-restates-diff
items.description: A commit body enumerating, file by file, what the diff already shows, instead of explaining why the change exists.
items.detection: Compare the body's content lines against the changed file and symbol names from git show --stat. High one-to-one overlap plus no causal connective (because, so that, was breaking) is the flag. Also flag bodies whose bullets are '- **<filename>**: <restated change>'.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model has the diff in context and nothing else, so restating it is the only content it can safely produce. Humans write commit bodies precisely for the information that is NOT in the diff.
items.fix: Delete the enumeration. Keep one paragraph: the problem, why this approach, what you rejected. If the body only restates the diff, use a one-line subject and no body.
items.before:
This commit introduces a comprehensive authentication system.
- **auth/login.py**: Added the login() function
- **auth/models.py**: Added the User model
items.after:
Add password login

Sessions were cookie-only, so the mobile client had no way in. Issues a 24h JWT; refresh comes in a follow-up.
items.false_positive_when: A long body is correct on a large or subtle change. The tell is restatement, not length.
items.evidence: grain anti-slop linter rules VAGUE_COMMIT / NO_CONTEXT; astronomer-cosmos AGENTS.md ('explain what and why, not how').

items.name: commit-subject-scale-adjective
items.description: A commit subject reaching for scale words the diff does not earn: comprehensive, robust, enhanced, complete, production-ready, streamlined, optimal.
items.detection: Closed scale-adjective set matched against git log --format=%s, joined with diff size. One of these words on a diff under ~50 lines is near-certain. Subjects over 72 characters are a second signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Models self-grade inside the artifact. 'Comprehensive' is a confidence assertion rather than a description, and it appears at a rate no human log matches.
items.fix: Cut every adjective. Verb, object, imperative, under 50 characters.
items.before: feat(retry): implement comprehensive and robust retry mechanism for enhanced reliability
items.after: Retry failed uploads with backoff
items.false_positive_when: A genuinely comprehensive change can say so. Check the diff size before believing the adjective — that join is the whole detector.
items.evidence: grain VAGUE_COMMIT; NetExec AI policy on generated verbosity.

items.name: convention-drift-in-commit-style
items.description: Conventional Commits appearing in a repo whose history does not use them — or a bare sentence subject in a repo that enforces them. The mismatch is the tell, never the format.
items.detection: Share of the last 200 subjects matching the conventional-commit prefix. If that share is under 15% and the new commit matches, flag; if over 85% and it does not, flag. Same test for capitalization, trailing period, and imperative-versus-past mood.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Conventional Commits dominate training data, so it is the model's default whatever the repo does. A human reads git log before their first commit; a model does not unless told.
items.fix: Run git log --oneline -30 and match the house format exactly, including case and mood.
items.before: (in a repo whose log is all 'Fix crash when profile is missing') feat(profiles): add per-profile override script support
items.after: Add per-profile override scripts
items.false_positive_when: Conventional Commits in a repo that uses Conventional Commits is correct and often hook-enforced. Only drift from the repo's own log is a tell — which is exactly why this check is near-zero false positive.
items.evidence: astronomer-cosmos AGENTS.md forbids the prefixes; flclash enforces them via commit-msg hook. Both are right for their repo.

items.name: agent-attribution-trailer
items.description: Agent signature footers left in commits and PR bodies: 'Generated with <tool>', 'Co-Authored-By: <agent>', 'Assisted-by:', 'Codex Task'.
items.detection: Literal-string grep. Zero false positives on detection — but this is a POLICY question, not a quality one, so detect and ask rather than strip.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is a literal signature. It also injects a non-person into git shortlog and the repository's contributor graph.
items.fix: Check the repo first: grep -ri 'co-authored-by|generated with|assisted-by' AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md CONTRIBUTING.md .github/. Strip if unmentioned or banned; keep if mandated. Removing an honest disclosure line can violate a project's policy — roughly forty projects in the public contribution-policy survey REQUIRE disclosure.
items.before: Co-Authored-By: <agent> <noreply@example.com>
items.after: (removed, or replaced with the repo's mandated form, e.g. Assisted-by: <tool>:<model>)
items.false_positive_when: Repos that mandate the trailer. This entry exists to make you look it up, not to make you delete it.
items.evidence: matecat CLAUDE.md bans all AI references; libusb/hidapi AGENTS.md mandates an Assisted-by line; astronomer-cosmos wants visible credit. The correct behavior is repo-dependent.

items.name: agent-namespaced-branch
items.description: Branch names prefixed with an agent namespace (claude/, codex/, copilot/, cursor/, ai/, bot/) or suffixed with a session hash or timestamp.
items.detection: Regex on the branch name for the namespace prefixes and for a trailing hex or ISO-timestamp suffix.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Tool defaults, not human naming. They survive into the merge commit and the PR URL, so they outlive the diff.
items.fix: Rename to what the branch does: kebab-case, explicit, brief.
items.before: claude/fix-auth-20260914-a3f91c2
items.after: fix-session-expiry
items.false_positive_when: Teams that deliberately namespace agent branches for routing or cleanup are doing something sensible. Check the repo's branch list.
items.evidence: libusb/hidapi AGENTS.md explicitly forbids agent-derived branch namespaces.

items.name: pr-scaffold-without-template
items.description: The Summary / Changes / Test Plan scaffold appearing in a repo with no pull-request template asking for it, often where the repo's other PRs are two sentences.
items.detection: Check for .github/pull_request_template.md. If absent, flag bodies carrying two or more of the canonical headings. Second signal: heading count against the median of the repo's last 20 merged PRs.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is the default scaffold baked into agent PR-authoring prompts. It reads as ceremony imported from another repo, which is what it is.
items.fix: Read three recently merged PRs and match them. Most repos want what changed, why, and how you know it works — as prose.
items.before: ## Summary / ## Changes (7 bullets) / ## Test plan / ## Related, in a repo whose merged PRs average 30 words.
items.after: Sessions expired at 24h regardless of remember_me. Reads the flag now and sets 30d. Verified by logging in with the box ticked and checking the cookie's Max-Age.
items.false_positive_when: A repo WITH that template, obviously — and long descriptions on genuinely large changes. The check is against the repo's own norm.
items.evidence: Aurelia's AI stance: 'Tell us what changed and how you know it works.' llama.cpp rejects fully-generated PR descriptions outright.

items.name: unverified-test-plan
items.description: A Test Plan of ticked checkboxes where nothing was run, or where the 'tests' restate the change rather than record an execution.
items.detection: Structural pre-filter: ticked boxes under a Test heading with no CI run, no pasted command output, no attached artifact. Then judge: does each ticked line name a command, an environment, and an observed result?
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model cannot run anything, so it writes the SHAPE of verification. A ticked box is an affirmative claim a maintainer will act on, which is why this is the tell that actually burns trust.
items.fix: Only tick what you ran. Paste the command and its output. If you could not run it, say so explicitly — that direction of honesty is itself strong evidence a person wrote it.
items.before:
- [x] All 25 existing tests pass
- [x] Backward compatibility maintained
items.after: Ran `pytest tests/auth -q`: 25 passed in 3.1s. Did NOT run the e2e suite — no Docker in this environment.
items.false_positive_when: A thorough test plan naming real commands, versions and what could NOT be verified is the opposite of a tell. Never flag a plan for being long.
items.evidence: Maintainer complaints across llama.cpp, curl and RPCS3 threads; the honest counter-example is codex-authored PR phodal/routa#158.

items.name: verbosity-disproportionate-to-diff
items.description: A PR description whose length bears no relation to the size or subtlety of the change.
items.detection: Ratio of description words to changed lines, against the repo's own median. A ratio, never a length cap.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generated prose has no cost function for length, so it defaults to thorough. Human effort tracks stakes.
items.fix: Cut to what a reviewer needs in order to start reading the diff.
items.before: 900 words on a 4-line config change.
items.after: Bumps the pool size from 5 to 20. We were queueing at 12 concurrent requests.
items.false_positive_when: 900 words on a 4,000-line migration is proportionate. This is a ratio check and breaks immediately if used as a word limit.
items.evidence: Identified in the engineering-lane survey as one of three highest-precision relative checks.

items.name: review-restates-the-diff
items.description: A review comment that describes back what the diff does, or praises it, without taking a position on whether it is right.
items.detection: Judge: does this comment contain a claim the author could disagree with? If not, it is not review.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model has the diff and no stake. Restating is the only safe output. 'LGTM! Great work!' on a 600-line change is the pure form.
items.fix: Delete it. A review comment should name a risk, a question, or a required change.
items.before: LGTM! Great work on this refactor — the new structure is much cleaner.
items.after: This drops the retry on 429. Was that deliberate? The upstream rate-limits us at 50rps.
items.false_positive_when: A short genuine approval after a real read is fine, and some teams require an explicit LGTM to unblock the queue. The tell is approval plus summary plus nothing else.
items.evidence: Maintainer commentary across HN threads on AI review bots; grain THANKS_OPENER rule.

items.name: confident-wrong-security-finding
items.description: A security or correctness finding, stated with full confidence and correct-sounding vocabulary, that is wrong about this codebase.
items.detection: Judge: does the finding cite a specific line, a specific reachable input, and a specific consequence? Generated findings name a vulnerability CLASS and assert it applies.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Security vocabulary is highly patterned, so it generates fluently without any of the reasoning that would make it true. This has been costly enough that curl's maintainer publicly documented the burden of AI bug-bounty slop.
items.fix: Require a proof of reachability before filing: the input, the path, the observed effect. If you cannot produce one, do not file it.
items.before: This code is vulnerable to SQL injection via string concatenation.  (the line uses a parameterized query)
items.after: (not filed — the query is parameterized at db/users.py:42)
items.false_positive_when: Real findings also sound confident. Judge the presence of a reachability proof, not the tone.
items.evidence: Daniel Stenberg's public accounts of AI-generated curl bug-bounty reports.

items.name: try-catch-just-in-case
items.description: Defensive exception handling wrapped around code that cannot meaningfully fail, or that should fail loudly.
items.detection: Count broad handlers (except Exception, catch (e)) per file; three or more in one file is the documented working threshold. Join with whether the wrapped call touches a real boundary.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model cannot run the code, so it hedges. The result converts a crash you could debug into a silence you cannot.
items.fix: Validate at boundaries, trust types internally. Handle the exception you can actually name.
items.after: total = a + b
items.false_positive_when: Network, IPC, subprocess, file I/O and user-input parsing all need handling. The rule is 'no try/catch just in case', not 'no try/catch'.
items.evidence: slop_scan P1 threshold (>=3 except Exception per file); Paseo's contributor rules.

items.name: single-impl-abstraction
items.description: An interface, abstract base class or strategy pattern with exactly one implementation and no named second one coming.
items.detection: Count concrete subclasses or implementors per declared interface.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generated code performs architecture. The abstraction is a pattern the model has seen rather than a seam the problem has.
items.fix: Inline it. Add the interface when the second implementation exists.
items.before: class StorageBackend(ABC): ...  # one subclass: LocalStorage
items.after: class LocalStorage: ...
items.false_positive_when: A plugin interface with one bundled implementation plus a real external one is justified, and test doubles count as a second implementor. This is a warning in every linter that ships it, for exactly that reason.
items.evidence: grain SINGLE_IMPL_ABC (severity: warn).

items.name: hallucinated-import-or-api
items.description: Calls to functions, flags, endpoints or packages that do not exist — including imports of packages never published, which is the attack surface behind slopsquatting.
items.detection: Resolve every import against the lockfile and every called symbol against the installed package. Fully mechanical.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model generates the API it expects to exist. Plausible names are exactly what it is good at.
items.fix: Run the resolver. Then check the package actually exists on the registry and is the one you meant — a hallucinated import name is a supply-chain hazard, not just a bug.
items.before: from requests.utils import parse_retry_after
items.after: from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
items.false_positive_when: Optional dependencies behind a try/except ImportError, and symbols added in a newer version than the lockfile pins.
items.evidence: aicodeaudit ACA4xx rule class; published slopsquatting research.

items.name: stale-training-api
items.description: Code written against an API version that was current in the training data and has since changed — deprecated call signatures, removed flags, superseded client libraries.
items.detection: Judge against the installed version's changelog. Deprecation warnings at runtime are the cheapest structural signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model's knowledge has a date. It writes the most-represented version, which is the most-documented one, which is rarely the newest.
items.fix: Check the installed version's docs, not the first search result. Pin the version in the file's header comment if the API is volatile.
items.before: openai.ChatCompletion.create(...)
items.after: client.chat.completions.create(...)
items.false_positive_when: Deliberately pinned old versions, and compatibility shims that support both.
items.evidence: aicodeaudit ACA3xx stale-training-data API rule class.

items.name: idiom-drift-within-file
items.description: A block of code whose idiom does not match the file around it: different naming convention, different error handling, different import style, different comment density.
items.detection: Compare the changed hunk's conventions against the rest of the file: naming case, quote style, type-annotation coverage, comment density, error-handling shape. Purely relative.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model writes its own idiom rather than the file's, because it optimizes the snippet rather than the codebase. A human who reads the surrounding code passes this automatically.
items.fix: Read fifty lines above and below, then rewrite the hunk in that idiom.
items.before: A snake_case file gaining a camelCase helper with full type hints and a docstring, where nothing else is annotated.
items.after: The same helper, snake_case, unannotated, matching its neighbours.
items.false_positive_when: Deliberate modernization is real, and a file mid-migration is legitimately mixed. Check whether the drift is toward a documented target.
items.evidence: One of the three highest-precision relative checks in the engineering survey; kubb's deslop skill frames the whole class as making the diff 'match the surrounding file and this repo's conventions'.

items.name: mock-assertion-test
items.description: Tests that assert a mock was called rather than that behavior happened.
items.detection: Count assertions that are assert_called / toHaveBeenCalled against assertions on returned values or observable state.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model can see the implementation and mirrors it. The test then passes for any refactor that keeps the call and breaks the behavior — which is the exact inverse of what a test is for.
items.fix: Assert the outcome. If the outcome is unobservable, the seam is in the wrong place.
items.before: assert mock_send.assert_called_once_with(user.email)
items.after: assert outbox[0].to == 'sam@example.com'
items.false_positive_when: Verifying an interaction with a genuine external boundary (an email really was queued, a webhook really fired) is legitimate mock assertion.
items.evidence: slop_scan and grain test-quality rules.

items.name: hollow-assertion
items.description: Assertions that cannot fail: assert True, assert result == result, assert x is not None as the only check, tests with no assertion at all.
items.detection: Mechanical pattern match on the assertion expression.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Test-shaped output. The file satisfies a coverage target and proves nothing.
items.fix: Assert the value you expect. If you do not know what to expect, you do not yet know what the function is for.
items.before:
result = parse(payload)
assert result is not None
items.after: assert parse(payload).currency == 'EUR'
items.false_positive_when: A smoke test whose only job is 'this import does not explode' is legitimate, if it says so.
items.evidence: slop_scan P-class hollow-assertion rules.

items.name: fabricated-doc-claims
items.description: Documentation describing an architecture the code does not have, platforms nobody tested, or features that are restatements of function names.
items.detection: Judge each claim against the code. Feature bullets that are function names with spaces inserted are the reliable structural signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model documents the system it would have built. Nothing in the generation loop checks the doc against the repo.
items.fix: Delete every claim you have not personally verified. A short true README beats a long aspirational one.
items.before:
## Features
- Robust caching layer
- Seamless cross-platform support (Windows, macOS, Linux, BSD)
items.after:
## Features
- In-memory cache with a 60s TTL
- Tested on macOS 15 and Ubuntu 24.04. Windows is untested.
items.false_positive_when: Roadmap sections clearly marked as planned. The tell is aspiration presented in the present tense.
items.evidence: Widely reported in maintainer AI-contribution policies.

items.name: unwired-badge-row
items.description: A README badge row advertising CI, coverage, npm version or a license that is not wired up, points at a different repo, or renders broken.
items.detection: Resolve each badge URL and each link target. Mechanical.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Badges are the most-represented README ornament in training data, so they generate whether or not the services exist.
items.fix: Delete any badge whose service you have not configured. A broken badge is worse than no badge.
items.before: ![build](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/other-org/other-repo/ci.yml)
items.after: (removed until CI exists)
items.false_positive_when: Badges for services that are configured but temporarily failing. Check the target, not the color.

items.name: narrated-theme-statement
items.description: The story stops to explain what it means. A character, or the narration, states the theme outright near the end, usually as a short italicized realization.
items.detection: Find the sentence that tells the reader what the story was about. If cutting it loses nothing but the explanation, it is this.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Fiction earns meaning through event and consequence. A model optimizes for the reader understanding, so it states the conclusion rather than staging it. Discourse-level narrative features like this separate human from AI fiction at 93% macro-F1 with every stylistic cue removed, which is the strongest evidence in this catalog for weighting structure over phrases.
items.fix: Delete the statement. If the story does not already carry the meaning, the problem is upstream in the events.
items.before: She looked at the empty chair and understood, finally, that grief was just love with nowhere left to go.
items.after: She looked at the empty chair. Then she moved it into the hall, where she would not have to see it.
items.false_positive_when: Some literary traditions and most fables state their theme on purpose, and a first-person narrator reflecting is a legitimate mode.
items.evidence: StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136: 61,608 stories, 93.2% macro-F1 from discourse-level narrative features with stylistic cues removed.

items.name: uplift-closing-line
items.description: The piece resolves upward regardless of what came before: a final line of quiet hope, acceptance, or gentle forward motion bolted onto an unresolved story.
items.detection: Read only the last two sentences. Do they belong to this story, or to any story?
items.why_it_reads_ai: Alignment training rewards endings that leave the reader well. The model resolves because resolution is preferred, not because the story reached one.
items.fix: Cut the last paragraph. Most of the time the real ending is two sentences earlier and harder.
items.before: It wouldn't be easy. But for the first time in a long while, she felt ready to try.
items.after: She locked the door behind her and did not check whether it caught.
items.false_positive_when: Plenty of good fiction ends hopefully, and whole genres require it. The tell is uplift that contradicts the story it ends.

items.name: body-sensation-emotion-substitution
items.description: Emotion rendered exclusively as somatic report: her chest tightened, his stomach dropped, a knot formed in her throat, breath she didn't know she was holding.
items.detection: Count somatic-reaction clauses per thousand words and check whether any emotion in the piece is conveyed any other way.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is 'show don't tell' applied as a compulsion. The model has learned the surface rule and applies it uniformly, so every feeling arrives through the same three organs.
items.fix: Let emotion show in what the character does, says, or refuses to say. Keep one somatic beat if it is the right one.
items.before: Her chest tightened. Her stomach dropped. She let out a breath she didn't know she'd been holding.
items.after: She read it twice, put the phone face down, and went back to chopping onions.
items.false_positive_when: Somatic detail is a legitimate and much-taught technique; romance and thriller conventions lean on it hard. Density is the tell, not presence.

items.name: single-register-cast
items.description: Every character speaks in the same voice. Vocabulary, sentence length, humor and hedging are indistinguishable across the cast.
items.detection: Strip the dialogue tags from a scene and ask whether you can still tell who is speaking.
items.why_it_reads_ai: One model, one register. Producing genuinely different idiolects requires holding several different competence and personality models at once, and the default collapses them toward the mean.
items.fix: Give at least two characters a verbal habit the others do not have: a filler, a register, a thing they will not say.
items.before: Two characters who both speak in measured, complete, faintly explanatory sentences.
items.after: One of them interrupts, swears, and never finishes a clause.
items.false_positive_when: Stylized work where uniform dialogue is the point, and some authors genuinely write one voice throughout.

items.name: simile-stacking
items.description: Figurative language arriving in clusters, often two or three comparisons for one image, none of them load-carrying.
items.detection: Count 'like' and 'as if' constructions per page and check whether any of them changes what the reader understands.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Simile is the most legible marker of literary writing, so a model optimizing for literary output produces more of it than any writer would.
items.fix: Keep the one that does work. Delete the others.
items.before: The silence hung like a held breath, like a curtain about to fall, as if the room itself were waiting.
items.after: The silence went on a beat too long.
items.false_positive_when: Some prose stylists genuinely stack figures, and certain genres reward density.

items.name: no-cultural-anchors
items.description: A world with no specific music, brands, slang, politics, or period detail. Everything is legible everywhere, which means it belongs nowhere.
items.detection: List every proper noun and period-specific reference in the piece. A long story with almost none is this.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Specific references risk being wrong or dated, and the model's training rewards safe generality. The result is fiction set in a beige everywhere.
items.fix: Anchor one scene hard: a real song, a real chain restaurant, the year.
items.before: They met at a coffee shop downtown and talked about work.
items.after: They met at the Dunkin' on Mass Ave and argued about whether the Sox should have kept Betts.
items.false_positive_when: Secondary-world fantasy, fable, and allegory deliberately float free of cultural anchors.

items.name: substitutable-reply
items.description: A comment that would fit unchanged under thousands of other posts: it restates the question, offers balanced general advice, and ends with encouragement.
items.detection: Ask whether the reply contains one fact that could only have come from reading THIS post. If not, it is substitutable.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model answers the category, not the post. It is the social equivalent of specificity starvation, and it is what people actually mean when they say a comment feels like a bot.
items.fix: Quote the specific thing you are responding to, and say the thing only you would know.
items.before: That sounds really difficult, and it's completely valid to feel that way. Have you considered talking to a professional about it?
items.after: The part about your manager copying HR on everything is the bit I'd document. Same thing happened to me and the paper trail is what saved it.
items.false_positive_when: Plenty of humans write generic supportive comments, and on advice subreddits that is often the socially correct move.

items.name: credential-persona-opener
items.description: An opener claiming standing that the rest of the comment never uses: 'As someone who has worked in this field for fifteen years', followed by advice available on any search engine.
items.detection: Judge whether the claimed experience produces anything in the body that a non-expert could not have written.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The frame is a rhetorical move the model has learned to perform. A person with fifteen years in a field leaks specifics without being asked.
items.fix: Drop the credential and lead with the specific thing the credential would have taught you.
items.before: As someone who's worked in commercial insurance for over a decade, I'd say it's important to read your policy carefully.
items.after: Check whether your policy has a 72-hour reporting window. Most commercial ones do and it's the single most common reason these get denied.
items.false_positive_when: Establishing standing is a real and useful convention, especially on technical subreddits where it tells readers how to weight the answer.

items.name: textureless-anecdote
items.description: A personal story with no texture: no names, no weather, no dialogue, nothing that could be checked or misremembered. It has a beginning, a lesson, and nothing in between.
items.detection: Ask what detail in this anecdote the teller would have had to actually be there to know.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A model generating an anecdote produces the SHAPE of one, because the details it would invent are the details most likely to be wrong.
items.fix: Add the wrong-seeming detail: the thing that does not serve the point but happened anyway. Real memories have those; invented ones do not.
items.before: I had a manager once who never gave feedback, and it taught me how important communication is.
items.after: Priya gave me exactly one piece of feedback in two years, in a stairwell, about a slide I'd already presented.
items.false_positive_when: Anonymized professional anecdotes are deliberately stripped of detail for good reasons, and some people simply do not tell stories well.

items.name: synthetic-consensus
items.description: A comment asserting what 'most people' or 'the community' thinks, in a thread where that consensus is visibly not present.
items.detection: Check the assertion against the thread it is in.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model reports the aggregate of its training rather than the state of the conversation in front of it. It cannot see the room.
items.fix: Cite the comment you are agreeing or disagreeing with, by what it said.
items.before: I think most people here would agree that the original approach was the better one.
items.after: The top comment says the opposite, and I think it's wrong because...
items.false_positive_when: Sometimes a consensus really is obvious, and long-standing community members can speak to norms accurately.

items.name: subreddit-register-mismatch
items.description: Formal, structured, correctly punctuated prose posted into a venue that runs on fragments, in-jokes and lowercase.
items.detection: Compare the comment's register against its five neighbours in the same thread.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Register leveling, localized. The model writes its one register regardless of where it is posting, and the mismatch is visible because the surrounding comments are right there.
items.fix: Read the room, then write in it.
items.before: A three-paragraph structured answer with a bolded summary, posted in a shitposting thread.
items.after: lol no. the connector melts at like 40 amps
items.false_positive_when: Some people write formally everywhere, including in casual venues, and non-native speakers often write more formally than natives. This is the single most socially destructive check in this catalog to get wrong.

items.name: rhetorical-question-hook
items.description: An opening question the reader did not ask and cannot answer: 'Ever wonder why some teams ship faster than others?'
items.detection: Judge whether the piece opens by asserting something or by asking permission to assert it.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is the safest possible opener: it commits to nothing and flatters the reader's curiosity. Models default to it because it never offends.
items.fix: Open with the claim the question was circling.
items.before: Ever wonder why some teams ship faster than others?
items.after: Teams that ship fast almost always have fewer people in the approval chain, not better engineers.
items.false_positive_when: A genuine question the piece then genuinely answers is a legitimate and old device.

items.name: false-precision-statistic
items.description: A specific-sounding number with no source: '73% of teams report improved collaboration', 'studies show a 3x increase'.
items.detection: Look for the citation. A statistic with a decimal point and no source is the strongest form.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Precision is cheap to generate and expensive to verify. The model produces the shape of evidence because evidence-shaped claims are what its training rewarded.
items.fix: Find the source, or cut the number and make the qualitative claim honestly.
items.before: Studies show that 73% of distributed teams struggle with async communication.
items.after: Every remote team I've worked on has had the same problem with async, and none of us solved it well.
items.false_positive_when: Real statistics are also specific. The tell is the missing source, not the number.

items.name: paragraph-length-monoculture
items.description: Every paragraph is roughly the same length, usually three to four sentences.
items.detection: Coefficient of variation of paragraph length in sentences. Human documents have a one-line paragraph somewhere, and a long one.
items.why_it_reads_ai: People break a paragraph where the idea breaks, which is irregular. A model breaks on a rhythm. Unlike sentence-length variation, this has no published baseline behind it, so the threshold is a judgment call and the severity is capped to match what the evidence actually supports.
items.fix: Put a one-sentence paragraph where the argument turns. Let another run long.
items.before: Six consecutive paragraphs of exactly four sentences.
items.after: Four sentences, then one, then seven, then two.
items.false_positive_when: News writing, house styles that cap paragraph length, and documentation all enforce evenness deliberately. A six-paragraph document has too few samples for a variance claim at all, which is why this needs eight.

items.name: nothing-at-stake
items.description: The whole-document version of the complaint. Nothing in the piece could be wrong, nothing costs the author anything, and removing any paragraph would change nothing.
items.detection: Ask two questions. What claim here could turn out to be false? What did the author risk by writing it? If both answers are nothing, this is the finding, and it outranks every phrase-level item in the catalog.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This is what readers mean when they say a piece 'says nothing' despite being well formed. The largest community analysis of what makes writing sound like AI concluded against its own premise on exactly this point: cosmetic AI-isms are mostly noise, and the discourse-level absence is the signal.
items.fix: Cut to the one claim worth defending and rebuild around it. If there isn't one, the piece should not exist yet.
items.before: A 1,200-word post about the importance of communication in teams.
items.after: A 400-word post arguing that standups are worse than a written update, with the two cases where that's wrong.
items.false_positive_when: Reference material, documentation and explainers are not supposed to have stakes. Scope this to anything meant to persuade or to be read for its own sake.
items.evidence: ~90,000-post community analysis of what makes writing sound like AI, whose author concluded that cosmetic AI-isms are mostly noise; StoryScope's discourse-only 93.2% macro-F1 is the quantitative counterpart.

items.name: cream-serif-sage-tasteful-default
items.description: The SECOND-generation default: what models produce when you ask them not to look AI-generated. A warm off-white ground (#faf8f5, #f5f1e8, bg-stone-50, bg-amber-50), a display serif (Instrument Serif, Fraunces, Playfair Display, Spectral, Cormorant, DM Serif), and a deep sage or forest primary (#15573a, #1a4d3a, emerald-800).
