items.detection: Grep for those grounds, for the serif list in font imports, and for a primary in the emerald 700-900 band. All three together is close to conclusive.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is the model's stored idea of taste, the look of a well-funded 2024 DTC brand, applied without reference to what the product is. A payroll API and a meditation app get the same cream-and-Fraunces treatment, so it reads as a costume rather than an identity.
items.fix: Treat it as a palette you have to earn. If the product has no reason to be warm, don't be warm. Choose the serif for what it does to your longest headline, and don't pair cream with green unless the brand is about growing things.
items.before: bg-[#faf8f5], Instrument Serif h1, --primary #15573a, one generated photo of hands holding a ceramic mug.
items.after: White ground, one grotesque at two optical sizes, the brand's actual color, and a real screenshot of the product.
items.false_positive_when: Editorial and publishing sites, food and hospitality, wellness and skincare, independent bookshops. Cream, serif and green is a genuinely correct and long-standing set there. Also any brand whose guidelines predate 2023 and happen to land here.

items.name: allcaps-letterspaced-eyebrow
items.description: A small all-caps, wide-tracked, often monospace label above the H1, repeated above every section on the page.
items.detection: Count elements combining uppercase, wide tracking, small size and a mono family. More than two on a page is the fire condition.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Free-looking hierarchy. It adds a level above the headline without requiring a decision, and because it costs nothing it appears above every section, destroying the hierarchy it was meant to create.
items.fix: Allow one eyebrow per page, and only where it carries information the H1 cannot: a category, a date, an issue number.
items.before: A mono uppercase tracked kicker above each of six sections.
items.after: No eyebrows; section boundaries carried by whitespace and H2 size.
items.false_positive_when: Editorial layouts where a kicker is a real typographic convention, conference sites where it carries track and date, and Swiss-modernist systems that use caps labels as a grid element.

items.name: shadcn-defaults-unmodified
items.description: shadcn/ui shipped exactly as generated: default radius, default zinc neutrals, default hairline borders, lucide as the only icon set, no token overrides.
items.detection: Check whether components.json and the CSS variable block differ from the scaffold defaults at all. Zero diff is the signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The library is excellent and the defaults are fine, which is why nobody changes them. A site that has not overridden one token has not made one decision.
items.fix: Change the radius, the neutral ramp, and the primary. Three token edits move a page further than a redesign.
items.before: A components.json and theme block byte-identical to the scaffold.
items.after: Custom radius scale, a neutral ramp mixed toward the brand hue, one real accent.
items.false_positive_when: Internal tools, admin panels and prototypes are exactly what unmodified defaults are for.

items.name: ambient-background-stack
items.description: Two or more decorative background layers stacked behind the hero: a dot or line grid, a noise overlay, an aurora or spotlight wash, a blurred gradient orb.
items.detection: Count decorative absolutely-positioned background layers behind the hero that carry no content.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Each layer individually is a legitimate technique. Stacking them is what happens when nobody decided which one the page needed.
items.fix: Keep at most one, and only if it does something for legibility or depth.
items.before: Grid background, plus noise, plus two blurred orbs, plus a radial spotlight.
items.after: A flat ground and one well-judged shadow.
items.false_positive_when: Some design systems genuinely layer texture, and a grid plus noise is a real and old print-derived treatment.

items.name: fade-up-on-scroll-everything
items.description: Every section, card and heading enters with the same fade-and-rise animation on scroll, usually staggered.
items.detection: Count elements carrying the same scroll-triggered entrance variant. Uniformity is the tell, not animation.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Motion applied as a finish rather than as meaning. When everything animates, the animation stops telling the reader anything.
items.fix: Animate the one thing whose arrival matters. Let the rest be present when the page is.
items.before: Twelve elements sharing one fade-up variant with a 0.1s stagger.
items.after: A static page with one deliberate transition where state actually changes.
items.false_positive_when: Motion systems with a documented entrance token are doing this on purpose, and a long marketing page can legitimately use entrance motion for pacing.

items.name: amber-white-balance-cast
items.description: A global warm cast across generated images: whites drifting to cream, shadows muddy brown, skin pushed slightly yellow. It compounds, adding a layer with each edit round.
items.detection: Compute the chromaticity of the brightest 1% of pixels. Neutral highlights sit near equal R/G/B; this skews R>G>B. A consistent cast across unrelated subjects from one source is close to conclusive.
items.why_it_reads_ai: No camera and no photographer produces the same white balance across a kitchen, a beach and an office. A cast invariant to the scene implies a single rendering stage.
items.fix: Neutralize white balance in post by sampling a known-white object and correcting globally. Prompting alone is unreliable, because the cast is applied late in rendering.
items.before: Product shot on a white seamless that samples at #F6EEDC.
items.after: Same shot with the seamless corrected to #FAFAFA.
items.false_positive_when: Golden-hour photography, tungsten interiors, deliberate warm grading across most commercial and film work, film-emulation looks, and anything shot under sodium light. The tell is a warm cast INVARIANT TO THE SCENE, not a warm cast. It is also trivially corrected, so its absence means nothing.

items.name: uniform-detail-no-focus-falloff
items.description: Detail distributed evenly rather than optically: everything equally sharp regardless of distance, or a flat Gaussian background wash that does not deepen with distance from the focal plane. Mid-tones perfectly smooth.
items.detection: Look at whether sharpness falls off as a gradient or as two flat zones. A partial structural assist is available by computing high-frequency energy in depth bands.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A lens has one focal plane and a circle of confusion that grows with distance. Diffusion models learned background blur as a style token rather than as geometry, so the blur has no depth structure. A real sensor also never produces perfectly smooth mid-tones, because it produces noise.
items.fix: If you must use the image, add real grain and a depth-aware blur. Better: use a photograph.
items.before: A portrait where the subject and the wall four metres behind are equally crisp.
items.after: A photograph, or a render with a real depth pass.
items.false_positive_when: Deep-focus photography, focus stacking, macro work, and small-sensor phone images with computational depth all break this. Heavy noise reduction also smooths mid-tones.
items.evidence: Reported by practitioners as the strongest purely visual tell surviving into 2026, now that hands and text no longer work.

items.name: provenance-absent-or-stripped
items.description: The file's provenance record: a C2PA manifest naming a generator, a manifest naming a camera, or nothing at all, plus EXIF that is present, absent, or implausible.
items.detection: Read the JUMBF box for a C2PA manifest, verify the signature against the C2PA trust list, and read EXIF and XMP. This is the only genuinely scriptable provenance test, and the asymmetry is the whole point: a signed generator manifest is close to proof of synthesis, and its absence proves nothing.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A signed manifest from a generator is a positive fact about the file. Most 2026 guidance goes wrong by reading the converse.
items.fix: If you are PRODUCING work, sign your real photography. Lightroom and Photoshop emit Content Credentials, and several camera bodies sign at capture. It is the only durable way to prove your work is yours as detectors get less decisive.
items.before: A hero image shipped as a stripped JPEG with no manifest and no EXIF.
items.after: Signed at capture or export, with the manifest preserved through the build pipeline.
items.false_positive_when: Constantly, in the negative direction. Every social upload, screenshot, re-save, CMS resize and CDN transform strips the manifest. Midjourney does not embed C2PA at all as of early 2026, so the most-used generator produces clean files. The standard has documented holes too: timestamps can be replaced without detection, and different validators return contradictory results. Never read a missing manifest as evidence of anything.

items.name: eight-second-shot-ceiling
items.description: Every shot runs five to ten seconds, because that is the generation window, and the piece is assembled entirely from cuts at that interval.
items.detection: Measure shot lengths. A whole piece with no shot outside the five-to-ten-second band is the signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The edit rhythm is the tool's constraint rather than an editorial choice. No human edit has that little variance.
items.fix: If you must use generated footage, cut against the grain: hold one shot long, and cut one hard and short.
items.before: A ninety-second piece of twelve eight-second shots.
items.after: A piece with a twenty-second hold in it.
items.false_positive_when: Music videos, trailers and social edits use fast uniform cutting deliberately. This is also expiring fast as generation windows lengthen.

items.name: no-idle-micro-behavior
items.description: People in generated video do the thing they were asked to do and nothing else. No blinking at the wrong moment, no weight shift, no glance off-camera, no hand doing something absent-minded.
items.detection: Watch a person who is not the focus of the shot. Real people are never doing only one thing.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model animates the prompt. Idle behavior is what a body does when nobody is directing it, and there is no instruction for it.
items.fix: Cut to the background actor and see whether the shot survives. Usually it does not, which tells you what to keep.
items.before: A conference room where everyone not speaking is perfectly still.
items.after: Real footage, or a tighter shot that does not show the room.
items.false_positive_when: Direction, and staged corporate footage, both produce unnaturally still extras. This is an underrated tell precisely because people look at the main subject.

items.name: breathless-uniform-prosody
items.description: Synthetic narration with even stress, no breath, and emphasis landing on function words. Sentences all start at the same pitch and fall the same way.
items.detection: Listen for a breath. Then listen for where the emphasis lands: 'the RESULTS were surprising' rather than 'the results were SURPRISING'.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Prosody encodes what the speaker means, and a system that has not understood the sentence stresses it by rule. Breath is the other giveaway, because a voice that never needs air has no body.
items.fix: Record a person, or at minimum hand-mark emphasis and insert breaths. Proper nouns need a pronunciation pass regardless.
items.before: Ninety seconds of even, breathless narration over stock footage.
items.after: A take with a person in it, including the place they stumble.
items.false_positive_when: Trained broadcast narrators are extremely even, and heavy compression removes audible breath. Radio and audiobook professionals get flagged by this constantly.

items.name: plausibly-wrong-chart
items.description: A chart that looks right and is wrong: axes that do not start where they should, percentages that do not sum, a trend line fitted to points that do not support it, labels that do not match the data.
items.detection: Read the numbers off the chart and check them against the source. This is arithmetic, not taste.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generating a chart means generating its appearance. The model produces a convincing picture of an analysis, and nothing in the loop checks the picture against the data.
items.fix: Rebuild the chart from the data. If there is no data, there is no chart.
items.before: A pie chart whose wedges sum to 112%.
items.after: The same comparison as a bar chart, from a CSV anyone can open.
items.false_positive_when: Humans make chart errors constantly too, which is the point: this finding is about the chart being wrong, not about who drew it. Like citation pathology, act on it with full confidence.

items.name: unfilled-placeholder-residue
items.description: Template scaffolding shipped live. Two mechanically identical families: merge tags that never resolved ('Hi {{first_name}}', 'Hi FNAME', 'Dear Customer Name', 'Hi null,') and model bracket placeholders nobody replaced ('the [Job Title] position at [Company Name]', '[insert metric here]').
items.detection: Regex for merge-tag and bracket-placeholder syntax. This should be a hard fail rather than a score.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is the one item in this catalog that is proof rather than inference: unreviewed generated or templated output reached a recipient. Nothing else here is that certain.
items.fix: Block send or publish on any placeholder pattern. Set fallbacks on every merge field, and grep the final artifact before it leaves.
items.before: Hi {FirstName}, I'm reaching out because [Company Name] is doing interesting work in [industry].
items.after: Hi Priya, I saw Northwind shipped the SOC 2 attestation last month.
items.false_positive_when: Documentation, template libraries, tutorials and code samples show unrendered merge tags on purpose, which is the point of them. Never fire inside fenced code, or in content whose subject IS templating. Some CRMs also render the braces in preview panes.

items.name: no-detail-only-you-could-know
items.description: The unifying rubric. A passage fails when it contains no detail that could only have come from the specific author, recipient, or object in front of it.
items.detection: Ask one question of any passage: what fact here could ONLY have come from this writer, this reader, or this thing? If the answer is none, the passage is generic regardless of how well formed it is.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Five separate communities converged on this independently: LinkedIn slop-flaggers, Amazon fake-review researchers, Reddit moderators, cold-email testers and dating-app users all describe the same failure in their own vocabulary. The academic version is that synthetic reviews emphasize generic product merits rather than idiosyncratic experiences. If this skill only ever ran one judge rubric, it should be this one.
items.fix: Add the one thing only you know: the name, the number, the room, the defect, the moment it went wrong.
items.before: I came across your profile and was truly impressed by your background and expertise.
items.after: Your talk on partial index maintenance is the reason we stopped rebuilding ours nightly.
items.false_positive_when: Reference material and general explainers are supposed to be general. Scope this to anything addressed to a specific person, about a specific object, or drawn from personal experience.

items.name: hook-break-lesson-list-close
items.description: The LinkedIn macro-frame, distinct from broetry: a standalone hook line, a blank line, a labelled transition ('Here's what I learned:', '3 things I'd do differently:'), a list of three, then an interrogative close. It survives re-flowing the paragraphs, which is what makes it a different tell from the line spacing.
items.detection: Judge the skeleton rather than the line breaks. The labelled transition plus a list of exactly three plus a question close is the shape.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is the highest-engagement post structure in the training data, so it is what a model produces when asked for a LinkedIn post. It is also what a lot of humans produce, which is why it needs its base rate attached.
items.fix: Keep the story, drop the scaffold. Tell what happened and stop when it's told.
items.before:
I got rejected 47 times.

Here's what I learned:

1. Persistence matters
2. Feedback is a gift
3. Rejection isn't personal

What's your experience?
items.after: I got rejected 47 times before Northwind said yes, and the only useful feedback came from the 31st, who told me my deck buried the number.
items.false_positive_when: This is a native LinkedIn convention that predates LLMs, and plenty of humans write it sincerely. Weight it by platform: LinkedIn long-form runs around 40% fully generated, so the prior is high there and nowhere else.

items.name: engagement-bait-close
items.description: The closing line that asks for interaction rather than ending the thought: 'What's your take?', 'Agree?', 'Drop a comment below', 'P.S. Follow me for more'.
items.detection: Closed phrase bank over the final line, plus a judge call on whether the question is real.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is a growth tactic learned as a writing convention. The model appends it because the corpus rewards it, regardless of whether a question is warranted.
items.fix: End on the last real sentence. If you genuinely want an answer, ask a specific question only your readers could answer.
items.before: What's your take? Drop a comment below.
items.after: If anyone has made the Postgres side of this work above 10k writes a second, I'd like to know how.
items.false_positive_when: Asking readers a genuine question is normal and good, and community managers do it professionally.

items.name: markdown-scaffolding-in-casual-comment
items.description: Bold headers, numbered sections and horizontal rules inside a threaded comment, where the surrounding replies are two sentences of lowercase.
items.detection: Count markdown structural constructs in a comment and compare against the thread's other replies.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model formats every answer as a document. A person typing into a reply box does not reach for an H3.
items.fix: Write it as you would say it. One paragraph, no headers.
items.before:
**TL;DR:** yes.

### Why

1. **Cost** — it's cheaper
2. **Speed** — it's faster
items.after: yeah, mostly cost. it's about a third the price and marginally faster, which surprised me
items.false_positive_when: Long technical answers on technical subreddits legitimately use structure, and some communities expect it. And the base rate matters enormously: Reddit replies measure around 1.7% generated against LinkedIn long-form at 40.5%, so the same formatting deserves very different weight in the two places.

items.name: synthetic-review-shape
items.description: The generated review arc plus its content signature. Skeptic-conversion opener, three generic merits, recommendation close. It praises category virtues such as quality, value and convenience, and never names a use, a room, a defect, a comparison, or a moment.
items.detection: Judge: does this review contain a single detail that could only come from owning the item? A corpus-level signal is stronger than the text: star-rating skew and burst timing at the product level.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Fake and generated reviews emphasize generic product merits rather than idiosyncratic experiences. A measured 3% of front-page Amazon reviews are generated, skewing toward five stars, and 93% of those carried a verified-purchase badge, so the badge does not save you.
items.fix: One concrete artifact per review: what you did with it, where it sits, what went wrong, what you compared it to, how long you have had it. Drop the recommendation sentence, because the star rating already says it.
items.before: I was skeptical at first, but this exceeded my expectations! The quality is excellent and the value is great. Highly recommend!
items.after: Third one of these I've owned. The hinge on the previous two gave out around 14 months; this revision uses a metal pin. It does not fit a 15-inch laptop with a case on, despite the listing photo.
items.false_positive_when: 'I was skeptical' describes a genuinely common purchase experience, and most people are simply not good reviewers. Seeded and sampled reviews are legitimately labelled and legitimately glowing. Text alone on a single review is weak evidence.

items.name: mirror-back-research-opener
items.description: An opener that personalizes by reciting the recipient's own public information back at them: 'I came across your profile and was truly impressed by your background', or a paraphrase of their homepage hero.
items.detection: Judge whether the opener contains one fact that is NOT on the recipient's public profile headline or homepage.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It signals the opposite of what it intends. Reading someone's homepage is not research, and the recipient knows what is on their own homepage.
items.fix: Lead with something you noticed that they would not expect you to have noticed.
items.before: I noticed your company helps businesses scale their operations.
items.after: Your changelog says you moved off Elasticsearch in March. How did the reindex go?
items.false_positive_when: Referencing a specific piece of someone's public work is good outreach. The tell is reciting their own summary of themselves.

items.name: power-verb-metric-bullet
items.description: Resume bullets built from a verb bank and an invented percentage: 'Spearheaded cross-functional initiatives resulting in a 40% increase in operational efficiency'.
items.detection: Hit rate against the standard power-verb bank, joined with round-number percentages the candidate cannot source.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Resume-writing advice is heavily represented in training data, so the model produces its distilled form. The percentages are generated because the corpus contains percentages, not because anyone measured anything.
items.fix: Name the actual thing and the actual number. If you don't have a number, describe what changed instead of inventing one.
items.before: Spearheaded cross-functional initiatives resulting in a 40% increase in team efficiency.
items.after: Rewrote the nightly batch so it finished before standup instead of at 11am. Four teams stopped waiting on it.
items.false_positive_when: Real achievements have real metrics, and resume conventions genuinely favor this shape. Career coaches teach it. The tell is the unverifiable round number attached to an abstract noun.

items.name: scripted-empathy-opener
items.description: Support and advice replies opening with acknowledgement boilerplate: 'I completely understand how frustrating this must be', 'I'm sorry you're going through this', before any engagement with the actual problem.
items.detection: Judge whether the empathy line references anything specific to this person's situation.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Alignment training rewards acknowledging feelings first, so the model performs the move whether or not it has understood the problem. Recipients read it as a script because it is one.
items.fix: Lead with the specific thing that went wrong for them. Demonstrated understanding reads as far more sympathetic than stated sympathy.
items.before: I completely understand how frustrating this must be. Let me look into it for you.
items.after: Your invoice ran twice on the 3rd because the retry fired after the first charge settled. I've refunded the duplicate.
items.false_positive_when: Genuine acknowledgement is good support practice and many teams require it by policy. The tell is empathy that could precede any ticket.

items.name: synthetic-executive-quote
items.description: A press-release quote attributed to a named executive that no executive said, containing no information: 'We're thrilled to partner with X to deliver best-in-class solutions to our customers.'
items.detection: Judge whether the quote contains a fact, an opinion someone could disagree with, or a voice. Attributed quotes with none of the three are manufactured.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The quote slot is a template field, and the model fills it with the average of every quote it has seen. Putting a real person's name on it is the part that matters.
items.fix: Get a real sentence from the real person, or drop the quote. A release without a quote is better than one with a fabricated one, and putting invented words in a named person's mouth is its own problem.
items.before: "We're thrilled to partner with Acme to deliver best-in-class solutions," said the CEO.
items.after: "We bought them because we'd already rebuilt half of what they do, badly," said the CEO.
items.false_positive_when: PR quotes have been ghostwritten and approved for a century, and an approved quote is not fabricated. The line is whether the named person saw and agreed to it.

items.name: framework-look-without-responsive
items.description: The page wears the visual idiom of a modern utility-CSS framework — flex rows, rounded cards, spacing scale, shadows — and contains not one responsive variant or width media query.
items.detection: Count utility-class tokens against responsive prefixes (sm:/md:/lg:/xl:) and width-based @media rules. A high idiom count with zero of either is the signal. Purely static, decidable from source.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The look was copied; the part that does work was not. A generator produces the class names that make a screenshot look right, and responsive behaviour only shows up if someone resizes the window, which nothing in the generation loop does.
items.fix: Pick the three widths that matter — roughly 390, 768 and 1200 — and make the page correct at each. Concretely: every multi-column grid needs a single-column form below the first breakpoint (grid-template-columns: 1fr by default, columns added at min-width); every fixed pixel width becomes max-width plus width:100%; horizontal padding lives on one container rather than on each child; and replace repeat(3, 360px) with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr)), which needs no breakpoint at all. Then open it at 390px before you believe any of it.
items.before: <div class="grid" style="grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 360px)">
items.after: <div class="grid" style="grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))">
items.false_positive_when: Embedded widgets, email templates, print stylesheets, and admin tools with a documented desktop-only support policy. Also a fragment that inherits its responsive behaviour from a parent layout — check whether the file is a whole page.

items.name: missing-viewport-meta
items.description: No viewport meta tag, so a phone renders the page at desktop width and scales the whole thing down.
items.detection: Absence of a meta viewport tag in a document that has a head. Binary and static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It is one line that every framework scaffold includes and that only goes missing in hand-assembled markup. Its absence is close to proof nobody opened the page on a phone.
items.fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the head. Do not add maximum-scale or user-scalable=no with it — that blocks pinch zoom, which people rely on.
items.before: <head><title>Product</title></head>
items.after: <head><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Product</title></head>
items.false_positive_when: HTML fragments, partials and email templates have no head and should not have one.

items.name: horizontal-overflow-at-mobile
items.description: The page scrolls sideways at phone width. Content is literally off screen.
items.detection: Rendered check only: load at 390px and compare documentElement.scrollWidth against innerWidth, then walk the DOM for the outermost elements extending past the right edge. scripts/render_check.py does this and names the culprits.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This is the lived form of the previous entry. It is also the single most common failure of a site styled to look like a framework without being built with one.
items.fix: Fix the named elements outermost-first; a wide child inside a wide parent is one bug. The usual four causes, in order of frequency: a fixed pixel width that wants max-width:100%; a grid with a hardcoded column count that needs a single-column form below the breakpoint; 100vw where 100% was meant, which overflows by the scrollbar width; and a long unbroken string (a URL, a token, a code sample) that needs overflow-wrap:anywhere. Add `html { overflow-x: clip }` only after you have fixed the cause — as a first move it hides the bug rather than solving it.
items.before: .wrap { width: 1180px; margin: 0 auto }
items.after: .wrap { max-width: 1180px; margin-inline: auto; padding-inline: 1.5rem }
items.false_positive_when: Deliberate horizontal scrollers (a carousel, a wide data table in its own overflow container) are correct. The finding is about the PAGE scrolling, not a component.

items.name: div-soup-no-semantics
items.description: Everything is a div. No main, nav, header, footer, section or article anywhere.
items.detection: Ratio of div elements to semantic landmark elements. Static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A generator emits the box it needs to style. Semantic elements pay off only for people using a screen reader or reader mode, and nothing in the loop represents them.
items.fix: It is a rename, not a rewrite, and usually twenty minutes: one <main> around the page content, <nav> for the nav, <header> and <footer>, and <section> wherever a heading introduces a region. Then tab through the page and use the browser's accessibility tree to check the landmarks read sensibly.
items.before:
...
...
items.after: <nav>...</nav> <main>...</main>
items.false_positive_when: Component fragments, design-system primitives and rendered subtrees legitimately return divs; the landmark lives in the layout that composes them. Judge whole pages.

items.name: clickable-div-not-button
items.description: A div or span with a click handler and no button role, so it is unreachable by keyboard and unannounced by assistive tech.
items.detection: Elements matching div/span with an onClick attribute and no role=button, tabindex or key handler. Static, near-zero false positive.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It looks identical on screen and works for a subset of people, which is exactly the class of defect that survives a visual review.
items.fix: Use <button type="button">. Strip its default styling with `all: unset` plus your own if you need it to look like a div. If it genuinely must stay a div it needs role="button", tabIndex={0}, and onKeyDown handling Enter AND Space — which is the argument for using a button.
items.before: Get started
items.after: <button type="button" onClick={open} className="cta">Get started</button>
items.false_positive_when: A click handler on a container for event delegation, or for dismissing a modal by backdrop click, is not a control and needs no role.

items.name: dead-anchor-href
items.description: Navigation links pointing at href="#" or nothing.
items.detection: Count anchors with an empty or hash-only href. Static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The generator produced the SHAPE of a nav without destinations, because the template has slots and the site has no pages.
items.fix: Point each link at a real destination or delete it. A nav with three real links beats one with eight dead ones, and the dead ones are the first thing a visitor clicks.
items.before: Docs
items.after: Docs
items.false_positive_when: href="#" on a control that JavaScript intercepts is a long-standing (if dated) pattern, and a skip-link legitimately targets a fragment. Check whether a handler is attached.

items.name: scaffold-title-residue
items.description: The framework's default document title shipped: "Create Next App", "Vite + React", "Untitled", "Document".
items.detection: Match the title text against the closed set of scaffold defaults. Static, near-zero false positive.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Proof rather than inference, like an unfilled merge tag. It is what the browser tab, the search result and every shared link will say.
items.fix: Write the title: product name, then what it is, under about 60 characters so search does not truncate it. Set a distinct one per route, and while you are in the head add a meta description and an og:image — they are missing for the same reason.
items.before: <title>Create Next App</title>
items.after: <title>Northwind — invoice reconciliation for finance teams</title>
items.false_positive_when: A scaffold that genuinely has not shipped yet. That is a reason to fix it before it does, not to ignore it.

items.name: placeholder-copy-residue
items.description: Template filler reaching a reader: lorem ipsum, "Your Company", "Acme Inc", "Product Name", "Your logo here".
items.detection: Closed-set literal match. Static, and proof rather than inference.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Nobody read the page end to end. This is the visual-design sibling of the unfilled merge tag.
items.fix: Replace with real copy, or delete the section until you have some. An honest three-section page beats a seven-section one with two sections of filler.
items.before: Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit.
items.after: Northwind matches bank lines to invoices and flags the 2% that need a human.
items.false_positive_when: Design-system documentation, component galleries and Storybook stories use lorem deliberately to avoid implying real content.

items.name: missing-or-placeholder-alt
items.description: Images with no alt attribute, or alt text that describes the file rather than its job: "image of a laptop", "screenshot.png".
items.detection: Images missing alt, or whose alt starts with image/photo/picture/screenshot, or is a filename. Static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generated alt text describes the picture because that is what the model can see. Useful alt text describes what a reader would lose, which requires knowing why the image is on the page.
items.fix: For each image ask what a reader loses if it does not load, and write that. If the answer is nothing, use alt="" so screen readers skip it rather than announcing a filename. A product screenshot's alt should carry the thing the screenshot proves.
items.false_positive_when: Decorative images correctly carry alt="", and an adjacent caption can legitimately carry the description instead (with the image marked decorative).

items.name: focus-outline-removed
items.description: outline:none or outline:0 with no :focus-visible replacement anywhere.
items.detection: Presence of an outline-removal rule with no :focus-visible selector in the same stylesheet. Static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The ring is ugly in a screenshot and invisible in the generation loop, so it gets removed. Keyboard users then cannot see where they are.
items.fix: Replace it, do not remove it: `:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px }`. :focus-visible only shows for keyboard focus, so you get the clean mouse appearance you wanted. Then tab the whole page and confirm you can always see where you are.
items.before: button { outline: none }
items.after:
button { outline: none }
button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px }
items.false_positive_when: Removing the outline while supplying a different visible focus treatment (a ring, a border, a background shift) is fine — the detector looks for :focus-visible specifically, so a box-shadow-based ring under a different selector may read as a false positive.

items.name: wcag-fail-from-generated-palette
items.description: Text below WCAG AA contrast: 4.5:1 for body, 3:1 for large text. Usually muted grey on white or on a tinted ground.
items.detection: Rendered: compute relative luminance of computed foreground against the nearest opaque ancestor background. scripts/render_check.py reports ratios per element. Partial static detection is possible for known low-contrast utility tokens on a known ground.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A palette chosen for how it photographed in a hero mock rather than for whether anyone can read it. Muted grey secondary text is the default because it looks calm in a screenshot.
items.fix: Darken the foreground token until it passes rather than patching each element — there is almost always one --muted token behind every failure. On white, grey needs to reach about #595959 for body text. Check the states too: placeholder, disabled and hover are where this recurs after the fix.
items.before: color: #9ca3af on #ffffff  (2.54:1)
items.after: color: #595959 on #ffffff  (7.0:1)
items.false_positive_when: Genuinely decorative text, disabled controls (exempt from AA), and text over an image where the real background is a scrim the checker cannot resolve. Verify the computed background before filing.

items.name: tap-target-too-small
items.description: Interactive controls smaller than about 44x44 CSS pixels at phone width.
items.detection: Rendered at 390px: measure bounding boxes of anchors, buttons and form controls.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Desktop-first styling that was never checked with a thumb. Padding tuned for a cursor is too small for a finger.
items.fix: Give controls a minimum 44x44 hit area with min-height and min-width, or put the padding on the control rather than on its container. Nav links set to display:inline with tiny padding are the usual offender — make them inline-block or flex items with real vertical padding. Inline links inside a paragraph are exempt.
items.before: .nav a { padding: 2px 6px; font-size: 11px }
items.after: .nav a { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; min-height: 44px; padding-inline: 12px; font-size: 15px }
items.false_positive_when: Inline text links within prose, and dense data tables on desktop, are legitimate exceptions the guideline itself carves out.

items.name: body-text-below-readable
items.description: Text rendering under about 12px.
items.detection: Rendered: computed font-size on elements with direct text content.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Small type reads as refined in a zoomed-out mock and is unreadable at arm's length. Generated pages inherit the look of a design shot rather than of a page someone reads.
items.fix: Floor body text at 16px and secondary text at 14px. Note iOS zooms the page when a form input under 16px receives focus, so inputs specifically must be 16px or larger. If the layout only works at 11px, the layout is too dense — cut content rather than shrinking type.
items.before: .eyebrow { font-size: 11px }
items.after: .eyebrow { font-size: 14px }
items.false_positive_when: Legal footnotes, chart axis labels and dense tabular data have long-standing conventions below 12px.

items.name: no-reduced-motion-guard
items.description: An animated page with no prefers-reduced-motion media query.
items.detection: Count animation, transition and motion-library declarations; flag when several exist and no prefers-reduced-motion block does. Static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The motion was added as a finish. Honouring the OS-level preference requires knowing the preference exists.
items.fix: Add the guard, which is four lines: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: .01ms !important; animation-iteration-count: 1 !important; transition-duration: .01ms !important; scroll-behavior: auto !important } }. For a motion library, read the preference and pass a zero-duration variant.
items.before: (twelve scroll-triggered fade-ups, no guard)
items.after: (the same, wrapped so reduced-motion users get instant state changes)
items.false_positive_when: A page whose only transitions are sub-100ms colour or opacity changes on hover does not trigger vestibular symptoms and is not what the preference is for.

items.name: image-without-dimensions
items.description: Images with no width and height attributes, so the layout shifts as they load.
items.detection: Rendered or static: images over about 40px in either dimension with no width/height attributes.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The attributes matter only while the page is loading, which nothing in the generation loop observes.
items.fix: Set width and height to the real intrinsic pixel dimensions and let CSS scale with `height: auto`. The browser then reserves the space from the aspect ratio before the bytes arrive. Add loading="lazy" to anything below the fold and fetchpriority="high" to the hero image.
items.false_positive_when: Images in a fixed aspect-ratio container, or with an explicit aspect-ratio CSS property, already reserve their space.

items.name: important-escalation
items.description: Heavy use of !important.
items.detection: Count occurrences. Static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Specificity fought rather than designed — what happens when rules are added without reading the ones already there.
items.fix: Find the rule being overridden and change it. Where you genuinely need to win, raise specificity deliberately or use a cascade layer (@layer) rather than the nuclear option. Keep !important for utility overrides, print styles and the reduced-motion guard, where it is correct.
items.before: .card p { color: #333 !important }
items.after: (the base rule corrected, so nothing needs to win)
items.false_positive_when: Utility-first frameworks and the reduced-motion guard use !important by design; a generated utility stylesheet will have many legitimately.

items.name: z-index-escalation
items.description: z-index values in the hundreds or thousands.
items.detection: Maximum z-index value in the stylesheet or utility classes. Static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Stacking resolved by bidding. A z-index of 9999 means nobody knows what it is competing with.
items.fix: Define a small named scale and use only it: base 0, sticky 10, dropdown 20, overlay 30, modal 40, toast 50. Put them in CSS custom properties so the scale is visible in one place. Most stacking bugs are actually stacking-context bugs — a transform or filter on an ancestor — which a bigger number will never fix.
items.before: z-index: 9999
items.after: z-index: var(--z-modal)  /* 40 */
items.false_positive_when: Third-party widgets sometimes require a high value to sit above host content, and a documented single high value is not escalation.

items.name: unearned-prior-reference
items.description: The piece points at a history the reader was never present for: 'building on our previous approach', 'unlike the v2 design', 'as we discussed', 'you'll recall'. The referent exists only in the writer's context, not on the page.
items.detection: A closed set of deictic and anaphoric frames, scoped to the opening third of the document, where by construction nothing has been established yet. Closed grammatical forms measured positionally, not a topic list.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A model writes from its context window. That window holds the previous versions, the internal thread and the repo, and nothing in the loop marks which of it the reader has seen. The sentence reads fine to everyone who was in the room and as noise to everyone who was not.
items.fix: Either establish the prior thing in one sentence before you improve on it, or cut the comparison and state what the current thing does. 'Faster than our v2 pipeline' means nothing to someone who never saw v2; 'processes forty thousand invoices an hour' means something to everyone. The test: could a reader who arrived from a search result follow this sentence?
items.before: Building on our previous approach, Quantum Lane is a significant step forward from the v2 pipeline.
items.after: Our scheduler used to hand the same job to two workers about once every forty thousand runs. Quantum Lane is the fix.
items.false_positive_when: Part three of a numbered series, an internal memo, release notes for existing users, and any piece that links the prior thing in the same sentence. The tell is an unlinked, unexplained back-reference in something addressed to newcomers.

items.name: repo-context-leak
items.description: File paths, function names, ticket ids and branch names in prose meant for someone who does not have the repository open.
items.detection: Density of repo-shaped tokens outside code fences: path/like/this.ext, snake_case(), ABC-123, feat/branch-name. Countable, and specific to prose regions.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The writer had the repo open and the model had it in context. Neither noticed that an identifier is a pointer into a workspace the reader cannot see.
items.fix: Name the thing by what it does, and move the identifier into a code block or a link if it is genuinely needed. 'The scheduler' beats 'lib/fleet/conductor.ts' in a sentence someone reads on a phone. Ticket ids almost never belong in outward-facing prose at all.
items.before: This removes the contention we saw in lib/fleet/conductor.ts, which PD-4471 tracked.
items.after: This removes the contention in the scheduler, which we had been chasing since March.
items.false_positive_when: Engineering blog posts written for contributors, internal docs, changelogs, and any piece whose subject IS the codebase. Scope this to outward-facing writing.

items.name: definition-after-use
items.description: Terms of art used before they are defined, or never defined at all. The reader meets a concept with nothing to attach it to.
items.detection: For each candidate term of art appearing three or more times, compare the line of first use against the line of the first definitional frame ('X is a', 'X refers to', 'X, which is', 'we call this X'). Flag terms defined well after first use, and terms never defined. Matching spans singular and plural, so a piece that uses 'Soft Leases' and defines 'A Soft Lease' counts as defined.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The curse of knowledge with a context window behind it. The writer already holds the concept, so the sentence reads fine to them; the model holds it too, because it was in the prompt. Nothing in the loop represents a reader who does not.
items.fix: Define a term at or before its first substantive use, usually with an appositive in the same sentence. Introduce one new idea at a time and let each earn the next. If a term appears three times and is never defined, either define it or stop using it. Read the piece imagining a competent stranger: the first place you would have to stop and look something up is the place to fix.
items.before: Quantum Lane sits between the Drift Broker and the Lane Coordinator.
items.after: Jobs are handed out by a scheduler we call the Lane Coordinator, which takes work from a queue (the Drift Broker) and decides who may run it.
items.false_positive_when: Writing for a named expert audience, reference documentation with a stated prerequisite page, and terms defined in a glossary the piece links. Also common nouns that merely happen to be capitalised in a product context.

items.name: signposting-without-structure
items.description: Meta-navigation substituted for structure: 'First we'll explore... Next we'll examine... Finally we'll conclude.' The outline is read aloud instead of being enacted.
items.detection: Count sentences matching an ordinal plus a first-person-plural intention verb plus an exploration verb. A closed frame set, not a topic list.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model was given an outline and emits it as prose, because announcing a structure is cheaper than building one. It costs the reader a paragraph before anything is said, and it promises a shape the piece often does not deliver.
items.fix: Delete the announcements and let headings and prose do the work. Where a transition is genuinely needed, make it carry information: say what changed or what the last section established, not that a new section is beginning.
items.before: First, we'll explore the architecture. Next, we will examine performance. Finally, we'll look at what comes next.
items.after: The fix had two halves, and the second one is the interesting part.
items.false_positive_when: Tutorials and long reference documents legitimately tell the reader what the path looks like, and a single roadmap paragraph in a long piece is a kindness. Three or more is the signal.

items.name: hundred-vw-overflow
items.description: 100vw or w-screen used for width, often with the -50vw full-bleed hack.
items.detection: Regex for 100vw width declarations, w-screen utilities, and margin-left:calc(-50vw...) full-bleed patterns.
items.why_it_reads_ai: 100vw is the viewport INCLUDING its scrollbar; 100% is the space actually available. On any browser that reserves scrollbar space the element is wider than its container, and paired with the -50vw trick it overflows twice. It is the most common single cause of a page scrolling sideways.
items.fix: Use width:100% and let the element fill its container, or 100dvw where you genuinely mean the dynamic viewport. For a full-bleed section inside a padded container the modern form is `margin-inline: calc(50% - 50vw)` with `overflow-x: clip` on a wrapper — and verify at 390px either way.
items.before: .hero { width: 100vw }
items.after: .hero { width: 100% }
items.false_positive_when: 100vw on a position:fixed overlay does not participate in document flow and cannot cause page overflow.

items.name: static-vh-full-height
items.description: 100vh or h-screen used for a full-height section.
items.detection: Regex for 100vh height declarations and h-screen utilities.
items.why_it_reads_ai: On mobile browsers 100vh is the viewport with the URL bar hidden, so a 100vh hero is taller than the screen until you scroll and its bottom is cut off on first paint. Visible instantly on a phone, invisible in a desktop screenshot.
items.fix: Use 100dvh with a 100vh fallback: `min-height: 100vh; min-height: 100dvh`. Better still, stop pinning the hero to the viewport — let the content decide the height.
items.before: .hero { min-height: 100vh }
items.after: .hero { min-height: 100vh; min-height: 100dvh }
items.false_positive_when: Desktop-only applications, and any layout already using dvh/svh/lvh units alongside it.

items.name: missing-html-lang
items.description: The root html element has no lang attribute.
items.detection: Absence of a lang attribute with a value on the html element. Binary and static.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Screen readers choose a voice and pronunciation model from it; without one they guess, and often read the page in the wrong phonology. One attribute, always in the scaffold, only missing in hand-assembled markup.
items.fix: Set it on the root: <html lang="en">. Use the real language, and a region subtag only where it changes pronunciation or formatting.
items.before: <html>
items.after: <html lang="en">
items.false_positive_when: Fragments and partials have no html element.

items.name: tailwind-play-cdn-in-production
items.description: A runtime-compiled CSS or JS CDN on a shipped page: the Tailwind Play CDN, babel-standalone, and their relatives.
items.detection: Script src matching the known runtime-compiler CDNs.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The Play CDN compiles your stylesheet in the visitor's browser on every page load, and its own documentation says it is for prototyping. Shipping it means the build step was never set up — the page was assembled to be looked at rather than deployed.
items.fix: Install the framework as a build dependency and ship a compiled stylesheet. For Tailwind that is the CLI or the Vite/PostCSS plugin; output is typically a few kilobytes against the CDN's several hundred, and it removes the flash of unstyled content.
items.before: <script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"></script>
items.after: <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.css">
items.false_positive_when: Genuine prototypes, CodePen-style demos, and documentation examples, where it is the correct tool.

items.name: h1-absent-or-competing
items.description: A page with no h1, or with several competing for the role.
items.detection: Count h1 elements in a document that has a body. Anything other than exactly one is the signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Headings get chosen for size rather than structure, because in the generation loop a heading is a type scale. The h1 is what a screen reader announces first and what search results lean on.
items.fix: Exactly one h1 per page, naming the page rather than the brand. Everything below steps down one level at a time without skipping. If you needed a second h1 for its size, style the h2 instead.
items.before:
Flowstate

...

Ship faster
items.after:
Flowstate: invoice reconciliation for finance teams

...

Ship faster
items.false_positive_when: Some documented design systems permit an h1 per landmark section; and a fragment legitimately has none.

items.name: no-meta-description-or-og-image
items.description: No meta description, no og:image, or both.
items.detection: Absence of the meta tags in a document head.
items.why_it_reads_ai: What the page looks like when shared or found, which is never visible while building it. Without an og:image a link unfurls as a grey box, which reads as abandoned.
items.fix: Write a meta description that says what the page offers in about 150 characters, and set an og:image at 1200x630 showing the actual product rather than the logo on a gradient. Check it with a link-preview debugger rather than assuming.
items.before: (no description, no og:image)
items.after: <meta name="description" content="..."> <meta property="og:image" content="...">
items.false_positive_when: Pages deliberately excluded from sharing and indexing, and documents whose meta tags are injected by a framework at build time rather than present in source.

items.name: input-without-label
items.description: Form inputs with no label element and no aria-label, relying on a placeholder to say what the field is.
items.detection: Count real inputs (excluding hidden, submit, button, reset) against labels and aria-label attributes.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A placeholder looks like a label in a screenshot, which is the only view the generation loop has. It disappears the moment someone types, and screen readers do not reliably announce it.
items.fix: Give every input a <label for> pointing at its id, or an aria-label where a visible label genuinely does not fit. Keep the placeholder for an example of the format rather than the field name. Then fill the form out with a keyboard only.
items.before: <input type="email" placeholder="Email">
items.after: <label for="email">Email</label><input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@company.com">
items.false_positive_when: A single search field with an adjacent icon and an accessible name supplied elsewhere, and inputs whose labels are composed by a wrapping component the detector cannot see.

items.name: form-without-destination
items.description: A form with no action and no submit handler. It looks complete and goes nowhere.
items.detection: Form elements carrying neither an action attribute nor a submit handler.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This one is genuinely model-flavoured rather than merely unreviewed. A generator produces a complete, convincing front end for a back end nobody asked for, and the failure is invisible until a real person types into it and presses send.
items.fix: Wire it to something, then submit it yourself and confirm the message arrives. If there is no destination yet, replace the form with a mailto link so the page makes an honest promise instead of a broken one.
items.before: <form><input name='email'><button>Notify me</button></form>
items.after: <form action="/api/subscribe" method="post">...</form>
items.false_positive_when: Forms whose handler is attached later in JavaScript, or bound by a framework directive the detector does not recognise. Verify by submitting it.

items.name: debug-residue-in-production
items.description: console.log, console.debug and debugger statements on a shipped page.
items.detection: Count console and debugger calls.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Working notes shipped to visitors. Harmless in itself, and a reliable sign nothing was reviewed on the way out.
items.fix: Strip them, or route logging through something that compiles out in production. While you are there, check whether any of them log a request or user object.
items.before: console.log("user", user)
items.after: (removed)
items.false_positive_when: Deliberate console banners (hiring messages, self-XSS warnings) are a long-standing convention, and development builds are expected to be noisy.

items.name: barrel-icon-import
items.description: An entire icon library imported as a namespace for the handful of icons actually used.
items.detection: Namespace imports from the common icon packages.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The import that makes every icon available is the one a generator reaches for, because it cannot know in advance which icons the page will end up using.
items.fix: Import by name: `import { Check, X } from 'lucide-react'`. Then confirm the bundle actually shrank — some of these packages need a per-icon path import before they tree-shake at all.
items.before: import * as Icons from 'lucide-react'
items.after: import { Check, X } from 'lucide-react'
items.false_positive_when: A dynamic icon picker that genuinely needs the whole set at runtime.

items.name: unbacked-social-proof
items.description: Trust signals with nothing behind them: 'join 10,000+ teams', star ratings with no reviews, a 'Trusted by' bar of logos belonging to companies that are not customers, badges for certifications not held.
items.detection: Judge: for each trust signal, can you name the thing it counts? A number with no source, a logo with no relationship, a rating with no reviews.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The template has a social-proof slot and the generator fills it, because an empty slot looks unfinished and a populated one looks successful. It is the visual-design sibling of the fabricated statistic.
items.fix: Delete anything you cannot substantiate. Real specificity beats invented scale: 'the four finance teams at Northwind run their month-end on this' is worth more than '10,000+ users' and has the advantage of being true. An empty section is better than a false one, and using a company's logo without permission is its own problem.
items.before: Trusted by 10,000+ teams  [six logos]
items.after: Used daily by the AP teams at Northwind and Calder. (Both agreed to be named.)
items.false_positive_when: Real numbers and real customers, obviously. The tell is a claim the site's own operator could not source if asked.

items.name: missing-interaction-states
items.description: The happy path only: no empty state, no error state, no loading state, no 404.
items.detection: Judge, or probe: request a bad route, submit an invalid form, throttle the network, and view a list with no items. Four states, four checks.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Generation optimises the screenshot, and the screenshot is always the full, successful, populated view. The other four states never appear in a design shot so nothing in the loop produces them.
items.fix: Build the four: an empty state that says what to do next, an error state that says what went wrong and what to try, a loading state that reserves the final layout, and a 404 that offers a route back. The empty state is the highest-value one, because every user sees it on day one.
items.before: A dashboard that renders a table. With no rows it renders headers over blank space.
items.after: With no rows it says what data goes here and links to the import flow.
items.false_positive_when: Static marketing pages have no states to miss. This applies to anything that loads or submits.

items.name: duplicated-component-markup
items.description: Three near-identical card or row blocks written out longhand instead of mapped over data.
items.detection: Judge, or diff sibling blocks for near-identity. Static detection is possible by normalising whitespace and text and comparing structural hashes of siblings.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A generator emits what the page looks like. Extracting a component requires deciding what varies, which is a modelling step the visual output does not require.
items.fix: Move the varying parts into an array and map over it. The test is whether adding a fourth item is one line of data or twenty of markup.
items.before: Three <div class='card'> blocks differing only in their heading and body text.
items.after: features.map(f => <Card key={f.id} {...f} />)
items.false_positive_when: Static HTML with no templating available, and blocks that only look similar while differing in ways a shared component would have to special-case.

items.name: eyebrow-with-no-information
items.description: The small uppercase label above a headline carrying no fact: INTRODUCING, FOR MODERN TEAMS, AI-POWERED, THE FUTURE OF WORK.
items.detection: Locate small uppercase or letterspaced elements; convict the ones containing no digit, no acronym or standard name, and no link. Capitalisation is deliberately NOT used as the signal, because 'For Modern Teams' is title-cased and says nothing.
items.why_it_reads_ai: An eyebrow is an editorial device that presumes a hierarchy: a publication, a section, an issue. A landing page with one section has nothing for it to be above. The slot exists in the template, so the generator fills it, and the filling has to come from somewhere when no fact is available. It is among the most-cited visual giveaways in practitioner threads for exactly this reason.
items.fix: Delete it and raise the headline. If the page reads identically you have proved it was decoration. If you keep one, make it carry the specific the headline cannot: SOC 2 TYPE II - FEB 2026, WORKS WITH POSTGRES 14+, OPEN SOURCE, AGPL-3.0. The rule of thumb is that an eyebrow must contain a proper noun, a number, a date or a licence. Then delete the eyebrow slot from the component itself, or the next generated section will fill it again.
items.before:
Introducing

The AI-powered workspace for modern teams
items.after: Turn Figma files into React components
items.false_positive_when: Editorial and documentation contexts where the eyebrow is a real taxonomy label (ENGINEERING, CHANGELOG, API REFERENCE, ISSUE 47) and navigates somewhere; conference pages carrying date and place; and brands whose whole system is editorial and where every eyebrow resolves to a real section. The question is not whether there is an eyebrow but whether it resolves to something a reader could navigate to or verify — which is why a linked eyebrow is never flagged.

items.name: pull-quote-that-quotes-nothing
items.description: A styled pull-quote block containing a sentence that appears nowhere else on the page and is attributed to nobody. An aphorism in quotation marks that no one ever said.
items.detection: Unusually clean, because a pull quote is DEFINED by a provenance relation: it is an excerpt of the document it sits in. So normalise the quote's text and search for a six-word window of it in the rest of the body. Flag when it appears zero times elsewhere AND carries no cite, figcaption or trailing attribution.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The pull quote is the one typographic device whose definition is a provenance relation, and a generator emitting it as visual rhythm breaks that relation invisibly. A pull quote is an excerpt; a block quotation cites something external. Generated text is neither — it is new text, from nowhere, wearing the costume of a quotation. The form makes a promise the content cannot keep, and a reader who goes looking for the speaker and finds none has learned something true about the page.
items.fix: In an article, replace it with the sharpest eight to fifteen words already in your body copy, and leave them in the body too: the pull quote is a trailer, not a scene. On a landing page there is no document to pull from, so it is a testimonial with a full name, role and company, or it is the founder's words attributed to the founder, or it is deleted. There is no fourth option. Mechanically: make the component require a source prop and fail the build when it is absent or does not appear in the page body.
items.before: "The best products don't just solve problems — they anticipate them."
items.false_positive_when: Epigraphs — a quotation at the head of a chapter from an external source, correctly attributed — are legitimate and by definition do not appear in the body, so a quote carrying a cite naming an external author is never flagged. Also quote-collection pages, walls of love, Tufte-style marginalia (authorial commentary, not quotation), and lyric fragments used as section openers. The discriminator: cited-but-external is an epigraph, uncited-and-internal is a pull quote, uncited-and-external-to-everything is the tell.

items.name: hero-with-nothing-to-look-at
items.description: A hero with no screenshot, photograph, illustration, diagram or video — only type on a gradient or a flat ground. The visual budget goes entirely to a background treatment carrying no information about the product.
items.detection: Within the hero region, count img, picture, video, canvas, iframe and substantial svg elements, excluding logos and small icons. Zero is the signal.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Two causes, both diagnostic. A generator cannot screenshot a product it has never run, so the visual slot resolves to the only thing it can synthesise from CSS: a gradient. And placeholder copy produces placeholder layout — the hero has no image because there is nothing real to show yet. An image-less hero is a claim that nothing is worth showing, which for a working product is always false, and the reader correctly infers that the product does not exist, is ugly, or has not been used by anyone involved.
items.fix: Show the product, in descending order of what it proves. A real screenshot of a real screen with real data in it, cropped to the one view that makes the value legible, shipped at 2x through a picture element. Or a five-to-fifteen second silent loop of it doing its one thing, which beats a still for anything streaming or animated. Or a diagram of the mechanism, which is the honest answer for infrastructure with no interface. If there genuinely is no product yet, say so and make the hero the argument for the waitlist — that is not a tell. Hiding pre-product status behind a gradient and a Get Started button is. Never fix this by generating an illustration.
items.before:
...

...
items.after: The same hero plus a screenshot of the actual migration diff view, three real table names visible, one shadow, no device frame.
items.false_positive_when: Products with no visual surface (a DNS provider, a payments API, a law firm); type-led brand systems that commit fully, where the typography IS the demonstration and is doing something rather than being Inter at 64px; deliberately minimal utility pages where the working tool is the hero, which is the strongest version of this pattern rather than a fault; search-first homepages; and pre-launch pages that admit it.

items.name: undifferentiated-section-padding
items.description: Every section on the page padded identically. Hero, feature grid, testimonial, FAQ and footer all get the same vertical space.
items.detection: Collect vertical padding values across sections; flag when four or more sections share exactly one value.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Spacing used as a constant rather than as a relationship. Nothing is grouped with anything and nothing is separated from anything, so the page becomes a stack of equally weighted slabs and the reader gets no signal about what belongs together. Choosing one value is what you do when you have not decided which sections matter.
items.fix: Vary it by role. Give the hero more room than it needs and the sections after it less; tighten the gap between a heading and the thing it introduces; widen it between unrelated sections. A three-step scale used deliberately reads as designed. One value everywhere reads as a default, which is what it is.
items.before: Five sections, every one py-24.
items.after: Hero py-32, feature grid py-20, and eight of those units between a heading and its own paragraph.
items.false_positive_when: Documentation and long-form article templates legitimately use one rhythm throughout, and a design system with a documented spacing scale may deliberately standardise section padding.

items.name: mechanism-never-named
items.description: The page describes outcomes and never says how the thing works. You finish it unable to explain the product to someone else.
items.detection: Judge: after reading the page, write one sentence explaining the mechanism. If you cannot, the page never gave you one.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Placeholder copy produces placeholder layout, and the causal arrow runs that way. A generator writing from a product name and a category has outcomes available to it and no mechanism, so it writes the half it has.
items.fix: Add the sentence that says what actually happens: what goes in, what the system does, what comes out. It is usually one sentence and it is usually the most valuable one on the page.
items.before: Empower your team to do more with less.
items.after: We watch your bank feed and match each line to an invoice; the 2% we cannot match go to whoever owns that ledger.
items.false_positive_when: Brand and campaign pages that deliberately withhold detail, and products whose mechanism is genuinely the category (a font shop sells fonts).

items.name: numerology-of-three
items.description: Three features, three tiers, three testimonials, three steps — regardless of how many real ones exist.
items.detection: Judge: is three the true count, or the count that fills a row? Ask what the fourth would be and whether the third earns its place.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Three is what you pick when the number of real things is unknown, and it happens to fill a grid. The layout chose the content rather than the other way round.
items.fix: Count the real things and show that many. Two strong features beat three where the third is padding, and a five-item list that does not fit a grid is a reason to change the grid.
items.before: Three feature cards, the third of which restates the first.
items.after: Two features, each with a screenshot.
items.false_positive_when: Plenty of products genuinely have three tiers, and the rule of three is a real compositional device. The tell is a third item that restates or pads.

items.name: subhead-restates-the-h1
items.description: The line under the headline says the headline again in different words, spending the most valuable position on the page on nothing.
items.detection: Judge: does the subhead add a fact the h1 lacks? If deleting it loses nothing, it was restatement.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The template has a subhead slot and the generator has one idea, so the idea gets said twice.
items.fix: Make the subhead carry what the headline could not: who it is for, what it costs, what it replaces, or the number that makes the claim credible.
items.before: H1: Ship faster with AI-powered workflows. Sub: Empower your team to do more with less.
items.after: H1: Turn Figma files into React components. Sub: Ships typed props and variants; works with your existing design tokens.
items.false_positive_when: A subhead that deliberately expands a deliberately terse headline is doing its job, not restating.

items.name: cta-names-the-click-not-the-outcome
items.description: 'Get Started', 'Learn More', 'Get Started Free' — buttons that describe the act of clicking rather than what happens next.
items.detection: Judge: does the label say what the reader will have, or only that they will proceed?
items.why_it_reads_ai: The most-represented button label in the training corpus, and the one that commits to nothing. A model that does not know what the next screen is cannot name it.
items.fix: Name the outcome and the cost: 'Start a 14-day trial, no card', 'See it run on your repo', 'Book 20 minutes'. If you cannot name the next screen, that is worth knowing before you ship the button.
items.before: Get Started Free
items.after: Start a 14-day trial — no card
items.false_positive_when: 'Get started' above a genuine multi-step onboarding is accurate, and established products can rely on a bare label the reader already understands.

items.name: uniform-explanatory-depth
items.description: Everything explained at the same level of detail, so nothing is marked as hard. The reader cannot tell which two ideas actually needed the effort.
items.detection: Judge: name the two hardest ideas in the piece, then check whether they got more room than the easy ones. Equal room is the finding.
items.why_it_reads_ai: This is altitude lock, and it is the strongest evidence that context leakage is not the whole story: it persists when the audience is stated in the prompt. Explanations generated for different stated audiences come out indistinguishable in reading level, and match their intended level about half the time against roughly four-fifths for human-written ones. A model has a set readability range and does not move off it on request.
items.fix: Supply the depth plan yourself, because prompting will not produce one. Decide which two ideas are hard, give each a worked example, and cut the easy ones to a sentence. The shape of good exposition is uneven on purpose, and the unevenness is the signal to the reader about where to slow down.
items.before: Six sections, each three paragraphs, covering install, config, the consistency model, logging, the CLI, and the consistency model's failure mode.
items.after: Two paragraphs on install. Nine on the consistency model, with a worked example. One line each on logging and the CLI.
items.false_positive_when: Reference documentation is uniform by design and correctly so — every entry gets the same treatment because readers arrive at one and leave. Scope this to anything meant to be read start to finish.
items.evidence: ELI-Why, arXiv:2506.14200 (13.4K why-questions, two human studies); Know Your Audience, arXiv:2312.02065.

items.name: no-worked-example
items.description: Abstractions with no concrete instance. The piece defines, categorises and qualifies, and never once shows the thing happening.
items.detection: Judge: count the places the text moves from a general claim to a specific instance with real values in it. Zero in a long explanatory piece is the finding.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Also altitude lock. A worked example requires committing to particular values, which is where a model is most likely to be wrong, so the safest output stays general. The reader is left holding a definition they cannot apply.
items.fix: For each hard idea, show one instance end to end with real numbers, real names, real output. If you cannot produce one, you have found something you do not understand yet, which is worth knowing before publishing.
items.before: Exponential backoff increases the delay between retries to reduce contention.
items.after: Exponential backoff increases the delay between retries: 1s, then 2s, then 4s. Our third retry lands at 4s, by which point the dogpile that caused the failure has usually cleared.
items.false_positive_when: Reference pages, API listings and conceptual overviews that explicitly hand off to a tutorial.

items.name: abstraction-jump-no-rung
items.description: The prose moves between levels of abstraction with no transition: a sentence about business outcomes followed by a sentence about a mutex, with nothing between them.
items.detection: Judge: read consecutive paragraphs and ask whether each is at the same altitude as its neighbour, or whether a rung is missing.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Altitude lock again. Holding a ladder of abstraction requires modelling where the reader currently stands, and the model has one register it returns to regardless.
items.fix: Add the missing rung, which is usually one sentence naming the mechanism that connects the two levels. Read consecutive paragraphs aloud and listen for the place your voice would have to change.
items.before: This cuts month-end close from five days to two. The scheduler takes a lease with a ninety-second TTL.
items.after: This cuts month-end close from five days to two, because nothing waits on a human to unblock a stuck job any more. The scheduler does that by taking a lease with a ninety-second TTL, so a dead worker's claim expires on its own.
items.false_positive_when: Deliberate rhetorical juxtaposition, and pieces that establish the ladder early and can then move freely on it.

items.name: how-it-works-that-says-what
items.description: A 'How it works' section that describes what the system does rather than how or why, restating the feature list in longer sentences.
items.detection: Judge, or compute: the ratio of sentences stating a mechanism or a reason to sentences restating a capability. This is the single most-quoted complaint in the reader corpus.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Template completion. The heading is a slot and the model fills it from what it has, which is the feature list. Mechanism requires knowing the implementation; capability can be inferred from the name.
items.fix: Every sentence under that heading should answer how or why. If a sentence would survive unchanged under the heading 'Features', it belongs there instead or nowhere. Name the data path, the decision, the trade-off you took.
items.before:
## How it works

Flowstate automatically syncs your data and keeps everything up to date in real time.
items.after:
## How it works

We hold a logical replication slot on your primary and stream the WAL. That means we see a row change about 200ms after your database does, and it also means we cannot see anything that never hits the WAL, like a truncate.
items.false_positive_when: Marketing pages where the section is deliberately non-technical, and products whose mechanism is genuinely proprietary — though in that case say so rather than filling the space.

items.name: promised-idea-never-delivered
items.description: The piece sets up an idea it never returns to. A question posed in the opening, a tension introduced, a 'we will come back to this' that never comes back.
items.detection: Judge: list every promise the opening makes, then check each against the body. An unclosed loop is the finding.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Template completion. An opening that raises a question is a learned move; closing it requires holding the promise across the whole document, which nothing in the generation loop enforces.
items.fix: Close the loop or cut the setup. Usually cutting is right, because the setup was rhetorical furniture rather than a real question. If it was a real question, answering it is probably the best part of the piece.
items.before: The interesting part is what happens when the clock skews — more on that below. [no more on that below]
items.after: The interesting part is what happens when the clock skews. [three paragraphs on clock skew]
items.false_positive_when: Part one of a stated series, and pieces that explicitly defer to a linked follow-up.

items.name: decision-without-alternatives
items.description: 'We decided to go with X' where the reader never learns what else was on the table or what criteria settled it.
items.detection: Judge: for each stated decision, is there a named alternative and a reason one won?
items.why_it_reads_ai: Context leakage. The alternatives were discussed in a thread the reader was not in, and the conclusion is the only part that reached the page.
