items.fix: Name the alternative and the thing that decided it, in one sentence. That sentence is usually the most useful in the piece, because it is the part a reader facing the same choice can actually reuse.
items.before: We decided to go with Postgres.
items.after: We went with Postgres over DynamoDB because our access pattern needs joins across four tables and we were not willing to denormalise them.
items.false_positive_when: Pieces about a decision already documented elsewhere and linked, and contexts where the alternatives are obvious to the stated audience.

items.name: dead-internal-cross-reference
items.description: 'See the section on X' where there is no section on X; a link to an anchor that does not exist; a reference to a page that was never written.
items.detection: Pure name and link resolution: every internal anchor, every 'see the X section', every relative link. Zero judgment required, and it belongs in CI.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The model refers to the document it would have written. Nothing in the loop resolves the reference against the document that exists.
items.fix: Resolve every internal reference mechanically and fix or delete each miss. This is the highest yield-per-effort check in the whole exposition family because it needs no taste at all.
items.before: See the configuration section below for details. [there is no configuration section]
items.after: [section written, or the sentence deleted]
items.false_positive_when: Documents generated into a larger site where anchors resolve at build time rather than in source. Resolve against the built output in that case.

items.name: obligatory-dual-cta
items.description: The hero always carries exactly two buttons side by side, one solid and one ghost: 'Get Started Free' plus 'Learn More'.
items.detection: Count buttons and anchors in the hero; flag a pair where one is filled and one is outline or ghost.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The hero component has two button slots, so two buttons appear. It is not two audiences with two next steps; the secondary almost always points at the section immediately below it, which the reader would have reached by scrolling.
items.fix: Decide what the one next step is and offer that. Keep a second action only when it serves a genuinely different reader, and then make its label name that reader's outcome rather than 'Learn more'.
items.before: Get Started FreeLearn More
items.after: Start a 14-day trial — no card
items.false_positive_when: Products with two genuinely distinct entry points (self-serve and sales-assisted) legitimately offer both, and a documented design system may standardise the pair.

items.name: triplicate-grid
items.description: The same three-column card grid used for features, then benefits, then testimonials, then pricing. One layout answering every content shape.
items.detection: Count three-column grid containers on the page.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The grid was chosen once and reused, because choosing per section requires knowing what each section contains. It is the layout equivalent of one register for every genre.
items.fix: Let each content shape pick its own container. Two features with screenshots want something different from five testimonials, and a pricing table is not a card grid. When every section looks the same the reader stops distinguishing them.
items.before: Four sections, all grid-cols-3.
items.after: Features as two wide rows with screenshots; testimonials as a single quote; pricing as a table.
items.false_positive_when: A deliberate modular system, and pages where the content genuinely is three parallel things three times over.

items.name: magnitudes-without-a-baseline
items.description: '10x faster.' 'Cut costs by 40%.' A comparative claim with no comparand, no method and no source.
items.detection: Match multipliers and improvement frames attached to numbers, then check the surrounding block for a comparison target, a measurement method, a date or an outbound link. A bare percentage is deliberately NOT matched: a proportion is not a claim.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The figure does the rhetorical work of evidence while carrying none of the risk, which is exactly what a generator reaches for when it has no measurement to report. It is the visual-design sibling of the fabricated statistic.
items.fix: Give every number its denominator and its method, or delete it. 'Median build time fell from 4m12s to 1m50s across our own CI over March' beats '3x faster' and cannot be doubted the same way.
items.before: 10x faster. Save 40% on costs.
items.after: Median build time fell from 4m12s to 1m50s, measured across our own CI over March.
items.false_positive_when: Claims with the comparand and method already attached pass and should. Regulated industries often have approved comparative language with the substantiation held elsewhere and linked.

items.name: testimonial-with-no-traceable-source
items.description: A quote attributed to 'Sarah C., Product Manager' with a generated face. A first name, a job title, no company, no link.
items.detection: Placeholder avatar hosts (pravatar, randomuser, ui-avatars, thispersondoesnotexist) are the cleanest signal, plus first-name-plus-initial attribution patterns. Near-zero false positive on the avatar hosts: no real customer has a portrait served from a random-face API.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Nothing in the attribution can be checked, which is the design rather than an oversight. The template has a testimonial slot and a testimonial needs a face, so a face is fetched from wherever faces come from.
items.fix: Get a real name, role, company and a link, or take the section down. One checkable quote outperforms five unfalsifiable ones, and a page with no testimonials is more credible than a page with invented ones.
items.before: Sarah C., Product Manager
items.after: Priya Raman, Staff SRE at Calder — read the write-up
items.false_positive_when: Design-system documentation and component galleries use placeholder avatars correctly. Anonymised testimonials from regulated or security-sensitive customers are legitimate when the page says why the name is withheld.

items.name: one-family-no-contrast
items.description: Display and body set in the same typeface, differentiated only by size and weight. Headlines are body text made large.
items.detection: Count distinct non-monospace font families in use; flag a page with exactly one and a display heading.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Pairing is a decision and a single family is a default. Nothing in the generation loop rewards the second choice.
items.fix: Pair a display face with the text face, or at minimum set an optical-size axis so the headline is drawn for headline sizes. One good pairing does more for a page than any amount of spacing work.
items.before: Inter for everything, 400 and 700.
items.after: A display serif at the headline, the grotesque kept for body.
items.false_positive_when: Single-family systems are a real and respected choice, especially with a variable font carrying genuine optical sizing. This is low severity for exactly that reason.

items.name: centred-body-copy
items.description: Centring applied to paragraphs and not just headings, so every block has a ragged left edge.
items.detection: Count centred text blocks across the page.
items.why_it_reads_ai: It looks balanced in a thumbnail, which is the view the generation loop optimises. It reads badly at full size because the eye loses the line start.
items.fix: Centre headings if you like; left-align anything over two lines. The left edge is what the eye returns to, and a ragged one costs the reader on every line.
items.before: Every card body centred.
items.after: Headings centred, bodies left-aligned.
items.false_positive_when: Short hero subheads, pull quotes, and genuinely centred editorial layouts. The threshold is set high because a few centred blocks are ordinary.

items.name: untouched-default-icon-set
items.description: The default icon library at default stroke width, with the worn glyph set: Sparkles beside anything AI, Zap beside anything fast, ArrowRight on every button.
items.detection: Library import signature plus the specific glyph names.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Not the library, which is good, but the glyph choice. These are the icons a generator picks because they are the icons the training data picks, and they name the adjective rather than the thing.
items.fix: Choose glyphs that name the actual noun: if the feature is scheduling, the icon is a calendar, not a lightning bolt. Drop Sparkles entirely, which now reads as a label saying AI went here.
items.before: Sparkles, Zap, ArrowRight across the feature grid.
items.after: Calendar, Database, ArrowUpRight — each naming what its card is about.
items.false_positive_when: A well-chosen icon set used consistently is good practice, and these libraries are genuinely good. The tell is the specific worn triad, not the library.

items.name: reveal-animation-on-everything
items.description: Every element fades and rises into view on scroll, so the motion marks nothing and delays everything.
items.detection: Count scroll-entrance animation usages.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Motion applied by rule rather than to direct attention. Deciding which one element deserves an entrance requires knowing which one matters.
items.fix: Animate the one element whose arrival is the point and let the rest be present when the page is. Then add the prefers-reduced-motion guard, which a page with this much motion needs and almost never has.
items.before: Twelve elements sharing one fade-up variant with a stagger.
items.after: A static page with one deliberate transition where state actually changes.
items.false_positive_when: Motion systems with a documented entrance token, and long marketing pages that use entrance motion deliberately for pacing.

items.name: h1-names-a-category-not-a-product
items.description: The headline is a value proposition or a category description rather than a statement of what the thing is. The canonical form is a mad-lib: 'The AI-powered X for modern Y.'
items.detection: Judge: after reading only the hero, can you name one thing the product does? A structural pre-filter is possible on the template shapes and on headlines containing no verb describing an action the software performs.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A generator given a product name and a category has the category available and the mechanism not. The reader finishes the hero knowing which aisle the product is shelved in and nothing else.
items.fix: Say what it does, with a verb and an object. 'Turn Figma files into React components' beats any arrangement of platform, workspace, and modern teams. Test it by asking whether a competitor could use the same headline unchanged.
items.before: The AI-powered workspace for modern teams
items.after: Turn Figma files into React components
items.false_positive_when: Category-defining products genuinely name a category, and established brands can lead with positioning because the reader already knows the mechanism.

items.name: mockup-of-nothing
items.description: A hero visual that is chrome without a product: a browser frame or device bezel around an interface that does not exist, with invented chart shapes and plausible-but-fictional nav items.
items.detection: Judge: is this a screenshot of a running application or an illustration of one? Look for data following a real distribution, labels naming domain-specific nouns, scrollbars, focus rings, timestamps, truncation, and empty states. A structural hint: a hero 'screenshot' built as a DOM tree or inline SVG rather than a raster, because a real screenshot is almost never hand-rebuilt in markup.
items.why_it_reads_ai: More dishonest than the image-less hero, because it makes a claim. A generator cannot screenshot software it has never run, but it can draw something that looks like one.
items.fix: Replace it with a real screenshot, cropped to the view that makes the value legible, with real data in it. If the product is not built, an honest diagram of the intended mechanism is better than a fake of the finished thing.
items.before: A MacBook bezel around a hand-drawn dashboard with Project Alpha, Project Beta, Project Gamma.
items.after: A screenshot of the real queue with three real table names in it.
items.false_positive_when: Deliberate illustration clearly presented as illustration, and pre-release products showing a design mock labelled as one.

items.name: bullet-restates-its-own-title
items.description: Each feature card has a two-word title and a body that is the title again as a sentence. 'Real-time sync — Keep everything in sync, in real time.'
items.detection: Content-word overlap between a card's title and its body, discounting stopwords. Flag when most of the title's content words reappear and the body adds no proper noun, numeral or unit.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The card has a body slot, so a body is generated, and the only guaranteed-relevant content for that slot is the title it sits under.
items.fix: Make the body say the thing the title cannot: the mechanism, the limit, the number. If you cannot, delete the body and let the title stand alone.
items.before: **Real-time sync** — Keep everything in sync, in real time.
items.after: **Real-time sync** — Changes land in about 200ms; we stream the WAL rather than polling.
items.false_positive_when: A deliberately redundant summary line for scanning, and accessibility patterns where the body expands an abbreviated title.

items.name: fixed-section-order
items.description: Hero, logo bar, three features, testimonial, pricing, CTA, in that order, regardless of what the product is or what a visitor needs to believe first.
items.detection: Classify top-level sections and compare the sequence against the canonical order. Report once per page rather than per section.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The order is the template's, not the argument's. Deciding what a reader must believe first requires knowing who the reader is.
items.fix: Decide the one thing a visitor must believe before anything else, and put the section that establishes it first. For a product nobody has heard of that is usually the demonstration, not the logo bar.
items.before: The canonical six-section stack.
items.after: Demonstration, then the objection it raises, then the answer, then pricing.
items.false_positive_when: The canonical order is canonical because it often works, and a page following it deliberately is not at fault. The tell is following it without having considered an alternative.

items.name: stock-collaboration-photography
items.description: The diverse team around a laptop, mid-laugh, pointing at a screen that is not the product. Or its generated successor: same composition, same lighting, nobody real.
items.detection: Judge: is this a photograph of this company's people, customers or product in use, or a generic image of work happening? Structural hints include stock-CDN filenames and hosts, and the same image on several pages.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The image occupies the space where evidence would go. It is the visual form of copy that names no mechanism.
items.fix: Photograph your actual team, your actual customer, or your actual screen. A worse photograph of a real thing beats a better photograph of nothing.
items.before: Smiling team around a laptop, stock CDN.
items.after: The three people who built it, at their desks, badly lit.
items.false_positive_when: Licensed stock used knowingly for mood on a brand page, and industries where showing real customers is not permitted.

items.name: measure-past-75-characters
items.description: Body text running the full width of a wide container: 100, 130, 160 characters per line. No constraint on the text column, so the layout's width became the text's width.
items.detection: Rendered: measure a sample string in each paragraph's own computed font on a canvas, divide the element's content width by the resulting advance width. scripts/render_check.py reports the actual characters-per-line rather than estimating from font size.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Nobody decided the width. A generator sets a container and puts prose in it; constraining the text column is a separate decision that only matters once someone reads a full paragraph on a wide screen, which nothing in the loop does.
items.fix: Constrain the text column rather than the page: max-width around 65ch on the element holding prose, or a grid whose text column is narrower than its media column. 45 to 75 characters is the conventional range and 66 the usual target. Note ch units track the font's zero-width, so check the result rather than trusting the number.
items.before: .wrap { padding: 2rem }   /* measured 167 characters per line at 1280px */
items.after: .wrap { padding: 2rem; max-width: 65ch; margin-inline: auto }
items.false_positive_when: Data tables, code blocks, and dashboard cells are not prose and want the width. Deliberately wide editorial layouts with large type can exceed the range legibly, which is why this measures characters rather than pixels.

items.name: hand-rolled-div-dialog
items.description: A modal built as a div wearing role=dialog with a hand-written overlay, instead of the native dialog element or a maintained primitive.
items.detection: Flag role="dialog" or role="alertdialog" in a file containing no <dialog> tag and no dialog primitive import. The highest-confidence static check in the app-interior lane.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The most empirically model-flavoured tell available. In a 720-trial baseline, 673 generated modals hand-rolled role=dialog on a div and about 2% used native <dialog>, with native use essentially confined to one model family. The mechanism is training distribution: the web's modal corpus is overwhelmingly pre-<dialog> overlays. The consequence is measurable, because native dialogs closed on Escape 98% of the time against 31% for hand-rolled ones.
items.fix: Use native <dialog> opened with showModal(), or a maintained primitive such as Radix Dialog or React Aria. Both supply focus trap, Escape, top-layer stacking and background inertness with no hand-written code, so delete the overlay, the keydown listener and the tab-cycling logic. With native <dialog> you should NOT hand-trap focus: absent trap code there is correct, not a finding.
items.before: ...
items.after: <dialog ref={ref}>...</dialog>  // opened with ref.current.showModal()
items.evidence: Featherstone, ~720-trial markup baseline and ~3,000-trial operability study, six-model panel.
items.false_positive_when: Rare. This is a defect you can reproduce by opening the page, not an inference about who built it — but check whether the file is a fragment, a template, or a generated artifact before filing it against an author.

items.name: escape-and-focus-declared-not-wired
items.description: Escape handling, a focus trap or focus restoration written in source and not working at runtime.
items.detection: Static detection can only find the DECLARATION and say so. Settling it needs a browser: open by keyboard, press Escape, assert closed; reopen, Tab past the last control, assert focus never leaves the dialog; close, assert focus returned to the trigger.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The canonical model signature, with the cleanest numbers anywhere in this catalog. Escape handlers were present in 79% of generated modals and worked in 59%, and 1,031 of 1,032 failures threw no console error, so the failure is invisible to every non-interactive check. Focus containment was worse: only 12% held focus on a bare prompt.
items.fix: Stop hand-writing it: native <dialog> with showModal(), or Radix or React Aria with their defaults left alone. If custom code must stay, the required set is focus in on open, Tab and Shift+Tab contained, Escape closes, focus restored to the trigger, background scroll locked and background content inert. Then drive it in a browser, because this is the one entry where source review provably does not suffice. Note that asking a model for accessibility can reduce basic function: 'make it accessible using <dialog>' scored 80% working opens against 98% for the plainer instruction.
items.before: a useEffect adding keydown on document, registered on the wrong element or shadowed by a stopPropagation in the overlay
items.after: native <dialog>, plus the Playwright assertions above running in CI
items.false_positive_when: Non-modal dialogs and popovers have a different keyboard contract, and stacked dialogs move focus to the topmost layer on purpose. Crucially: with native <dialog> you do not need to hand-trap focus, so ABSENCE of trap code there is correct. Only ever flag on driven behaviour, never on missing trap code.
items.evidence: Featherstone operability study: handlers present 79% / working 59%; 1,031 of 1,032 failures silent; focus fully held 12% bare, 64% guided.

items.name: missing-autofill-attributes
items.description: Form inputs with no autocomplete tokens, so the browser cannot fill a form it could otherwise complete in one tap.
items.detection: Ratio of typed inputs carrying an autocomplete attribute to those without.
items.why_it_reads_ai: Invisible in a screenshot, which is where the generation loop looks. The field renders identically with and without it.
items.fix: Add the standard tokens: autocomplete="email", "given-name", "family-name", "street-address", "postal-code", "tel", "current-password", "new-password", "one-time-code". Pair with inputmode and the right type so mobile keyboards match the field. This costs everyone and costs people with motor and cognitive disabilities most.
items.before: <input type="text" placeholder="Email">
items.after: <input type="email" autocomplete="email" inputmode="email" id="email">
items.false_positive_when: Search fields, one-off inputs with no autofill meaning, and forms deliberately opting out for security reasons such as a passphrase confirmation.

items.name: table-without-sort-filter-paging
items.description: A multi-column table with no sort, no filter and no pagination.
items.detection: Column count against the presence of sort, filter or pagination affordances.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A table's usefulness depends almost entirely on behaviour, and a generated one arrives with the markup and none of it. It renders correctly with the eight rows in the mock and becomes unusable at eight hundred, which is a state no mock contains.
items.fix: Decide what a user does with this table and build that: sort on the columns people order by, a filter for the field they scan, and pagination or virtualisation past a few hundred rows. Show the row count so people know what they are looking at, and keep the sort control a real button.
items.before: <table> with eight columns and no controls
items.after: sortable headers as buttons with aria-sort, a filter on the one field people scan, a row count, and pagination
items.false_positive_when: Small fixed tables (a pricing comparison, a spec sheet) neither need nor want controls. This keys on column count as a proxy for a data table; a four-column spec table is a false positive worth ignoring.

items.name: sort-header-not-button-no-aria-sort
items.description: A sort affordance announced with aria-sort but not operable from a keyboard, or a sort caret with no aria-sort at all.
items.detection: aria-sort present on a header containing no button element.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A pure declared-but-unwired case: the visible and announced half of the pattern shipped and the interactive half did not.
items.fix: Put a real button inside the th and keep aria-sort on the th itself, updating it between ascending, descending and none as the state changes. Announce the change in a live region if the sort happens without a page transition.
items.before: <th aria-sort="none">Name</th>
items.after: <th aria-sort="none"><button type="button" onClick={sortByName}>Name</button></th>
items.false_positive_when: Header cells made interactive by a table library that injects the control at runtime rather than in source.

items.name: unbounded-spinner-no-error-path
items.description: A loading state with no corresponding error state, so a request that never returns spins forever.
items.detection: Presence of loading indicators with no error handling in the same component.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The request that never returns is the commonest real-world failure and the one a mock never shows. The generated component has a state for waiting and none for having waited too long.
items.fix: Give every async surface three states rather than two: loading, loaded, and failed with a message naming what failed and a control to retry. Add a timeout so the failed state is reachable without needing a server error to produce it.
items.before: if (isLoading) return <Spinner />
items.after: if (error) return <Failed onRetry={refetch} reason={error.message} />; if (isLoading) return <Spinner />
items.false_positive_when: Error handling supplied by a parent boundary, a framework-level error route, or a data library's global handler.

items.name: settings-flat-toggle-wall
items.description: Every configuration key rendered as a switch, in schema order, with no grouping and no indication of which values are defaults.
items.detection: Toggle count against the presence of fieldset, legend or group roles.
items.why_it_reads_ai: The screen is a faithful rendering of the data model rather than a designed view, which is what you get when the model is the only thing available to design from. One of the three recurring app-interior signatures, alongside declared-but-unwired and content whose cardinality matches a layout constant.
items.fix: Group by what a person came to change, label each group with a legend, and mark defaults. Most settings screens halve once you ask which of these anyone has ever needed to touch, and the ones that survive deserve an explanation of what changes when they do.
items.before: Nine switches in a column, in the order the config object declares them.
items.after: Three labelled groups, defaults marked, the four nobody uses removed.
items.false_positive_when: Advanced or developer settings panels are legitimately exhaustive and flat, and power users often prefer them that way.

items.name: kpi-card-without-comparison
items.description: A KPI tile rendering one number and a label, with no delta, no prior period, no target and no unit context. 'Revenue $48,291' answers no question, because the reader cannot tell whether it is good.
items.detection: Judge, or count: a stat card whose content is exactly one interpolated value plus a static label, with no comparison affordance. Ratio form: comparison-carrying cards over total cards in a KPI row.
items.why_it_reads_ai: A number is renderable from a single query; a comparison requires deciding what it should be compared against, which is a judgment about the business rather than the data. The generated dashboard shows what is easy to fetch.
items.fix: Every metric needs a comparand: the prior period, the target, or the distribution. If you cannot say what good looks like for a number, it does not belong on a dashboard, because nobody can act on it.
items.before: Revenue  $48,291
items.after: Revenue  $48,291   +12% vs last month   target $52,000
items.false_positive_when: A live counter or a status readout where the current value genuinely is the whole answer, and dashboards whose comparison lives in an adjacent chart.

sources.note: 8,290 parallel human/LLM texts over a 66-feature Biber tagset. Present participial clauses at 5.3x the human rate (d=1.38) is the top-ranked discriminating feature; nominalizations at 2.1x. The authors explicitly refuse the detector framing and argue for 'teachable moments in the revision of machine-generated text' — which is this skill's whole posture.

sources.note: 15M+ PubMed abstracts. 'Delves' excess ratio 28.0; at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts LLM-processed. The methodological finding matters more than the word list: pre-2024 excess words were 79% nouns (content), 2024 excess words 66% verbs (style).

sources.title: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu & Zou, 'GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers', Patterns 4(7):100779 (2023)
sources.note: Seven detectors, 61.3% mean false-positive rate on TOEFL essays; 19% flagged by all seven unanimously. Prompting for more native-sounding word choice dropped misclassification from 61.3% to 11.6% — proving the detectors measure fluency, not machine-ness.

sources.title: Weber-Wulff et al., 'Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text', International Journal for Educational Integrity 19:26 (2023)
sources.note: 14 tools, 756 tests. No tool exceeded 80% accuracy; GPTZero produced a 50% false-accusation rate on human text. Accuracy falls to ~45% on lightly human-edited AI text, so the detectors miss the machines and catch the people.

sources.title: van Nuenen, 'Voice Under Revision: LLMs and the Normalization of Personal Narrative', arXiv:2604.22142 (2026)
sources.note: The best study of what LLM EDITING does, with 13 markers and effect sizes: dashes +325.7%, commas +66.6%, contractions -31.4%, first-person pronouns -8.6%, lexical diversity +52.7%. Voice-preserving prompts recover only 10-15% of what is removed.

sources.title: Abdulhai et al., 'How LLMs Distort Our Written Language', arXiv:2603.18161 (2026)
sources.note: Adjectives +40-87% even under explicit minimal-edit prompts; pronouns -40-61%; a 68.9% increase in essays that take no position. Human-editor baseline is under 5% change in any POS category.

sources.title: Hart, Allred, Abbas & Alugo, 'The Deontic Gap', arXiv:2608.18144 (2026)
sources.note: Eleven-model replication. Personal deontic modals (should, have to, can't) sit at the 3.7th percentile of underuse — more underused than 96% of common vocabulary, so not a generic frequency artifact.

sources.title: Munoz-Ortiz, Gomez-Rodriguez & Vilares, 'Contrasting linguistic patterns in human and LLM-generated news text', Artificial Intelligence Review 57:267 (2024)
sources.note: The peer-reviewed basis for the sentence-length claim: human texts have more scattered length distributions, models cluster at 10-30 tokens, all differences p<0.001. Cite this rather than 'burstiness', which is a detection product's marketing vocabulary, not a term of art.

sources.title: Vanderbilt University, 'Guidance on AI detection and why we're disabling Turnitin's AI detector' (2023)
sources.note: The institutional arithmetic: a claimed 1% false-positive rate across 75,000 papers is 750 wrongly accused students. Northwestern, Michigan State and UT Austin followed.

sources.note: Withdrawn six months after launch 'due to its low rate of accuracy'. At launch it caught 26% of AI text and falsely flagged 9% of human text.

sources.title: Simon Willison, 'Delve' (2024), summarizing Alex Hern's Guardian TechScape
sources.note: The fairness problem at the root of the best-known tell: 'delve' is markedly more common in Nigerian formal English, and the RLHF annotation workforce that rewarded it was substantially Nigerian and Kenyan. A list that flags 'delve' is mechanically a list that flags a dialect.

sources.title: GIJN, 'Reporter's Guide to Detecting AI-Generated Content'
sources.note: Why the hands-and-text image heuristic is retired, and what replaced it: provenance first — C2PA/Content Credentials, EXIF, reverse image search, publisher sourcing.

Ask a model to design a landing page without giving it real content and it will invent placeholder copy - and placeholder copy produces placeholder layout.'

sources.title: Pull quote - Wikipedia
sources.note: The definition that makes pull-quote provenance checkable: 'a key phrase, quotation, or excerpt that has been PULLED from an article and used as a page layout graphic element.' A pull quote that appears nowhere else in its document is not a pull quote.

sources.title: Block Quotes and Pull Quotes: Examples and Good Practices - Smashing Magazine
sources.note: Draws the line the detector implements: pull quotes are excerpts of the presented text, while block quotations refer to an external citation not already in the article. Also the density guidance: an ordinary article should carry at most one or two.

sources.title: ELI-Why: benchmarking the pedagogical utility of LLM explanations (arXiv:2506.14200)
sources.note: The evidence that breaks the tidy unification of the exposition family. 13.4K why-questions and two human studies: GPT-4 explanations match their intended educational background only 50% of the time against 79% for lay human-curated ones, and explanations generated across model families for different informational needs remain indistinguishable in grade level. Prompting the audience does not fix altitude lock.

sources.title: Know Your Audience: do LLMs adapt to different age and education levels? (arXiv:2312.02065)
sources.note: Corroborates the same finding independently: current LLMs have set readability ranges and do not adapt well to different audiences even when prompted.

sources.title: The Curse of Knowledge: Pinker Describes a Key Cause of Bad Writing - APS
sources.note: The human mechanism the context-leakage family is the machine analogue of: 'It simply doesn't occur to the writer that readers haven't learned their jargon, don't seem to know the intermediate steps that seem to them to be too obvious to mention.' Underlying literature: Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber 1989; Nickerson 1999.

sources.title: Featherstone, AI UI accessibility: operability under browser-driven testing
sources.note: The evidence behind the declared-but-not-wired signature, and the best numbers in the whole catalog: ~3,000 browser-driven trials across a six-model panel. Escape handlers present in 79% of generated modals and working in 59%; 1,031 of 1,032 failures threw NO console error; focus fully held in 12% of bare prompts. Also the counterintuitive finding that asking for accessibility can reduce basic function.

sources.title: Featherstone, AI UI accessibility: the markup baseline
sources.note: 720 trials. 673 generated modals hand-rolled role=dialog on a div; about 2% used native <dialog>, essentially all from one model family. Native dialogs closed on Escape 98% of the time against 31% for hand-rolled ones.

sources.title: A11yN and the systematic review of LLM-generated accessibility
sources.note: LLMs replicate accessibility flaws from their training data rather than inventing new ones, which is why the fix is changing what they reach for (native elements, maintained primitives) rather than prompting harder.
